on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. the eyes of the world have been on yemen recently, after al qaeda claimed responsibility for the, thankfully, failed christmas attempt to blow up an american airliner. but we've known for a long time that the ever-decreasing security in this country allows terrorist groups to find sanctuary where they can plan and organize their next operation. terrorism in this region had been spreading for many years before the memorable 9/11, just as al qaeda's attack on the american ship uss cole on october 12, 2000. yemen is a very important country, primarily because of its geographical location. we must be aware that the 26.5 kilometers of the bab al-mandab strait between yemen and djibouti transport almost 3.5 million barrels of oil a day, or 4% of the world's production. at the same time, it is a country with a very complicated internal situation. in addition to the growing power of al-qaeda, there is a serious shia rebellion in the north of the country in sada province and an outbreak of violence by secessionist movements in the south. if we add to this the negative effects of the global food crisis two years ago, the recent financial crisis, the depletion of oil supplies that generate three quarters of the country's income, and finally the increasingly severe water shortage, we have a picture of a failed country, ideal for al qaeda, which is looking for a new base in the face of the troubles in afghanistan. therefore, apart from military action, which, given the inaction and incompetence of local authorities, seems inevitable in one form or another, the international community, including the european union (and here the appeal to the commissioner), must above all be very active in the process of rebuilding state institutions.

on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i too will give an example, as did mrs hautala: a young polish man was sentenced to life imprisonment in the uk for rape in a trial that was conducted under intense press pressure and which, according to some observers, did not meet at least polish fair trial standards. he is currently serving a life sentence in poland, although polish law does not provide for life imprisonment for rape, only for murder (for rape, a maximum of 12 years). so we are dealing with a situation where a man is in a polish prison for a punishment that is not in accordance with the principles of polish law. i give this example as an illustration of the problem and an argument for the urgent need to define some general standards both in terms of criminal procedure and, in my view, also in terms of the rules for the enforcement of the sentence. because we are increasingly seeing a situation where criminals are tried in some countries and punished in others. that is why i support the idea of standards and the idea of a directive.

sense of responsibility on the part of the states, but also by giving the community institutions, in particular the commission, new powers of direction and of achieving objectives. in the last ten energy dependence reduced and we will encourage the development of renewable energies, which by their very nature require versatility in energy distribution. ladies and gentlemen, europe will not win in writing. − the strategy for the trans-danube region that we have developed and voted on today makes it possible to promote regional and crossborder cooperation. the danube river currently connects ten european countries germany, austria, slovakia, hungary, croatia, serbia, bulgaria, romania, moldova and ukraine most of which are member states and eu aspirant countries. the trans-danube region is therefore an important link between the various eu cohesion policy programmes and those for candidate countries and those covered by the european neighbourhood policy. what we have adopted today is a scheme to support the danube basin strategy, but whether the programme will remain on paper or whether this model will be filled with content depends on whether there are additional measures that will not compromise or reduce the pool of funds allocated to cohesion policy in individual countries. i hope that a coherent strategy for the danube region will contribute to increased prosperity, sustainable and sustainable development, generate new jobs and security in the region.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the european strategy for the danube region. territorial cohesion is one of the european union's priorities enshrined in the lisbon treaty. the actions of the strategy for the trans-danube region cover a number of areas of support, such as social policy, culture and education, environmental protection, infrastructure and sustainable economic development. the very fact that the strategy and its solutions have had a major impact on these areas is evidence that regional strategies should be developed and implemented. the trans-dunisian region needs a strategy, it needs our support and our action, because it affects many european countries. six of them are eu member states, and the others are potential candidates. the impact of the region is also important for other countries that are not directly linked to it. the idea of creating functional regions macro-regions was initiated by the baltic sea strategy. the danube strategy, like other planned eu macro-regional strategies, aims primarily at strengthening integration through cooperation at regional and local levels. it is vital that governments, local authorities, ngos and citizens work together with the european union, which they are building with us, to develop and implement the agreed solutions.
in writing. − any community initiative which aims to coordinate and strengthen regional initiatives and contributes to deepening economic cooperation, improving transport infrastructure and protecting the environment deserves support. the strategy for the danube region confirms the growing importance of the macro-regional approach to european union regional policy. the document voted today will strengthen the links between the old, new and possible future eu members on the one hand and central europe and the black sea region on the other. i believe that in the near future, the odra corridor concept will be given similar recognition. it would connect the baltic sea to the adriatic sea, running from sweden through poland, the czech republic, slovakia, hungary, all the way to croatia.

day-to-day reality. it must help us to fashion a new culture of partnership and purpose, to use our common leverage to offer a real advance for the european project. also several of these issues imply cooperation with the council. so i would very much welcome a broader agreement which unites the co-legislators, together with the commission, on a set of principles for interinstitutional cooperation. our institutions and help us achieve our goals, in full respect of our values. because let us never forget that our union is founded on values: respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights. today, a new chapter in our european adventure opens. let us work together to make it a real success for all our citizens. mr president, i want to refer to the framework agreement and a special partnership between the commission and parliament, which you addressed and we obviously welcome. parliament is fighting for its competence not for the sake of this house’s pride and glory. we want to fill the gap of democratic legitimacy after all the pain we witnessed when the referenda were held. we are entering a new era of community method so please do not defend the competences of the commission as we, parliament, were not part of this community method. i am referring here to the legislative monopoly of the commission. this monopoly existed when the european parliament was not what it is today, so i welcome the half-way solution which takes into account our initiatives in legislative matters, and which you have accepted. this house will be looking very closely at the practice of this half-way solution, taking into account our request to the commission to take legislative action. my second point is about the common external action service. it should draw its credibility from two sources – not only the council but also the european parliament – and so far we are not fully satisfied. i am looking at your vice-president, lady ashton. we deplore the fact that we are absent from the high level group. we think we should be involved in the process which was always requested by this house. we should be involved in the nominations of ambassadors and eusrs. perhaps there is still some room for left for manoeuvre because it is not for our glory but to give this service real credibility in the eyes of europeans. otherwise it will be weaker, whereas both sides want it to be stronger.
mr. chairman, please! the european union is in a completely new situation. the treaty of lisbon makes important changes. what can we say after two months of operation? well, actually, if you think about it, that's a good and important start. it is only now that these statutes and resolutions are to be put into effect. the allocation of competences between the institutions or newly created important high-level posts should be made accordingly and the political principles and rules for cooperation should be established. it is also a question of maintaining the principle of effective equality between member states, but also between member states and the union. it is important not to diminish the importance of the presidency of the individual member states. only a cohesive union that speaks with one voice will have its rightful place in the world. the first experience of the last two months raises various doubts. we must therefore think these problems through and take action to achieve the desired results and a new quality in the functioning of the european union.
president of the commission. − mr president, i will try to start by answering some concrete questions and will then address the more general ones. firstly, on the euro area, some members of this parliament raised issues relating to the euro area and some current problems we are facing in euro-area member states. first of all, let me recall that the euro is one of the major successes in europe’s history. since its creation with 11 participants, the euro area has grown to comprise 16 member states. the euro area has been an area of stability and job creation. of course it was affected by the crisis. non-euro-area countries were also affected by the crisis. i do not need to remind you that, just a few days ago, i received the prime minister of iceland, a country very close to us – and a non-euro-area member – which was indeed facing this crisis. i want to repeat that this crisis was not created in the euro area; it came from outside the euro area. but the truth is that the euro did protect the countries which share the single currency. i believe that the european situation would be much more difficult today if we did not have the euro. we have yet to reap the full benefits of the euro. to do so, we need to reinforce economic coordination in the euro area. it is true that we do not have just a monetary union. we should have a real economic union. the treaty gives new opportunities, which i intend to make use of. olli rehn, the new commissioner for these matters – if we get your support – will develop this line. looking ahead at how to reinforce the euro area is very important, but of course it does not prevent us from looking at the present. the period the euro area is going through is a difficult one. there is no point in denying it. other countries outside the euro area are also facing very difficult times. let us also recognise that. however, i must say that the situation in the financial markets is sometimes reported in a way that amplifies the problems, and does not always give an objective assessment of the situation. such analyses usually come from non-euro-area countries. but the euro area has the capacity to deal with the difficulties currently affecting it. we have our system of fiscal rules, the stability and growth pact, which must be properly implemented. in the case of greece, we have the capacity to assess and monitor its fiscal adjustment programme. we have the possibility of recommending bold structural reforms in greece which will also be closely monitored by the commission. on 3 february the commission adopted a package on greece which will go to the council early next week. naturally the solution requires, above all, action from the greek side. support for the determination of the greek authorities will increase confidence in the successful achievement of the ambitious programme they have adopted. member states, particularly those in the euro area, should always have in mind that the economic policies of each of them have an impact on the economies of others. i welcome clear indications that all member states are aware of the challenge and will act accordingly. there was a concrete question asked about consumer policy, i think by mrs gebhardt. there is a person with clear responsibility for consumer policy in the commission, namely commissioner dalli. he will be in charge of this policy, propose initiatives in this area and discuss them with you in the imco committee and in plenary. specific civil-law dimensions will be under the responsibility of the commissioner for justice, vice-president reding. this is normal in most executives around europe, where those specific issues are dealt with by the minister of justice. of course all decisions on new initiatives will have to be approved by the college. i am extremely committed to collegiality. in fact many of you have urged the commission to keep a strong accent on collegiality. under the treaties, the president of the commission is the guarantor of collegiality. in today’s policies this is a normal tendency. more and more issues are transversal or horizontal by nature. they need a common purpose and they require the integration of different sectoral policies. what happens in the commission is more or less the same as what is happening in national governance and in global governance. we see now that, very often, heads of state and government need to address, in a coordinated and coherent way, matters that were previously dealt with separately by those responsible in the different governments. so this is exactly what we intend to do. i want to underline this point with special pride because we are now building this new commission on the experience of the previous one. the previous one was the first commission of this enlarged europe – the first time we had a commission with 27 members from 27 different countries. the fact that that commission worked in a truly collegiate spirit with a sense of purpose is indeed a demonstration that the enlarged european union can work with 27 or more members. i think this is also critically important for the future. there were some concrete questions about cohesion policy and some community policies like fisheries and agriculture – for example, the question by mr capoulas santos. the cohesion policy has been enshrined in the treaty of lisbon. by its nature it is a european policy. we need to see how we can continue the process of reform so that we can continue to improve the policy’s value for money, and ensure that cohesion policy and regional policy are translated into a real increase in the competitiveness of all the regions of europe. we need to be sure that the policy can achieve that so that we can have a strong case in the next financing debate. let me assure you of my full commitment – and, i think i can say, the full commitment of the new commission – to the principles of social, economic and territorial cohesion that are also enshrined in the lisbon treaty. of course we will do everything we can to promote the common policies of europe. there were some concrete questions about social impact assessment – mr cercas’s question. i want to make clear what i have said publicly before. we are committed to introducing this social impact assessment in our work through the impact assessment board. we believe we have made a lot of progress on impact assessment. we are always ready to improve that work and we believe the social dimension should be properly addressed in our work. some members of this parliament put questions to me regarding energy security. i want to underline that we are going to include energy security in our proposal for the european union 2020 strategy. one of the innovations of the european union 2020 strategy is precisely to bring together some policies that were previously treated separately. i believe that promoting energy security and energy efficiency should be an important part of our agenda for competitiveness and for greener, sustainable and resource-efficient growth in europe. this underlines how important we believe this agenda is. some of you asked me about smes and the value of the internal market – mr hökmark and others. it is very important to relaunch the internal market now. it is important to make clear that the internal market is not just about a market, even if markets are important. some people believe that we defend markets because we are market fundamentalists. nothing could be further from the truth. we believe the internal market is, above all, the basis for the european project. without an internal market we will not have a strong european union. if you allow the internal market to be fragmented, we will see the ugly face of economic nationalism again in europe. we have to speak courageously and say that the internal market exists to defend the weakest – the consumers, to defend small and medium-sized companies against monopolies, and of course to defend the european project as a whole. that is why i asked mr monti to produce a report so that we can bring some new ideas and also create a larger consensus to relaunch and deepen the internal market as one of the great past and future achievements of our european project. j'aimerais maintenant évoquer quelques questions plus générales que certains d'entre vous ont abordées. joseph daul, martin schulz , alain lamassoure – qui a fait une intervention où il a bien insisté sur la question de l'audace –, juan fernando lópez aguilar, jaime mayor oneja et beaucoup d'autres ont soulevé la question de l'ambition. c'est, à mon avis, un point extrêmement important et nous devons avoir effectivement un débat honnête entre nous sur ce point. certains d'entre vous, notamment martin schulz, m'ont interrogé encore une fois sur la question du marché et du social. je tiens à vous le répéter: ce n'est pas la commission que vous devez convaincre du besoin d'avoir une vocation sociale. c'est avec nous que vous devez essayer de convaincre quelques capitales, parce que la vérité est très claire: certaines capitales pensent que l'europe, c'est le marché, et que, d'après le principe de subsidiarité, le social, c'est eux. je ne suis pas d'accord. je trouve que pour obtenir également une adhésion émotionnelle à l'europe, il nous faut une dimension sociale. il faut une dimension sociale qui combine effectivement ce qu'on peut faire au niveau communautaire avec ce que l'on peut faire au niveau national. personne ne veut créer de système de sécurité sociale européen, de système de santé centralisé en europe. ce n'est pas ce que nous proposons. d'ailleurs, il ne faut pas voir ça en termes de concurrence entre le niveau national et le niveau européen. mais si, en complément de ce que nous faisons sur le plan du marché intérieur, de la concurrence, de la politique des aides d'état, d'autres politiques comme la politique commerciale extérieure, il n'y a pas une dimension sociale de l'europe, nous aurons un problème de légitimité du projet européen. j'insiste donc. ce n'est pas nous qu'il faut convaincre du besoin d'une dimension sociale. travaillez avec nous pour renforcer la dimension sociale de l'europe, l'économie sociale de marché, qui est d'ailleurs inscrite comme objectif dans le traité de lisbonne. j'y tiens beaucoup et on doit lutter pour elle ensemble. cela ne fait aucun doute. (applaudissements) en ce qui concerne la question de la gouvernance – un problème qui est cher à m. verhofstadt et aussi à moi-même –, encore une fois, aidez-nous, appuyez-nous. je suis pour une gouvernance renforcée de l'europe et l'europe a besoin de cette gouvernance renforcée. mon discours – vous direz un discours, c'est un discours, mais c'est quand même un discours que je fais au nom du nouveau collège et qui traduit une ambition, une ligne politique – est clair. nous ne sommes pas en train de vivre des moments comme les autres. je l'ai dit: à l'intérieur de l'europe comme à l'extérieur, on a besoin de plus de détermination sur le plan européen. je suis absolument convaincu, intellectuellement, politiquement, que si l'europe n'agit plus de façon concertée, nous risquons informel, après-demain, car j'en suis convaincu. je pense que les développements récents n'ont fait que souligner cette situation avec plus d'acuité. la crise financière internationale a montré à quel point nos économies sont interdépendantes. les problèmes que connaît maintenant la zone euro montrent aussi combien nos économies sont interdépendantes. nous devons donc jouer un rôle accru en termes de coordination et de gouvernance européenne. il ne faut pas nécessairement donner à bruxelles des compétences nationales: c'est un débat du xxe siècle qui, je crois, est dépassé. c'est une erreur de poser ce débat en termes de "c'est pour bruxelles, c'est pour la commission, c'est contre les états membres...", car ce débat est ridicule. il est évident qu'aujourd'hui, si nous voulons compter dans le monde, nos états membres seuls n'ont pas l'influence nécessaire pour discuter d'égal à égal avec les états-unis, la russie ou la chine. nous avons besoin de cette dimension, non pas pour renforcer bruxelles, mais pour renforcer l'europe et surtout pour répondre aux intérêts concrets de chacun et de chacune de nos concitoyennes et concitoyens. c'est là qu'il faut travailler ensemble, et là aussi, je vous dis: appuyez-nous. nous avons besoin de votre soutien, non pas dans une logique de guerre entre les institutions – plus que jamais, nous avons besoin du partenariat institutionnel –, mais pour défendre l'intérêt de l'europe dans le monde. enfin, en termes de relations extérieures, là aussi, soyons absolument clairs. dans quel domaine l'europe compte-t-elle dans le monde? l'europe compte dans le monde là où elle a, effectivement, une position coordonnée. elle est respectée sur le plan commercial, cela je peux vous le garantir. nos lois de concurrence sont respectées par tous les grands conglomérats internationaux. nous avons une politique commune. nous avons des institutions. nous avons la base pour agir. mais attention! nous sommes à un moment, notamment en termes de sécurité internationale, où l'europe n'a pas aujourd'hui les instruments géopolitiques et de défense que d'autres ont. je vois très bien que, quand je parle avec quelques-uns de nos partenaires globaux, ils pensent surtout en termes de sécurité. ils pensent en termes d'équilibre stratégique. et là, il faut le dire clairement, l'europe ne peut pas être naïve. le problème de copenhague n'était pas un manque d'ambition de l'europe, comme certains le disent. au contraire, nous étions de loin les plus ambitieux. pour moi, ce que copenhague a montré, c'est que nous devions articuler un intérêt européen dans les différents domaines et le défendre de façon cohérente et stratégique, avec tous nos partenaires. il ne faut donc pas simplement mener une politique généreuse, qui est importante, mais il faut que nous ayons aussi la force de défendre notre générosité et la conviction de défendre nos intérêts. c'est cela que j'ai l'intention de faire, et j'espère aussi votre soutien en ce sens. in writing. − the new framework agreement between the european parliament and the commission contains several important elements. first, the principle of equal treatment between parliament and the council, which strengthens the democratic legitimacy of the european union. secondly, it gives parliament additional powers to scrutinise the commission's legislative initiatives, giving parliament greater influence over the law that is being made. the agreement includes a provision for the mandatory publication of the correlation table (as i mentioned in my report on the internal market scoreboard) and binding deadlines for the implementation of directives, which should not exceed two years. this will give a chance to complete the project of creating a common market faster. the agreement also strengthens the community approach and improves the functioning of the two institutions. it also obliges them to operate in a way that ensures that the european union is a genuine community.

in writing. − we have a new commission, which has taken up its mandate at a difficult time, but which is made up of professionals who have the responsibilities of all 27 member states. we have the treaty of lisbon which changes the configuration of power and requires flexibility on the part of the commission. the european union is therefore in a new and sensitive context, but one which requires performance, stability and dynamism in proposing and implementing coherent policies. we are facing a new financial perspective, and this implies a responsible response from the commission, through reform and new adjustments in all areas, starting with the economic one. all member states are feeling the impact of the financial crisis. the alarm sounded by greece is being heard loud and clear, from states with robust economic systems to those struggling for every step in reducing their budget deficits. a stable and coordinated economic policy at the level of the 27 countries is the chance to avoid a major imbalance at eu level and, in the second stage, to produce beneficial effects. the ec's actions are designed to reflect responses to crisis-related problems and to build, in order to restore stability in the member states, in other words to close the deficit, prevent discrepancies and, at the same time, consolidate.
the situation in some euro area countries calls for serious reflection. the economic crisis is only partly justified. many of the reasons lie elsewhere. first, the large variation in the level of economic development in the individual euro area countries has not been taken into account. secondly, the rigorousness of the stabilisation and growth pact was not respected. budgetary discipline was not adequately maintained, leading to a large increase in the government deficit. third, there was a lack of proper supervision of banks and other financial institutions - and not just in these countries. what can we do about it? the corrective programme drawn up by each country must receive, in accordance with the principle of solidarity, the support of the european union, which entitles the european commission and the european central bank to supervise its implementation. it is also unacceptable that the poorest should bear the brunt of the crisis, as was the case with the greek farmers' protests.

member of the commission. − mr president, the proposal we are debating today is a tangible sign of the commitment of all eu institutions to promote integration of extremely marginalised and deprived communities into mainstream society. the proposal meets the request of parliament and of the council and confirms that the structural funds have a role to play, not only by contributing financially but also by promoting an integrated approach to tackling social and economic conditions of marginalised communities. the proposal specifically targets the roma population, which in europe accounts for 10 million people. however, in accordance with the common basic principles on roma inclusion, the proposal does not exclude other marginalised groups sharing similar social economic circumstances. the current compromise proposal extends housing interventions for marginalised communities to all 27 member states and not only to the eu-12 as the commission initially proposed. the existing article 7 applies only to housing interventions in urban areas, while the amendment proposes that housing interventions also be allowed in rural areas. this extension is justified since the majority of the roma population in the eu-12 is settled in rural and not in urban areas. under the proposed amendment, both the renovation of existing housing and the construction of new houses are eligible. in fact renovation of houses of extremely poor quality might result in a waste of public resources. during the discussion of the proposal, the committee on regional development asked for a specific reference to desegregation measures. recital 6 of the proposal now includes such desegregation measures as examples of actions which should go along with housing interventions. indeed, segregated settlements imply insecurity, no easy access to education or employment as well as exposure to violent attacks and criminality. the creation of new marginalised areas, although with decent and erdf-supported houses, is definitively not our objective. we know that many member states have put in place integration policies of the roma communities with particular focus on housing. the implementation of these policies is not an easy task. the structural funds can participate in this effort supporting not only housing but more importantly actions improving the productive capacities of these communities, such as support for smes, women, entrepreneurship initiatives etc. in this respect i would like to stress that the main objective of the cohesion policy is to make the regional economies converge by fostering the productive capacities. as you are certainly aware, the new regulation will be accompanied by a declaration from the commission – and indeed most member states – stating that the eligibility of housing interventions in favour of marginalised communities throughout the european union under the erdf is of an exceptional nature. this exception should in no way be regarded as a general opening of cohesion policy to financing housing interventions. i would like now to refer to the proposal by the committee on regional development to insert a specific recital on comitology into the text. in this context i would like to remind you that a horizontal solution of transitional provisions relating to comitology has in principle been found between the three institutions. the aim of the declaration of the european parliament, the council and the commission concerning the implementation of article 291 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union is to avoid raising institutional discussions on each individual file during the interim period pending the entry into force of a new comitology framework regulation. the commission therefore regrets the introduction of the recital, but will not block – for this reason – the agreement in first reading between the co-legislators. i am looking forward to the debate.

acting president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by making a clear statement: spain has clearly and unequivocally supported the treaty of lisbon. from the very beginning. and he did so in the conviction that the implementation of this new treaty would mean, among many other things, bringing the european institutions closer to our fellow citizens. it is an objective which the treaty entrusts to a large extent to this parliament. the most important aspect of this treaty, its participation in matters such as the area of freedom, justice and security, is the way in which it aims to bring citizens and institutions closer together. the spanish presidency therefore begins this speech by assuring the honourable members of the commitment to joint work, to loyal collaboration between the council and this parliament, as a result of our firm commitment to the lisbon treaty and its objectives. the council also shares with this house its concern to ensure the security of all european citizens; security as a guarantee for the full exercise of freedom. this is the context in which our common fight against terrorism, against terrorism of all kinds, takes place. as stated in the resolution adopted on 17 september, 'the european parliament reiterates its determination to fight terrorism and its firm conviction that a proper balance must be struck between security measures and the protection of public freedoms and fundamental rights'. i couldn't agree more with that statement. this is the framework in which i would like this debate to take place, a new framework - the treaty framework - of open interinstitutional cooperation, and a shared concern, which is no longer new: that of fighting terrorism in accordance with the principles of proportionality and necessity, which are at the same time the guarantee of full effectiveness in this fight. it is commonly accepted, mr president, that international terrorism has posed new challenges to our societies. it is a relatively new form of terrorism, of diffuse organization, of extreme lethality and operating on a global scale. its eradication is therefore also being considered on a global scale. the lack of rigid structures, of hierarchical structures, can only be combated by an extraordinary effort of information. its lethality has led us to extreme surveillance in places of high public affluence. prevention, coordination and information are the three words that sum up our strategy to deal with this enormous threat. all the countries have therefore made efforts to coordinate themselves better, internally and externally, to be better and better informed, to cooperate, finally, with those who are facing the same struggle with us. the european union too: there has been a proliferation of joint research bodies and teams, exchanges of information and shared analyses. this is the context in which the agreement between the european union and the united states on the transfer of financial data which we are discussing today is situated. the exchange of data without an agreement has been operating for years without interruption. in my appearance in the libe committee two weeks ago, several members asked me about the results of this exchange of data. it was a pertinent question that appears to be addressed and answered in the second report of judge bruguière, which has been sent to this chamber and which i also quote verbatim: 'during 2009, the tftp has been a highly valuable instrument to assist in the preparation of terrorist maps, to complete missing elements in investigations, to confirm the identity of suspects, to locate their geographical location, to identify new suspects and to thwart, in short, attempts at terrorist attacks'. and i add, not just in 2009, but also before, in the united states, in europe and around the world: in barcelona in january 2008, in germany in the summer of 2007, in london after the 7 july attacks and in the investigations into the 11 march 2004 attacks in madrid, the bangkok murder in april 2005, or the 2002 bali bombings. these are some of the examples the judge cites in his report. the exchange of data has therefore produced good results. the exchange has allowed for the investigation of bombings. it's prevented a bombing. it has made it possible to arrest terrorists after they have committed attacks and, above all, before they can commit them. although swift had previously indicated in 2007 that it would change its databases, the decision was not taken until a few months ago. this necessitated a review of the protocols which, up to that date, had allowed the operation of financial data exchanges. it had to be done in a very short time. the mandate was adopted by the council in the summer of 2009, and had to be done at a time of uncertainty about the entry into force of the lisbon treaty. the decision that was taken is well known. a provisional, interim agreement was signed for nine months, which must be ratified in this house: a temporary agreement for nine months, during which time this house, the council and the commission should establish a new negotiating process to agree on a final treaty. that was the decision. it may not have been the best. but it should be made clear in this house that the agreement signed ad referendum, the agreement we are discussing today, is, as far as the defence of privacy is concerned, much better than the protocols in force up to the time before the agreement. that is because that interim agreement incorporated additional guarantees, among other things, recommended by this house and recalled by its rapporteur in the report we have just seen today. at this point i would like to say that the spanish presidency of the council has taken full account of the resolutions adopted in this house and the letters sent by the president of this parliament, as well as the report drawn up by mrs hennis-plasschaert, which was voted on in the libe committee on 4 february. that is why it adopted a declaration in the council and sent it to this house yesterday, the main points of which i would like to summarize here today. first, the council commits itself to fully incorporating in a final agreement the strong safeguards reinforcing effective protection, data suppression and greater concreteness with regard to the exchange of information obtained by the tftp with national authorities and with third countries. and it is, of course, committed to reinforcing the safeguards already contained in the current agreement and which should continue to appear 'reinforced', i insist, in the final agreement, as a strict limitation of the purpose of the use of data and an absolute ban on the extraction of data and the use of profiles. finally, in response to the new context created by the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the council undertook to negotiate an interinstitutional agreement to allow more rapid access to classified documents in international agreements. in this matter - and i want to state this very strongly in this house - the spanish presidency expresses its full commitment to the lisbon treaty and to the charter of fundamental rights, in particular article 8, and also takes on board the legitimate concerns expressed by this house. today we know that the compromise i have just formulated is possible. in the letter to the president of parliament from the us secretaries of state, hillary clinton, and of the treasury, timothy geithner, the us government has expressed its commitment to incorporate appropriate safeguards in accordance with the position expressed in this parliament. it is possible, ladies and gentlemen, that in the process of approving the agreement we are discussing today, the council did not do things quite right. but what is certain is that in this process the council has learned and that in this act the council takes note of parliament's concerns. as it is, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement we are discussing today has contributed - and i hope will continue to do so - to improving the security of our citizens all over the world and also in europe.

member of the commission. − mr president, let me start by thanking everyone for yesterday giving us and me your trust and confidence by voting ‘yes’ for the new commission. it is an interesting first day at work and i am grateful to share with you the important issue of sharing information with the us for the purpose of combating terrorism, this time in relation to the terrorist finance tracking program (tftp). the european parliament has, of course, shown great interest in this matter. this is quite right, since the tftp confronts us again with the challenge of reconciling data-sharing with data protection and, if we take up this challenge, this helps us to give citizens security, privacy and data protection. one of the aims of the interim agreement has been to ensure implementation of the conditions in the european parliament resolution of september 2009. we firmly intend to strengthen further the data protection part when negotiating the long-term agreement, particularly concerning the right to receive information about whether one’s rights have been respected under the agreement, and stronger guarantees about effective redress, lawful data processing and the deletion of data. the second bruguière report was made available to meps on monday last week, and it demonstrates the significance and the value of tftp in the investigation and disruption of terrorism, including in the european union. the report confirms that tftp has been used to identify and arrest individuals who have subsequently been convicted of terrorism within our member states. the report also highlights that tftp is a valuable source of reliable information necessary in the fight against terrorism. there are specific examples and the council referred to a few of them. we know that the threat of terrorism in some of our member states remains as high as ever, and i am sure that you can see that rejection of the interim agreement by this house would represent a serious blow to eu security. some of our member states have made it very clear that they want the tftp to continue because they have benefited from it in the past and will continue to do so. they have told us that the reliable information that the tftp provides on known and suspected terrorism is an important source of legitimate intelligence needed to address the complex threat, notably from al-qa’ida inspired terrorism. the interim agreement is not only a favour to the us; it is in our common interest. much has been said about the level of protection of data in the interim agreement and this is, of course, a key concern. i encourage members – and i am sure most of you have already done so – to look closely at the interim agreement. you will see that it contains significant and detailed legally binding commitments on the way that the us treasury department can process data under the agreement. they include, for example, a strict limitation on the purpose of processing, which is limited to the investigation, detection and prosecution of terrorism. it includes an absolute prohibition on data mining – searches of the database can only be undertaken where it is possible to show a reason to believe that the subject of the search is engaged in terrorism. that means that the data held on the tftp database are effectively anonymous. only if there is a reason to believe that one identified person is a terrorist can the data of that person be seen and extracted from the database. this is important. the interim agreement obliges the treasury department to delete data within five years of receipt – a period which is in keeping with the retention period in eu legislation on terrorist financing. the agreement also provides for a detailed eu review in which some of our own data protection authorities will participate to ensure that these and many other data protection obligations are complied with. the agreement does not involve the transfer of virtually all swift data to the us treasury department. i can assure you that only a fraction of swift data will be transferred under the interim agreement. it does not in any way affect the powers of data protection authorities with regard to processing activities performed in the eu by swift or financial institutions. refusal of consent will bring to an end the interim agreement, including the significant data protection safeguard it contains. if the us is able to access data by other means – for example through bilateral relations with the netherlands – those safeguards will no longer apply. if the interim agreement falls, it is likely to take considerable time before any alternative can be put in place. so refusal of consent risks leading to both a data protection gap and a security gap. finally, the interim agreement is only an interim agreement. it might not be the best agreement in the world. it can – and it will – be improved. the commission is now finalising the draft mandate and the guidelines for the long-term agreement and we will adopt them swiftly. i give a personal commitment to you to ensure that the european parliament’s concern will be addressed and that we shall seek a strong protection of privacy and data protection in the new agreement. the european parliament will be fully informed at all stages of this procedure. i hope that this answers a few of your questions.

acting president of the council. - mr president, the first thing i would like to say is that i have listened to all the honourable members with interest and i am grateful for all the speeches, those of support, which were the fewest, and those of criticism, which were the most, which i also thank. i should like to begin by saying that what i am most grateful for is that i have seen, once again, in this debate in this house, that there is perfect harmony between parliament, the commission and the council in defending our values and in facing with determination terrorism - as i said in my speech - terrorism of all kinds. i think that's a first consensus that should be clear. as regards the agreement we have discussed this afternoon, the agreement on swift, i would like to draw a distinction between the criticisms, which have been of two radically different types: criticisms of the form and criticisms of the substance. it is true that criticism of the form has been constant, even among those members who have explicitly supported the existence of an agreement such as the one we are discussing this afternoon. i have already said in my speech, and i say again, that things could probably have been done better, that they certainly could have been done better. but i have also said, and i repeat once again, that the deadlines - and the honourable members are well aware of them - were what they were and that the council and the commission had to act in a very short space of time. in any case, i want to make it very clear that the council's will, as i have expressed it here this afternoon, is that things should no longer be done this way, that things should be done differently. there have been some members who have said - probably on the basis of their experience - that this is a promise, a commitment, which has been made repeatedly in this house and then, repeatedly, has been broken. i would like to say that the council's commitment is based on a fundamental commitment to the treaty of lisbon, and that the treaty of lisbon sets as a fundamental objective that this house should play an increasingly important role in the institutional life of europe so that citizens feel better represented. and it is this commitment of my country, which is a fundamental commitment to the treaty of lisbon, which leads me to state here, emphatically, that the council, during the spanish presidency, will do things differently. if anyone does not take the council's word for it - that is their right - it should be remembered that the treaty requires that things be done differently. so if the political will of the council is not enough, there is the treaty, which is a law, to ensure that things will be done differently in the future, with this house, working with the commission and, of course, with the spirit that all the members have defended here, which is a spirit that seeks a balance between defending security and maintaining our values and it is a fully european spirit with which the council also fully agrees. i would like to make three comments on the substance of the matter. i shall not go into some of the more specific aspects which have been criticised - it is true that some of these aspects have been criticised which i consider to be ill-founded. for example, it has been said on several occasions that the swift agreement, as it stands at the moment in this house, allows for the transfer of raw data and it has not been said, and it should be made clear, that this is not the logic of the agreement, that such a raw transfer is only allowed under the swift agreement exceptionally and as long as there are justified suspicions (article 4 (6) of the agreement). i'm just giving you an example. there have been a number of other allegations which i believe are the result of a somewhat superficial analysis of the content of the agreement, but which i shall not answer at this stage. i would like to say two more things about the substance of the matter. first of all, i would like to stress - as the commissioner has done and as some of the honourable members in this house have done - that the agreement has been useful in the fight against terrorism. i have given some examples. there are more examples in the report by mr bruguière than are available to members. i can even give an example of what i have just said, from my own country, or rather two. it is true that the swift agreement was used to investigate the 11 march attacks in madrid, with good results. and it is no less true, too, that the swift agreement was used to prevent an attack in the city of barcelona just over a year ago. today, those who tried are all condemned in spanish prisons. so it has worked, it has allowed us to get results. and if so, you will agree with me that if the agreement were to be suspended, european citizens would indeed be at least a little less safe. if the agreement works and has worked and is interrupted, you will admit with me that the interruption would leave us a little less secure. i use this formula deliberately so that no one can accuse the council of being dramatic. we'd be a little less safe. it's like this. that is why i am very much insisting from the council - and i think the commission also agrees that it is essential - that this agreement is not interrupted, as i insist on recalling, once again, that this agreement may be open to criticism and i have heard the harsh criticism here this afternoon. but you will also agree with me that this agreement is much better than the protocol which has for years facilitated the exchange of data between the united states and the european union. the agreement we are discussing here today is probably not the best. it is certainly improvable, and i can even agree with some of the criticisms that have been made from these seats, but you must agree with me that it is better than what was before. the european union, the council and the commission have introduced some mechanisms into the agreement which are of concern to meps - and rightly so - and which are mainly concerned with ensuring that security does not come at the expense of freedom and fundamental rights. that is why i would stress the importance, as the commissioner said, of not interrupting the agreement. and i reiterate to parliament once again the council's willingness to negotiate a new agreement - this definitive agreement - in which many of the things we have heard here this afternoon can be incorporated and with which the council wants to publicly confirm that it agrees. that is the council's commitment. it is true that this commitment has also been expressed in a letter from the president of the council to the president of parliament, but it will have to be made more concrete in any case when the negotiations begin. we are therefore discussing today an interim, transitional agreement which improves the present situation. we are discussing an agreement which will last nine months, which are the months that the commission, the council and parliament will spend in reaching a new agreement - in writing. the threat of terrorism is not diminishing. the recent suicide bombing of a plane from europe to the united states showed that there are people who are willing to kill hundreds of innocent people in the name of their fanatical beliefs. however, it would be a mistake to view acts of terrorism as the mere acts of desperate individuals. for every terrorist is backed by an organization that has trained him, provided him with explosives, and financed him. terrorism needs to be well organized to survive, and to do so, it needs money first. we must not stop our efforts to track the financial flows and determine where the funds to support terrorism come from. the efficient exchange of information between governments, mutual assistance in identifying suspected individuals and organisations is of the utmost importance to ensure the safety of the citizens of our countries. efforts shall be made to ensure that the necessary protection of personal data is ensured in the final agreement. but we must not forget that our primary objective should be to reduce terrorism, which remains a real threat also in europe. when security is at stake, political games should take a backseat. the european parliament should not demonstrate its position by rejecting the interim agreement with the us on the transfer of financial communications data which contributes to the security of our continent.
mr. chairman, please! in light of today's debate, the use of scanners at airports still leaves many questions. the safety of travellers is of course paramount, but the proportionality of the protection measures used must not be forgotten. the use of such devices still leaves a number of questions unanswered. what effect do scanners have on the health of the passengers being scanned? how will the image protection of the scanned persons be guaranteed? is it not better to seal off an existing system than to spend billions of dollars on devices that are known to be incapable of detecting charges placed inside the human body? until we know the answers to these questions, we should oppose the mandatory introduction of scanners at european airports. and finally, one last note: i feel like we've found a solution, and now we're looking for a problem. if scanners are the answer, they certainly do not solve the problem of airport security.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen, listening to today's debate, one gets the impression that the main problem facing european countries today is whether to make body scanners more common at airports or to limit the possibility of introducing them. i don't think that's the right way to put it, though. nor is the issue of guaranteeing the protection of human rights so important in this respect. the fundamental question we should ask ourselves is whether the new measures and instruments proposed by the special services will be effectively used. do we really guarantee our freedom by sacrificing some of it for security? the information that we're receiving is very sceptical. if the relevant services are not even able to guarantee effective passport controls; if they cannot use the information they have (as the incident with the flight to detroit clearly showed), what guarantee do we have that they will be able to use the new instruments effectively? history teaches us that in times of crisis, the intelligence community tends to take the easy way out, demanding new powers, more money, better tools, but failing to take full advantage of the capabilities it already has. the european parliament has a very important role to play in this.
in writing. events in recent years have forced us to look for new solutions to ensure the greatest possible safety for travellers. the threat of terrorism makes it easier for us to accept restrictions on our freedom. i hope that before any decision is made to introduce body scanners in airports, a thorough analysis of their effectiveness, safety and the costs that will have to be incurred will be carried out. we don't want to see a repeat of the a1/h1n1 flu vaccine rollout, where governments panic and buy huge quantities of vaccines that are not yet used, without any manufacturer's safety guarantees. perhaps a more effective solution would be to use the israeli approach, where the emphasis is on observing the behaviour of passengers and the detailed control of those most suspicious, not all. this system has been proven to work for many years.
in writing. to fight terrorism effectively, we need harmonised action, including uniform eu rules on scanners. the rules adopted must take into account the protection of fundamental rights, personal data and, not least, the health of citizens. it is necessary to decide on the mandatory use of x-ray equipment. there's no point in even going into this if the controls are voluntary. because it's hard to imagine that terrorists would agree to an x-ray. and of course, the safety of health scanners is a very important issue. there are different opinions on this. from the opinion of the czech nuclear safety authority, which proves that the scanning devices emit radiation harmful to humans, to the french general directorate of civil aviation, which has declared them completely safe. further tests are necessary to identify the types of scanners that are safe for health and the possible side effects of their use. the studies should be coordinated by the european commission in full cooperation with the member states. the scanners used must have a safety certificate, which is the basis for their authorisation in all member states. this will avoid duplication of research costs between countries and ensure that the health of citizens is equally protected in each country.
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. at some european airports, a new way of screening passengers has been introduced. along with the usual forms of security, full-body scanners have been used. most airline passengers are strongly opposed to these checks and see them as a violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to privacy and the protection of personal dignity. and what's more, and this is very important, is that they're exacerbated by the lack of knowledge about the health effects of the scanners on the people who are being scanned. nor are there clear regulations on the storage and security of data collected as a result of scanning. it is also argued that scanners do not perform as well as their manufacturers claim. let's hope that this doesn't turn out to be as effective as the swine flu vaccine, which was ultimately only effective in increasing the revenues of the pharmaceutical companies. in view of all these legitimate concerns, i believe that the european commission should lay down strict rules to protect passengers' rights while ensuring their safety.

member of the commission. − madam president, if i were to try to give a balanced answer to all the questions that have been put and to all the matters that have been raised, i would need, i think, at least half an hour. i have only two or three minutes if i understand rightly. having said this, let me start with a general remark. i really do not believe that protectionism is a solution. whether you are a believer or not, looking back into history, it is thanks to international trade that our countries have become prosperous. secondly, europe has a transformative economy, which means that we have to import to be able to export. the idea that we could export without importing is completely false and contradictory to the facts. so i staunchly believe that we should have free trade agreements with major economic partners, that we should make a success of the doha round and that we should further liberalise international trade, but that does not mean that we should not take into account the fact that this international trade also has to be fair and that we are entitled to protect our interests. the commission is certainly going to do so when necessary and we will use the tdi mechanisms we have to have an impact on what we consider to be unfair distortions of trade. some very specific questions have also been asked, by mr jadot for example, on the meeting on 4 february at the wto and what the result of this was. well, the main message at that meeting was that the rules of the general agreement on trade in services are not an obstacle to the right of countries to ensure effective financial regulation. the reason is that gats has a very broad scope for financial prudential measures, so this financial regulation, be it at national or european level, is certainly not contradictory to the gats rules. that brings me to the origins of the crisis we are going through. hopefully the major part is behind us. i am firmly convinced that it has had a major impact on trade, but that the origin of this crisis lies with financial imbalances which resulted from completely wrong choices by financial institutions. the financial crisis did not originate in europe; it came to europe and to the rest of the world from the united states. i can agree that the food crisis of a couple of years ago, which was still not completely resolved and digested, let us say, has added to big imbalances, especially for the developing countries. you can say a lot about developing countries, about good governance and so on, but you certainly cannot lay the blame on the developing countries for being at the origin of the financial crisis. that is obvious, and they are very severely hit by that crisis, so we should take that into due consideration. there have also been some questions, the last time by mr caspary and one by mr jadot too, asking what are we going to do with the tec and with the strategic initiative for china? my personal opinion is that the only good response to the economic development of china – which we are not going to stop, by the way – the only good response is to become stronger ourselves. i think that is the only good response. when you look at this in terms of trade deficit, it is true that the trade deficit with china has gone up considerably, but when you look at the global trade deficit with asia, this did not go up that much. also, within asia, the other asian countries are facing very fierce competition from china. so what we should do is become stronger ourselves. i believe that achieving this transatlantic marketplace, for example, is one of the best answers we can give. we have a recent report, produced at the request of parliament, which shows that, if you were able to reduce by 50% the non-tariff barriers between europe and the united states, this would have an effect which would be much larger than the doha round. we should work on that, but, having said this, it is not easy at all. speaking of the doha round, i staunchly believe that we should try to close that round because it has a lot of important features, among them that the existing tariffs cannot go up any more, that we would be able to close them down. secondly, there is a strong developmental approach in the doha round, provided, of course, that we can keep it as it stands now, and that should be the goal of the european commission. in writing. to begin with, i would like to draw your attention to the importance of online gambling in today's world. in the debate which is currently taking place, there are a number of issues which i believe should be resolved as soon as possible, preferably at community level. in its judgment, the european court of justice stated that the regulation of gambling law is a matter for the member states, which tighten their legislation in this area. not only in poland but also in other countries, there are voices that online gambling should be significantly restricted. i believe this is a step in the right direction, aimed at introducing clear and uniform rules, including the principles of a secure internet. on the other hand, online gambling often extends beyond the territory of a single country. this has serious consequences, not only legally, but financially. the question of which legislation to apply and to what extent remains unanswered. i would argue that the european union, whose primary task is to ensure the safety of its citizens, should introduce regulations at european level and ensure that they are effectively enforced.

in writing. − marriages between people from different countries and cultures are increasing. the issue of disputes arising from the dissolution of international marriages has been a frequent subject of petitions to the european parliament for years. in 1987, the european parliament, aware of the seriousness of the problems facing children in the context of family disputes arising in so-called international relations, created the position of ombudsman for parental adoption. the signature of the convention on the maintenance of children and other family members is another step forward by the community in ensuring the proper protection of its citizens, and in particular children. the convention is intended to strengthen existing community rules on the recognition and enforcement of maintenance decisions and administrative cooperation between central authorities by creating a harmonised set of rules in the community for third countries that become parties to the convention. the entry into force of the convention will therefore ensure that maintenance creditors receive comprehensive assistance in the recovery of maintenance abroad through a central unit designated in their country of residence. the convention also addresses many practical issues that may affect the way claims are handled, such as language requirements, standard forms, the exchange of information on national law and the use of new information technologies to reduce costs and delays.
