acting president of the council. - mr president, on the 7th of this week there will be a meeting of the heads of state and government of the euro area and this is the debate in the european parliament concerning that important meeting, which aims to formalise the agreement reached on loans to greece, the financial support package to greece, to deal with the serious financial situation of that euro area country, and also to reflect on the lessons to be drawn from that situation, from those agreements, in relation to the future of the euro area and the european union as a whole. what the heads of state and government are going to do on friday is to confirm the financial solution that has been given to greece by the european union, that is to say, to formalize the commitment - ultimately, the political commitment - that was already made at the meeting of the heads of state and government of the european union on 11 february, a commitment of solidarity with greece to solve its very difficult financial situation. and so what the heads of state and government are going to do on friday is to present, to set out, to agree the availability of the remaining 15 members of the eurozone, once the greek government has approved a tough economic and financial adjustment programme, for this country to receive this aid, these loans aimed at its financial stability and also aimed at the financial stability of the euro area as a whole, which is something that was politically committed not only for the greek case, but was politically committed on 11 february in a resolution of the heads of state and government of the european union. this decision is important, politically very relevant, historically relevant, because it is a decision necessary for the credibility of the euro area, for the external credibility of the union as a whole from a financial point of view. it is important for fiscal consolidation, as required by the treaties of the european union, fiscal consolidation in the euro area and in the union as a whole, and it is very important for consolidating an effective and lasting economic recovery in the european union. today, commissioner olli rehn, who is present here, published the commission's spring 2010-2011 forecasts, which point to the gradual economic recovery of the european union as a message. the commission forecasts confirm that economic recovery is underway in the european union and that, after experiencing the deepest recession in its history, the european union as a whole is expected to grow by 1% in 2010 - this year - and by 1.75% in 2011. the economic recession in the european union ended in the third quarter of last year and the economic recovery has begun, to which the european economic recovery plan and the decisions of the member states have clearly contributed by injecting very large sums into the economies of the various countries, money coming from the national budgets and also from the community budget through the european economic recovery plan, and that is one of the reasons why, after having gone through - again - the worst recession in its history, we are already seeing an economic recovery in the union. these are the forecasts that the european commission has made, and the decision to lend to greece is undoubtedly a major contribution to the effectiveness and durability of the 'two-factor' economic recovery in the euro area and the european union as a whole. we believe that the european union has responded well to the current economic situation, to the economic crisis, by doing what it could to respond to that situation and, in particular, to the very serious financial situation in greece, because what the european union has done in the last few months is to take clear steps towards what has been called economic governance or the economic governance of the union. clear steps have been taken which at times may have seemed slow, too slow, but which have been taken with certainty and determination and which will culminate next friday in this meeting of the heads of state and government of the union. we believe that economic governance, the economic governance of the union, must have three solid bases. the first is responsibility for the commitments made, for example when a treaty on union is signed and ratified. the second is solidarity, which is a principle at the heart of the european union and all its policies. and thirdly, coordination in fiscal consolidation, coordination for the external representation of the european union - for example, in view of the g20 meetings - coordination also for growth and for overcoming the crisis. and i am convinced that this document which commissioner olli rehn is preparing and which the commission will present on 12 may will be in that spirit. finally, i would like to say that economic governance of the union, as it is being carried out, developed and laid down in the european union, requires effective instruments, requires an element of supervision. i am convinced that this is what the document being prepared by the european commission will be about. we need quality public finances. we need supervision of the financial system, european supervision of the financial system, and in this connection i would call on the european parliament to adopt as soon as possible the financial supervision package, the regulations and directives which are now being discussed in the european parliament and which will be discussed in the next few days in the committee responsible and then in the plenary. and we also need mechanisms to prevent possible crises and we also need, finally - as i said earlier - the ability to have a single voice in the union's external representation, and i am speaking clearly in this case of the g20 meetings. i believe that these are steps towards a government or economic governance of the union; aid, loans to greece are part of that, and that is why i believe that the european union is on the right track and has consolidated that good track. i am convinced that the heads of state and government will approve this package of financial aid to greece, which is, in short - as they said in their declaration of 11 february - a bet on financial stability, on the economic stability of the euro area and of the european union as a whole.
president of the commission. − mr president, i was asked to make a statement to this house ahead of friday’s meeting of the heads of state and government of the euro area. let me first say a word of condolence for the families of the victims of the violence in athens today. to disagree and protest is a right of citizens in our democratic societies, but nothing can justify the recourse to violence. let me address the financial support package for greece endorsed last sunday. then i will give you some of my views on what needs to be done to prevent a repetition of a crisis of this type. as regards greece, a multi-annual programme of fiscal consolidation and structural reform has been agreed by the greek authorities. this was jointly prepared with the commission, the european central bank and the international monetary fund. the greek government has put forward a solid and credible package that will steer its economy on a sustainable path and restore confidence. it is important that we acknowledge the courage that prime minister papandreou and his government have shown. greece will undertake painful efforts, but we all know that there are no alternatives to such efforts. in return, following the recommendation of the commission and of the european central bank, the coordinated european mechanism for assistance to greece has been activated. this is an unprecedented act of solidarity, unmatched anywhere in the world. this assistance will be decisive in helping greece to get its economy back on track and will preserve the financial stability of the euro area as a whole. allow me to stress that the commission has made sure that the mechanism, whilst being based on bilateral loans, is a european one. the commission was instrumental in setting it up and will play an important role in its management and implementation. the commission is, and will remain, central in assessing greece’s compliance with the package’s conditionality. the commission will also manage the bilateral loans from the member states. by the end of the week we will already have a critical mass of member states that have completed the process to provide those bilateral loans to greece. it is my firm conviction that the unprecedented financial support given to greece – eur 110 billion – and the adjustment programme are an adequate response to the greek crisis. we have no reason to doubt that it will be firmly implemented both by greece and by the euro-area member states. this view is shared by others who matter. i noticed, for instance, the supportive statement of the past, current and future chairs of the g20 finance ministers, issued just now. regrettably, not all market players seem convinced already. we have to say loud and clear that the doubters are wrong. i will come back to this in a moment. at the meeting of the euro-area heads of state and government on friday, we will look beyond this deal to what we need to do to draw the right lessons from this situation. the debate will of course be a starting point, because decisions need to be debated further and ultimately taken with all the 27 member states – the euro-area member states but also all the other member states of the european union. let me say this very clearly: discussing and taking decisions at 27 is a source of strength. whilst we have to speed up our processes, the fact is that the joint action of the 27 – unparalleled anywhere in the world – provides the best possible foundation for our joint future in an ever more interlinked world. i see two main strands for reflection and action: first, a reassessment of the rules for economic governance, including the stability and growth pact, and second, financial markets reform. the commission has been working intensively on economic governance and is ready to present its proposals on how to improve this next wednesday. there are three main building blocks to be considered. first, responsibility: we need to reinforce the stability and growth pact and, above all, member states’ compliance. the case for reinforcement of both the preventive and the corrective arm of the pact is obvious. i am pleased that most of those who have previously questioned – or even suggested weakening – the pact now accept the need for stronger rules and – most importantly – for their strict implementation. second, interdependence: we are all in this together. i think the crisis has clearly shown that we need to address the imbalances between our member states, in particular within the euro area. this includes divergences in their competitiveness, as this is one crucial element that causes other types of imbalances. this cannot, of course, mean that some become less competitive so that others look relatively more competitive. we are all competing on world markets. what we need is to enhance our overall competitiveness in a balanced, mutually reinforcing way. i also believe we need to look at the other causes of imbalances. to make progress, we will propose increased surveillance and increased economic policy coordination. i am also happy that i see more openness now when it comes to the member states for this purpose. third, coherence: we have to ask ourselves whether our system of fiscal rules is complete. i see merit in creating a permanent mechanism for dealing with disruptive situations. after all, it is better to be safe than sorry. i hope that we can seize the moment – and i count on you to help us deliver these reforms. i believe from a political point of view that, in terms of european integration, we are at one of those moments where, if we do not build up europe, we will fall behind. we cannot have a standstill. it is a very special moment, the moment we are living today in europe where our solidarity, our responsibility, is being tested every day. i hope the leaders of our member states will be able to rise to the occasion, not just to help the others but to show their responsibility to our common european project. these reforms will be introduced against the background of unprecedented efforts already under way. that deficit and debt levels in some member states need to be corrected with determination, and faster than targeted before the crisis, is undisputed. but it must also be said that we cannot ignore the fact that the budgetary deterioration in 2009 was largely due to the working of the automatic stabilisers in the face of an unprecedented decline in economic activity caused by a financial crisis not originating in europe. in other words, the overall situation in the euro area was largely the result of anti-recession policies advocated all over the world. it was always clear that the situation would subsequently be corrected, and most euro-area members have already undertaken bold reforms, for example of their pensions systems. the responsibility shown by the governments needs to be matched by financial-market players. this is why it is no less urgent to continue delivering a sustainable and responsible financial sector, at the service of the economy and its citizens. one must bear in mind that financial-market players are key actors in driving market sentiment. psychology also matters in markets. the financial crisis was born out of short-termism, pro-cyclicality and a lack of responsibility. that is what we must urgently correct.we need strong and stable european financial services markets to deliver the investments needed for future growth in line with the europe 2020 vision. we need responsible behaviour from all our market players. we have already been doing a lot as regards financial markets reform. i count on this house to make this clear to all. european institutions are acting, and must be seen as acting together: parliament, the council and the commission. we have prioritised work on responsible risk management, safer derivatives markets, better financial supervision and ensuring that banks hold adequate capital to cover their real risks. this work must be speeded up. in the coming weeks we will need to complete the reforms already under way. as i said to this house only two weeks ago, i hope to see a breakthrough soon on our proposal for hedge funds and private equity. i would also like early agreement on effective new european supervisory arrangements. the european systemic risk board and the three supervisory authorities should start working at the beginning of 2011. but they must not be mere paper tigers: we have a shared responsibility to ensure they have the tools they need to do their jobs. this includes binding decision-making powers to deal with genuine emergencies, to enforce european rules – and i insist on european rules, not only national rules – and to settle any disputes within the colleges of national supervisors. it is high time to deliver these decisions and make sure they are ambitious. more proposals are on their way this year to improve depositor and investor protection, to strengthen measures against market abuse, to further improve the quality and quantity of bank capital and discourage excessive leverage. over the past three months, and paradoxically still this week, the situation on the sovereign debt markets has brought new concerns to light. the commission is already working on a fundamental overhaul of derivatives markets to increase transparency and safety in these markets. in a first stage, we will present legislation to standardise eligible derivatives contracts, putting them through central counterparty clearing that is properly regulated and supervised. we are also now considering whether further specific measures are needed for sovereign derivatives markets. the crisis has also once again brought the role of credit rating agencies to the fore. these agencies play a pivotal role in the functioning of financial markets, but ratings appear to be too cyclical, too reliant on the general market mood rather than on fundamentals – regardless of whether market mood is too optimistic or too pessimistic. because credit rating agencies have such a key role and influence over the markets, they also have a special responsibility to ensure their assessments are both sound and comprehensive. that is why in 2008 the commission quickly put forward new legislation for these agencies, which will come into force in the next few months. these rules will ensure that credit rating agencies act more transparently, publish their methodologies and avoid conflicts of interest, but we need to go further. to strengthen the supervision of these actors of europe-wide dimension, the commission believes they should be put under the direct supervision of the future european securities markets authority, and that is exactly what we will propose. we have also launched a reflection on whether further measures may be needed to ensure the appropriate rating of sovereign debt in particular. we must get our own house in order while pushing others to do the same. the commission will do whatever is necessary to ensure that financial markets are not a playground for speculation. free markets constitute the basis for the functioning of successful economies, but free markets need rules and compliance, and rules and compliance need to be tightened if irresponsible behaviour puts at risk what cannot and should not be at risk. market behaviour must rest on sound and objective analysis, and financial services must realise that they are exactly that: a service, not an end in itself. they must not become detached from their economic and societal function. in fact, financial-market players are still in business because regulatory authorities and democratic institutions – ultimately the taxpayers – stabilised the markets in the financial crisis. we acted swiftly then, and precisely for that reason, we will also act swiftly in the future. so the message from this friday’s meeting of eurogroup heads of state and president of the commission. − madam president, europe has been presented with a stark choice. we could take a beggar-thy-neighbour approach to the economic and financial crisis, a sauve qui peut mr president, for any strategy to be effective, creating strong links between its objectives and available policy tools is, in my view, essential, and i see four main policy tools as delivery mechanisms for the eu 2020 strategy. firstly, the most important is internal market regulation that stimulates competition and economic dynamism and recognises social obligations that result from economic integration; mr president, first of all let me thank both our rapporteurs – kinga gál and ramón jáuregui atondo – and also the commission and the presidency. muchas gracias por el trabajo tan duro, pero necesario, realizado. when we were talking about the eu’s accession to the european convention on human rights – and we have been talking about it in the european union for the past 10 years, i think – there were quite a lot of worries that there would be competition between the european court of human rights and the european court of justice, that we would have problems when it came to jurisdiction, that the autonomy of the european court of justice might be questioned. but i think that what we have achieved in our work is that we are coming to a situation in which those two courts can be complementary. we were trying to do everything to avoid hierarchical thinking, but actually we have cross-fertilisation between those two systems of human rights protection. in the light of recent trends, where the ecj follows the case-law of the strasbourg court and vice versa, i think that the two systems coexist and actually there is no competition, and most of those fears have been dissipated. in the recent bosphorus judgment that we all know very well, the european court of human rights said that there was no need to re-examine the case because the eu, as such, offers an adequate level of protection of human rights. so then the question arises: why do we need accession to the convention? this question has been posed by our colleagues here and, yes, we do need it. why do we need it? not only because of the symbolic meaning, which is important, but because the whole system of protecting human rights in the european union will gain credibility in the eyes of citizens who will enjoy the protection from the actions of the eu, not only of the member states as is the case now. when there is no effective judicial review either at national or at community level – when, for example, the applicant is denied standing or the eu body concerned cannot be sued, those are the situations where we will have added value. we are acceding to the convention for the sake of greater coherence of the system of human rights protection, not to undermine the credibility of that system. we need loyalty, and that is why we postulate that inter-state applications should not be brought concerning an alleged failure of compliance when the act falls within the scope of union law. we postulate this and we should do our utmost to put it into law. finally, i would like to thank very much the commission for setting up a dg on human rights. i remember as a student reading joseph weiler’s articles about the protection of human rights. he came to the conclusion that you can do whatever you like in terms of applying for and acceding to the convention on human rights, but if there is no implementation and follow-up in the commission then it will be fruitless. so finally, thanks to you, we have it. hopefully we will go forward and have better protection of human rights in the european union than we have now.
the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms is one of the foundations of the european axiology that defends the rights of the individual, the rights of man. it was the foundation of the european union in terms of values. for many years, the european court of human rights has done a good job of defending the weak, defending the oppressed. however, recent rulings have raised questions about the court's understanding of the principle of individual liberty. last year, a wave of discussion and opposition swept through europe over a ruling that banned the display of crosses in public. i believe that the european union, by virtue of the treaty of lisbon, should at the same time, as a party to this convention, initiate a discussion and debate in the direction of a profound reflection so that such distortions of individual freedom and misunderstandings of human rights do not occur in the future.

in writing. ladies and gentlemen! the accession of the european union to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms has long been a priority on the agenda of the european parliament. the lisbon treaty, providing a legal basis for this, allows negotiations to begin. this is a very important step towards enabling the eu citizens to exercise their fundamental rights more effectively. however, we must be aware that there is still a lot of work to be done before the union becomes a party to the convention. there are many legal questions that will need to be answered during the negotiations. these include: should the union only accede to the convention itself or become a party to the protocols as well? how can the question of the union's representation in the council of europe bodies be resolved? and, most importantly, how to arrange the relationship between the two courts: the court of justice in luxembourg and the court of human rights in strasbourg? it is important to remember that a fundamental principle of the eu legal system is that the ets has exclusive competence to interpret eu law. i am pleased that the newly constituted commission has made accession to the convention one of its priorities in preparing a recommendation for negotiation. the key now is for member states to agree on the basic issues so that the negotiations can run smoothly.
in writing. europe still lacks an effective system for protecting human rights. the european convention on human rights (echr) is the most important instrument for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in europe. it is of particular importance to the citizens of my country, whose right-wing government has been deprived of the protection of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the eu's common agricultural policy. the strasbourg court, which is the guardian of the convention, has dealt with over 100 000 cases since its creation. each year, more and more of them arrive. in 2009, almost 60 000 cases were brought before the court, an increase of 20% compared with 2008. member states shall not be in a hurry to recognise the judgments of the court. if they did it quickly and efficiently, there would be far fewer complaints. the accession of the union to the echr will provide an additional impetus for the efficient implementation of the case-law of the court, which safeguards the rights of citizens and enables them to seek justice. the court will monitor the conformity of legal acts with the text of the convention. the case-law of the court should therefore also be reflected in union policy. perhaps this will help the polish right to understand, among other things, that the state should ensure religious neutrality in state educational institutions, where attendance at lessons is required regardless of religion (from the court's judgment in lautsi v. italy).

in writing. the motor vehicles block exemption regulation is a very important document for the european union, as it directly affects over 3.5 million people employed in the automotive sector in europe, both in the primary and secondary markets. this regulation introduced favourable conditions for the operation of the automotive market which strengthened competition. it has created new jobs and enabled the market to develop efficiently and sustainably, in the interests of consumers, large car companies and independent operators alike. it is also very important that it provides european consumers with a wide access to services and goods on the automotive market. this document is of particular importance for independent car repairers who need access to technical information to compete effectively with authorised repairers and for independent car parts manufacturers. i was all the more pleased to learn that the european commission had decided to extend this regulation. in its resolution b7 0245/2010 the european parliament calls on the commission to clarify the issues raised by me in my written question to the commission of 16 april this year, such as access to technical information for independent manufacturers, or the clarification of the concepts of 'comparable parts', 'quality parts', 'original parts' and 'technical information'. the addressees of the mvber, by virtue of their non-trivial role in the economy, need clear and precisely worded legal acts.

in writing. − the decision not to convene the convention was one of the most difficult decisions to make in the introduction of 18 new members to the parliament. but we are doing so out of respect for this instrument, which aims to give greater legitimacy to decisions affecting eu fundamental law. this is not a precedent for the future. all important matters concerning treaty changes, such as the electoral procedure, will still require the convention to be convened. i would like to thank inigo (the rapporteur) and the coordinators for making this decision. and it wasn't easy. we have a problem with the appointment of 18 new members because some countries have not provided for the procedure. but we decided that the most important principle is representation. this chamber should be balanced as soon as possible. we therefore call on the member states to complete this process as soon as possible, assuming at the same time that all members are elected by direct suffrage.
in writing. - as a co-author of the european parliament resolution on kyrgyzstan, i would like to thank my colleagues for voting in favour of this document today. particular attention should be paid to the intention of the transitional government to start work on constitutional reform and to quickly lay the foundations for the holding of democratic parliamentary elections. hence the call to the interim government to fulfil kyrgyzstan's international obligations and ensure a free and fair electoral process. we are following with concern the developments in kyrgyzstan, including with regard to securing the uninterrupted supply corridor for nato and other international forces involved in the mission in afghanistan. it is essential that the european union, including the european parliament, closely monitor the situation in kyrgyzstan, provide the necessary support and promote dialogue between all groups in kyrgyz society.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on kyrgyzstan because i believe that as a member of the delegation for central asia, i am obliged to give at least some support to a nation which has been in such a difficult situation in recent weeks. the resolution calls for an end to violence, dialogue between the parties to the conflict and respect for the rights to liberty, human rights and the rule of law, stressing the importance of a coherent and stable constitutional framework for ensuring democracy. i therefore believe that the international support programme should be implemented as soon as possible and that the eu should take a leading role in it.
in writing. - resolution rc-b7-0246/2010 of the european parliament of 6 may 2010 on the situation in kyrgyzstan is a common european voice in favour of kyrgyzstan and its authorities. the resolution on kyrgyzstan is an important signal from the european union and from europe as a whole. we should show both the citizens and the kyrgyz authorities, not just through such resolutions, that we support the strengthening of democracy and social development, the security of the population and sustainable growth. the european parliament must be the institution which supports all prospects of democratization and does not accept any lapses along the way. the changes in kyrgyzstan are the consequence of the past few years and the fleeting hopes of the tulip revolution. the electoral fraud and soft authoritarianism that has started to function in kyrgyzstan cannot and will not be tolerated. the only actions we can and will support are democratic actions, because they are the foundation of the european union. we cannot agree to any other solution. i hope that the resolution on kyrgyzstan is one of many things we will do. the whole of europe expects us to do so.
in writing. − as the author of written statement no 71/2009 adopted by parliament on the fight against breast cancer in the eu, i am very pleased with the european commission's communication entitled 'the fight against cancer: a european partnership'. this document identified the problem of cancer in the eu and set targets for the fight against cancer. although healthcare is de facto a matter for the member states, the eu can act as a complement and provide an excellent platform for exchanging good practice, for example. it will be up to the member states to make use of this additional tool developed by the commission. the proposal has a very specific target of reducing the burden of cancer in the eu by 15% by 2020. to achieve this, an integrated pan-european cancer strategy needs to be developed by 2013. the next step is to reduce the disparity in cancer mortality among europeans receiving treatment by 70%. the gap between the best and worst performing countries in the eu is still too wide. the communication also emphasises the need for prevention and for 100% of the eu population to be screened for breast, cervical and colon cancer. i am pleased that our recent appeal in written statement no 71/2009 has come at a favourable time for the commission's work, which i hope will lead to its swift and certain implementation.
in writing. - according to the world health organization, cancer is the leading cause of death worldwide. today, one in three europeans is diagnosed with cancer and one in four dies from it. unfortunately, the aging of our population will also increase the incidence of cancer in the coming decades. i believe that to prevent this upward trend we need to improve national cancer plans and to carry out an even more effective public information campaign in the union. healthy lifestyles should be taught to children from an early age, and this will reduce the number of illnesses in the future. experts say that one third of all cancers are preventable, but to do so, the eu needs to increase funding for cancer research and broad-based cancer prevention across the eu.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution 'fighting cancer: a european partnership'. all actions to combat cancer and minimise its effects need to be supported. medical progress has not yet been able to stop cancer, which is becoming one of the greatest scourges of mankind. the fact that cancer was the second leading cause of death in 2006 is frightening. cancers have many causes, or they often go undiagnosed. but there is a way to prevent cancer and reduce its effects by about 30 percent. this requires appropriate national testing mechanisms. the european union, guided by the well-being and safety of its citizens, must ensure that appropriate methods of early diagnosis, prevention and advanced treatment are developed. in many countries, progress has been made in the fight against cancer, including through the implementation of anti-smoking strategies and specific prevention. similar actions, but with increased strength and effectiveness, should be applied across the union. the prognosis for the next few years in terms of morbidity and mortality from cancer is not optimistic. the knowledge that many people will die of cancer despite the various ways of diagnosing and treating it is always bitter and sad. but let us make sure that our citizens feel that they have our full support in this regard.
in writing. - i strongly support the european parliament's report on the commission communication 'fighting cancer: a european partnership'. the international agency for research on cancer estimates that one in three europeans will be diagnosed with cancer and one in four will die from it. this year, 3 million europeans will develop cancer and nearly 2 million will die of cancer. in poland, about 100,000 people develop cancer each year, and 70,000 die. the fight against cancer is a permanent area of union action in the field of public health. the lisbon treaty has emphasised the union's competences to support, coordinate or complement member states' actions to protect and improve health. the commission's initiative 'a european partnership to fight cancer 2009-2013' gives more detail on this. the objectives of the partnership, including in particular preventive actions, are essential to reduce the incidence of cancer. the limited financial resources available for these purposes are a cause for concern. the communication sets targets for the next 10 years, while the community budget provides only short-term financial support. i therefore call for: increased funding, especially for regional policy and european social fund prevention programmes; more effective use of the resources available under the 7th framework programme (e.g. for better coordination of scientific research); more funding planned in the new financial perspective.
in writing. - today we voted on a resolution prepared by the slovenian mep alojz peterle (epp) on the fight against cancer. i voted in favour of the european commission's proposal to establish a european partnership to fight cancer for the period 2009-2013. this new form of cooperation is intended to support member states' efforts to combat cancer. medical statistics confirm that more than 3 million new cases and 1.7 million deaths are recorded in europe each year. thus, cancer is the second most common cause of illness and death each year. the european partnership calls on member states to draw up integrated plans to combat this deadly disease as soon as possible, with the aim of reducing the incidence by 15% by 2020. but we must not forget that prevention is the key to this unequal battle. it's the most cost-effective because one-third of all cancers are preventable. prevention should therefore be promoted both in medical practice and in increasingly healthy lifestyles.
in writing. − given that progress towards the 20% energy saving target for 2020 is too slow, there is a need to increase and accelerate innovation in ict and to significantly increase the share of renewable energy sources. it should be noted that the growth of the transport sector is accompanied by a rapid increase in carbon dioxide emissions. the emphasis should therefore be on the use of information and communication technologies in this sector, not only to reduce emissions but also to prevent them from increasing. ict solutions must be taken into account in the planning of a new european transport policy. this can lead to a reduction in traffic congestion, which has a positive impact on the environment. all these actions will not only bring tangible climate benefits, but also reduce energy costs and lead to the creation of green jobs. however, it should be borne in mind that the new member states are not able to adapt so quickly to the requirements imposed by the european union. the interests of these countries must also be taken into account, as they are a significant group that still uses traditional energy sources. it takes time and money to change that.
in writing. − inevitable climate change is forcing the european union's society and economy to adapt to the new reality. i believe that there is a need for an adaptation policy which should be appropriate to the nature and type of change taking place and which should include a strategy for protecting the most vulnerable areas. in order to better coordinate action, i fully agree with the rapporteur and consider it extremely important to implement a system of information exchange and monitoring at the interstate level, but also at the regional and local level. i am particularly pleased to highlight the important role of the common agricultural policy, which plays a key role in the process of adaptation to climate change as a watchdog for the protection of ecosystems and biodiversity. that is why i think it is very important to have projects that prevent or mitigate the effects of drought and floods, that support farmers in working in difficult conditions.
in writing. − the results of scientific work indicate that the effects of climate change will have an increasing impact on the environment, the economy and our daily lives. taking action to adapt to the current and future impacts of climate change is therefore a major challenge for societies around the world. decisions on how best to adapt to climate change must be based on sound scientific and economic analysis, but not all regions have access to information of the right quality. the creation of a climate change monitoring platform to exchange information, experience and best practice at european, regional and local levels is therefore a good initiative. i am not sure, however, that the eu's taking on the role of leader in the international fight against global warming, as recommended in the document, is not an attempt to take on too much responsibility for global affairs. i think that in the face of challenges like the economic crisis, or the need to create growth, we shouldn't prioritize spending on global warming. whatever action is taken to adapt to climate change, it should also be borne in mind that some countries will face exceptionally high costs for implementing adaptation policies and that leaving them without any financial support may lead to a widening of the development gap between member states.
in writing. − securing value for money, effective management, and the elimination of fraud are key priorities of the ecr group for the eu budget. we therefore support the thrust of the cozzolino report and most of its conclusions. the ecr group cannot, however, endorse the concept of a european public prosecutor. this office risks being a dangerous first step towards european competence for aspects of criminal law and the focus on its creation is a distraction from making existing systems and bodies work effectively. as the ecr amendment to remove the paragraph supporting progress towards a european public prosecutor was rejected, the ecr abstained on the final vote.
in writing. − it is worth noting that there was a significant drop in irregularities in 2008 compared to the previous year. the biggest improvement was in agricultural spending. the report shows that the estimated amount of irregularities has decreased by 34%. the biggest increase was in the area of pre-accession funds, where misspending increased by as much as 90.6%, but it should be remembered that these are not member states and lack experience. despite the improvement in 2008, a certain part of the union budget is still being misused. this is partly due to the lack of effective control and supervision mechanisms. the european anti-fraud office (olaf), which has been in existence since 1999, has had a number of successes in the fight against fraud, but it is necessary to ensure its full operational independence. i support the rapporteur's proposal to allow olaf to make greater use of internal controls carried out by the commission rather than relying solely on information from officials or member states. what is the role of the member states and their supervisory and control systems? the fight against fraud in european projects should be our priority. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european union's financial instruments for the period 2007-13 is based on the principle of the european monetary system (ems) and the principle of sound financial management. we must not forget that the money in the eu budget belongs to all of us - the taxpayers. therefore, it is necessary to ensure that they are spent as efficiently as possible.

in writing. energy consumption in buildings accounts for almost one third of all energy consumed in the european union. this segment therefore has significant potential for reducing energy consumption not only because of the commitments made to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but also because of the issue of energy security. the key provisions of the proposed directive include the concept of 'nearly zero energy buildings'. let us recall that by the end of 2020, all new buildings are to be nearly zero-energy buildings, and in the case of the public sector, which should set an example, two years earlier. on the other hand, two elements of the directive under discussion deserve a positive assessment. first, the creation by 2020 of an energy efficiency fund, which would act as a vehicle for increasing private and public investment in projects to improve the energy efficiency of buildings. this type of structural support gives the opportunity to achieve the intended objectives. secondly, the inclusion in the text of the draft directive of a provision on the introduction of smart metering systems and active control systems, aimed at energy saving. the widespread deployment of these devices can bring benefits to consumers in terms of price, energy efficiency and energy security.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank mrs ranner, on behalf of myself and my colleague siim kallas, whom i am replacing, for her report on a particularly important aspect of social regulation in road transport. the commission's initial report highlighted the very significant differences between the penalties applicable in the member states in the event of serious infringements of social legislation in road transport. the penalties vary in terms of both type, severity and amount of fines. for example, a driver who exceeds the maximum daily driving time risks a fine in spain that may be ten times higher than in greece. the commission welcomes the decision of parliament to act on its report. parliament stressed the unsatisfactory state of affairs, as drivers and businesses may wrongly consider that committing an offence is less serious in one member state than in another. this is clearly potentially harmful to road safety and competition. the parliament's report thus provides valuable support to the commission's efforts to coordinate the harmonization of the implementation of the existing regulations. the report of the parliament suggests, among other things, that minimum and maximum penalties should be set for each of the infringements of social legislation and stresses that the treaty of lisbon, as the rapporteur has said, opens up, through article 83, the possibility of establishing minimum rules on penalties. the commission will shortly be examining with the greatest care to what extent and in what form these new treaty provisions can be used to improve the implementation of social rules in road transport. i thank you for this particularly constructive report and i can assure you that the questions raised and the suggestions made by the european parliament will be examined by the commission with the greatest attention.

in writing. − the main factors shaping energy efficiency are: 1. conversion of one kind of energy into another so that specific useful work can be done. the longer the chain of change, the greater the loss. in practice, this is mainly the flow of heat energy released from primary energy sources, much of which is released into the environment. this effect can be reduced in cogeneration processes, which can reach an efficiency of up to about 90%. 2. the electrical resistance, called ohm's resistance, is important in electrical energy transfer. the heat resistance. the low resistance is a significant feature in heat exchangers, and the high resistance is a function of the low conductivity of the heat through the insulation. the use of these insulation materials (e.g. styropian, mineral wool, cellular concrete) significantly reduces the energy demand of the dwelling. it's currently large, about 40% of the total energy used. 4. friction in anti-friction processes, e.g. in bearings, or friction processes, e.g. in brakes, mainly affects vehicles and aircraft (turbulence). friction losses are about 30% of the total energy. i was in favour of the regulation without amendments, because energy losses in housing are next to conversion losses the biggest, and the savings will help poor people. in the case of poland, thermal modernisation, alongside cogeneration, can bring economic, social and environmental benefits. there should be some priority for implementation in this area, as new regulations often hamper the implementation of previous ones.
in writing. - given the need to help refugees in europe, i consider the european parliament's decisions on this matter to be of particular importance. the main objective of the fund is to support actions undertaken by member states, which often involve additional financial measures. they are designed to ensure that refugees have a decent standard of living and that their stay in the eu is regulated by law. i think it's necessary to increase financial aid to countries that are involved in helping refugees. we cannot support the charge that we, as developed countries, are trying to prevent the influx of refugees, rather than protect them at all costs. refugees coming to europe from third world countries, often facing enormous problems such as violence, lack of livelihood and access to medical care, should be surrounded by the best-organised care available in the member states.
in writing. - it is good that a common eu resettlement programme has been established. the number of refugees requiring resettlement is increasing, as opposed to the number of places available to them. on the other hand, the countries hosting refugees are often poorer and their resources are limited. resettlement should be considered as a last resort the only solution when a refugee cannot return to his or her home country or find safe refuge in a third country. member states should adopt a more ambitious programme to ensure the quality and effectiveness of resettlement. the establishment of private funding mechanisms and more frequent public-law initiatives to strengthen the european resettlement programme should be encouraged. particular attention needs to be paid to the human resources needed in the current and future eu resettlement programme in order to put in place a procedure that will enable good practices on the adaptation and integration of refugees into the host society. the aim is to establish a common eu resettlement programme to increase the number of people resettled and improve their situation in the eu through closer cooperation between eu governments. every effort should be made to involve more union countries in the union resettlement programme, which is the starting point for political and practical cooperation between the union countries for the permanent protection of foreigners.

we must avoid serious risks by all means in acceding to the european convention on human rights. we have a major problem with the competition between two tribunals: the one in strasbourg and the european court of justice. the two documents that are causing problems are the charter of fundamental rights and the european convention. it will be very difficult to explain to our citizens which tribunal will be appropriate for their complaints. the number of cases of refusal to deal with a case on the grounds of conflict of jurisdiction and legal basis will therefore increase. there is also a risk that the union's accession to the european convention will restrict respect for the constitutional traditions of the member states which today constitute the general principles of law. in particular, the union's accession to the convention should not be intended to circumvent the binding protocol to the treaty of lisbon, which excludes the unintended effects of the charter of fundamental rights vis-à-vis the united kingdom and poland.

i'd like to return to the subject of today's proceedings. it is worth recalling that africa is a continent where crimes and genocide are very common. the european union cannot be passive in this situation. fortunately, the international criminal court in kampala is becoming increasingly important in the fight against crime. criminals need to know that they will never, anywhere, get away with it. i am therefore one of those who strongly advocate the union's support for the activities of the tribunal. i don't think we can have too many doubts today. i think we need to discuss and think about what we can do to make the kampala tribunal work more efficiently and effectively.
in writing. in the context of the forthcoming negotiations on the accession of the union to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, i would like to draw attention to the aspect of external relations. this is an area which will be particularly marked by the union's accession to the convention. why would you do that? first, let me remind you that under the treaty of lisbon the european court of justice has very limited powers in the field of foreign policy. accession to the convention will partially compensate for these limitations by providing for external judicial review of all aspects of the union's activities. the european parliament and the council will be consulted on the draft budget for the financial year. secondly, it goes without saying that the need to respect human rights is a recurring theme in the union's relations with third countries, including in the ep. accession to the convention will therefore give the union credibility in its human rights dialogue with third countries. the eu has a chance to strengthen the human rights dimension of its foreign and security policy by submitting itself to the scrutiny of the european court of human rights in strasbourg, and thus to promote the idea more effectively in the world... if it takes its own commitments seriously. let's hope that's what happens.
the european union's accession to the convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms is certainly a step in the right direction towards ensuring equal and fair privileges for our citizens. we must ensure that its rules are respected in all the member states. it will also improve legislative coherence between the community and the council of europe countries and increase the number of institutions to which citizens can appeal in the event of a breach of their rights. it will also give greater prominence and credibility to the many initiatives of the european parliament in defence of the fundamental freedoms which belong to every human being. however, it should not be forgotten that, in addition to ensuring that the rights of third-country nationals are respected, the union must first ensure that they are not infringed in the member states.
in writing. when we talk about the european union's accession to the european convention on human rights, we are talking about a decade of work and about many concerns regarding, among other things, competition between the ets and the court of human rights. there will certainly be problems with the case law and the autonomy of the ets. but i think what we've achieved after 10 years is that there's a complementarity between the two systems, so let's move away from that hierarchical thinking. ets has long been following the work of the european court of human rights in strasbourg and vice versa. the two systems coexist and there is no competition between them, and perhaps these fears are unfounded. we need to join the convention for symbolic reasons, but above all, we need the convention because it will complement the human rights system in the european union and give it more credibility in the eyes of its citizens. they will be protected by the european union and its institutions, not just by the member states as they have been so far. yes, so let's be glad that this system is going to be strengthened. but we need a certain amount of loyalty to not question the credibility of this system. we therefore call on the member states not to bring any action against each other when eu law is at stake, using the possibility afforded to them by the convention.

member of the commission. - my first words will be to thank mrs geringer from oedenberg for her question. it's very much at the heart of the current copyright and internet debates. unfortunately, copyright is too often presented as an obstacle to the creation of a digital single market. i don't think that's fair. i don't think that's fair. i know that. copyright allows the creator to sell what he has created, guarantees him a return on investment. this is not only true in the field of cultural creation, which mrs geringer de oedenberg knows so well. this is also true in the field of industry, creation, industrial innovation; a return on investment that allows the creator to then continue to create other works and new content. this business model that underpins copyright has been around for hundreds of years, but rights management has evolved naturally with technology -- radio, television, cable, satellite, and now, the internet. each time, new technologies have led to new business models that have led to a change in the exploitation and commercialisation of copyright. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, rather than proposing radical changes to copyright, i want to protect creation while seeking a legal framework that allows the emergence of new economic models. i announced this at my hearing before you on 13 january, and it is this principle that will guide my action. this is the role which i envisage for the european legislator. the digital agenda that the commission adopted on 19 may, under the dynamic impetus of my colleague and friend neelie kroes, contains my roadmap, including copyright and the internet. and this year, i'm going to take three initiatives in that spirit. firstly, a proposal for a framework directive on collective management of copyright. firstly, it is a question of allowing collective management companies to better organise themselves to offer new internet services, such as tailor-made directories, one-stop-shops. in return, the rules on governance, transparency and supervision of collective management companies should be aligned to allow for more transparent pricing and return of income to members of collective management companies. secondly, a directive on orphan works: the aim is to create the legal certainty needed to support efforts to digitize our cultural heritage. i am thinking of a european definition of orphan works. thirdly, i will present a green paper on audiovisual content and the internet. the challenge here is to analyse the conditions for the emergence of new video-on-demand services in europe. in 2011, we will launch a dialogue with the various stakeholders on the issues that impact the emergence of new value-added content services on the internet to see how to clarify the existing rules. the aim is to see what role technology can play in identifying and monetising digital content, to identify the challenges of the digital press, and to find out how to combat the black economy of the pirated internet more effectively. my method will be simple: i want to be able to listen to the different stakeholders while i propose the movement. i want a europe which allows new economic models to emerge. i have no a priori idea of what kind of intervention will be needed - legislative or otherwise. i have no dogma or illusion either about the possibility of finding one-size-fits-all solutions, but i would like to use this new dynamic of the internal market and the digital agenda, which mario monti has also mentioned in his report, to develop a real economic policy for the cultural sector in europe.

conditions and at depths as in the gulf of mexico, we in the eu must be prepared for the possibility of an accident. we have the appropriate bodies and mechanisms to respond quickly to a possible accident. we have the european maritime safety agency, we have salvage vessels, we have civil protection mechanisms, we have good coordination of aid measures, and our colleague, commissioner georgieva, has therefore offered european aid early on for ongoing action in the gulf of mexico. our goal must be prevention, so that we don't have to deal with the big cleanup after a disaster. i have therefore asked the services, together with my colleague, commissioner potočnik, to review our applicable eu legislation. this european legislation provides the framework for safety and environmental protection measures, both in general and in the event of a specific accident. we are now examining all these laws to see whether they provide the best and most adequate instruments for a disaster of a similar nature, for a worst-case scenario. this is a matter of close cooperation with the national regulatory authorities, because a large part of the safety regulations in the field of promotion and health are in the hands of our member states and not directly with us. of course, a regulatory body does not offer a 100% guarantee. much depends on the attitude and behaviour of the operational sector in our industry. this is why we have every reason to come together: politics and business must work together to ensure that europe's environment and its citizens are as safe as possible. i want to put safety and sustainability in oil and gas production at the center of our stakeholder conversations. that is why i have already invited a high-level panel of the major energy similar accidents near european coasts. we have presented a catalogue of questions to be answered by the companies in the coming days: 12 questions which contain in concrete terms everything that is crucial for safety on the oil and gas platform and for the waters and the coast and the member states. i see this meeting with industry as the beginning of a process which will increase the transparency of industrial operations and encourage compliance with regulations and the application of best practice. we are planning a second meeting in the next few months, when we have a better understanding of the causes of the accident, to assess the situation and to draw the lessons for europe from the accident in the gulf of mexico. at the present time, when the causes and circumstances are still being analysed, it would be premature to draw any definitive conclusions or to call for new legislative initiatives. but if it should turn out that a regulatory response is necessary, then i can assure you that the commission will not hesitate to put forward proposals for european regulations. as you can see, ladies and gentlemen, there is a continuing effort in europe to prevent a similar tragedy in our own neighbourhood. if, however, a similar accident should occur, we have a variety of measures and mechanisms to respond effectively without delay and to minimise the impact on the citizens and the environment in europe. i shall be glad to tell you again what we have planned after the next meeting.
on behalf of the ppe group. the explosion of a platform in the gulf of mexico is the largest environmental disaster of its kind in history. every day, 800,000 liters of oil enter the gulf, and more than 22 million have leaked since the disaster began. the oil platform now covers over 17,000 square miles [43,000 sq km], more than the land area of the netherlands. at such a time, it is our duty to in writing. 56 000 sick eu citizens are waiting for a transplant, including 2 000 in poland. 12 people die every day from lack of organs for transplant. donation and transplantation rates range from less than 1 in bulgaria to 34-35 donors per million in spain. in poland, the rate is 11. most organs are harvested from the dead on the basis of consent (opt-in) or presumption of consent (opt-out). in poland, the removal of cells, tissues and organs from human cadavers is allowed if the deceased person did not register in the central register of objections during his lifetime. the development of transplantation requires the creation of an atmosphere of social approval for the completion of wills, allowing for the removal of organs after death, and the condemnation of objections. i am personally actively involved in the promotion of transplantation and i encourage all my fellow members of parliament to do so. in poland, i distributed stamps and bracelets to encourage the use of transplant medicine. with colleagues from other political groups, i was launching a nationwide social action "chain of relatives" to promote transplantation and honorary blood donation. promoting transplantation and coordinating the exchange of experience across borders could save thousands of lives. it is necessary to establish a common union database of organs intended for donation and transplantation and a database of all living and deceased donors. it would also be an important tool in the fight against organ trafficking and human trafficking.

the debate on europe 2020 must take account of the experience of the previous strategy. we all know that the failures that followed were due, firstly, to the fact that this strategy was based on the responsibility of the individual countries in the method of open coordination, and the successes were due, among other things, to the fact that it was lisbonised, that is to say that certain lisbon objectives were incorporated into cohesion policy. the question therefore arises as to how to approach the new strategy. it seems absolutely crucial at this point to first make it clear that we are dealing with so-called treaty policies, which are not policies designed for strategic purposes but function in the longer term, as for example cohesion policy. the idea is to integrate policies into the strategy, and the strategy, as previous experience has shown, will only succeed if the policies are integrated. any kind of action that separates policies, that separates funds, that separates actions, will end up with the same failure as the previous strategy. therefore, we need to connect, integrate and create synergies.

in writing. in the context of the debate on the effective use of all the european union's research and innovation funds, the issue of adequate promotion of innovative solutions emerging in individual member states should be raised. it is often the case that, because of the poor flow of information, investment is made in research projects that have already been carried out by scientists in one of the countries. this is a waste of eu money which we cannot afford in a time of economic crisis. more emphasis should be placed on improving communication and supporting the purchase of existing new technologies within the european union, which will also allow additional financial support for innovative enterprises. it is also important to finance soft projects such as training and dissemination of knowledge on the importance of innovation for economic growth, better information on available programmes to local actors, and flexibility in the definition of the conditions for granting support, so that countries with currently low levels of innovation can contribute to the european union's competitive advantage on a global scale by developing this sector. it is also necessary to create incentives for investment in local research centres. small and medium-sized enterprises cannot afford them, while large multinational companies do not want to use them, thus deepening the innovation disparities between the eu member states.

this report is consistent with the important objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. i would remind you that in 10 years' time the number of people with higher education is to increase by 10% (from 30% to 40%) and the member states' expenditure on research and development is to increase by 3%. the recipients and implementers of these tasks will be mainly universities. so we should really look at these mechanisms that have worked best in the world. i'm talking about the american partnership solutions: business and universities, how to market all the research results so that often the great scientific achievements don't just sit on the shelves, but are put into practice, and therefore into business. another issue is to effectively implement scholarships and to bring companies into the system. the doctorates should be strongly supported, the european social fund should be used and existing programmes such as marie curie should be used. how can we create clear public partnership schemes, particularly in the areas of technology parks and business incubators? how to get involved in small and medium-sized enterprises, including students? all these things are very important. i think it's important to also invest not only in the technological space, which is important, but also in the humanities system, which should also have its scope of cooperation with public elements and with business. one last note: china today has as many students as the entire european union. so talking about common goals is our common task, and i think that business participation in dialogue will be an effective solution to win the global competition.
the commission's university-enterprise forum, which strengthens cooperation between universities and enterprises to help universities build partnerships that harness scientific and technological knowledge, is the right solution if we want to make europe's economy dynamic and truly competitive. however, i would like to mention a few shortcomings in the commission's proposal. some of the recommendations are too general and leave too much room for interpretation, e.g. the use of the term 'university' for all higher education institutions irrespective of their status. there are no research instruments to identify skills shortages in the labour market. nor is there any education or training system that can reduce these shortcomings. the special situation of those without a university education is not taken into account in the lifelong learning programme. in conclusion, the direction taken towards closer cooperation between universities and enterprises seems to meet the current needs of the market. however, the most important tasks are those of the member states, which must ensure that the ideas proposed are effectively implemented if the intended objectives are to be achieved. (laughter) (applause)
research, scientific advancement, and the education of students are the main tasks of higher education. the lisbon strategy's priorities are, in short, the knowledge-based economy, innovation and research. even if we are not satisfied with the results of this strategy, the objectives set out therein are still valid. what are the forms of achieving the above objectives and objectives? first, cooperation between universities and the economy, specific companies, funding of research, internships by business. secondly, exchange of students, researchers between universities in different countries, increase of funds for scholarships. thirdly, the financing of student traineeships and research contracts by employers. fourthly, the mobility of these people is essential for the full use of the people who are trained. fifthly, the development of research centres in the economic field. and so in closing, i would like to say that the best investment is to invest in the education of the younger generation, which is lifelong learning.
in writing. the dialogue between academia and business aimed at modernising europe's universities should take account of their current state, adapted to the bologna system and the economic challenges of innovation. the bologna system allows considerable flexibility in the profile of the specialist, who at the engineering (bachelor) stage is practically prepared for the profession, at the master's stage can flexibly approach interdisciplinary knowledge of the economy in the developing world, and at the stage of the doctoral thesis introduces innovative solutions. conservative education institutions are putting people into the market who are not fit for the innovation economy. therefore, curricula must be continuously adjusted and coordinated to meet the needs of the different economic sectors. the university's activities are brought closer to the needs of industry by lectures on entrepreneurship and intellectual property. it is useful that theses and doctoral dissertations respond to the requirements of the economy or are directly generated by its needs. this is the best pretext for dialogue between the two worlds of science and business. the likelihood of innovation success could be further shaped if the practical part of this work was carried out directly at the site of its eventual implementation. an important element of university cooperation with the economy is student internships, which are currently reluctant to be organised due to the cost. in turn, universities should provide postgraduate studies on the latest scientific and technical developments for industry.

the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? it is an honour to present to you today the mandate for our trilateral negotiations with the european commission and the council, which are due to take place on 30 june. before i go on to present the mandate itself adopted by the committee on budgets, and which i hope will be adopted in our vote in plenary tomorrow, i would like to say a few words about the 2011 budget year because of its particularity. this will be a pioneering year, because the budget of the european union for 2011 will be the first budget adopted under the new provisions of the lisbon treaty. the lisbon treaty strengthens the powers of the european parliament and extends our co-decision powers on the eu budget to areas where we could not previously co-decide fully, such as agriculture. it's a big change in quality. the lisbon treaty also introduces far-reaching procedural changes, notably the abrogation of the first and second readings. we as the european parliament will have one single reading of the budget, just as the council will only read the budget once. what does that mean, practically? this means that we will probably meet again at the conciliation meeting in november, but above all that the new budgetary procedure under the lisbon treaty will require more discipline and greater restraint from all the parties concerned. we won't get a second chance, we won't get a chance to negotiate again. we as the european parliament must think carefully in advance about what we really want to achieve, because we cannot do as we have done in previous years, where we have raised our expectations and lowered them during the second reading. we have to think carefully, even in the first reading, about what we really want to achieve. i would like to thank the rapporteurs for the various committees for their contributions. the committee on budgets has received some very interesting and important opinions from the various thematic committees, which will certainly be taken into account in the next parts of the budgetary procedure. these thanks are primarily personal. i have to thank the authors and tell them that i have learned a lot about the priorities of their respective committees and that this knowledge will hopefully help me a lot as your rapporteur in the autumn when negotiating with the european commission and the council. at the same time, many of these specific requests from the various thematic committees could not be taken into account in my report, which came from the committee on budgets, because the mandate for the tripartite negotiations (those in june) could not be extended. we need to focus on a few key issues, and we can work out the details in september as we go through the amendment process. we can't go into that level of detail in these first negotiations. so please understand that i was against many of the amendments. i would now like to say a few words about these priorities which are the key to our negotiations at the end of june and about the most important issues which i would like to see you support in the vote tomorrow as the issues which the european parliament will put forward. first of all, i would like to mention the most important thing in the first talks with the commission and the council: the current multiannual financial perspective is running out. what was agreed in 2006 is slowly becoming insufficient for the new priorities. we have two parallel, but at the same time, slightly opposite processes. on the one hand, the european union's growing ambitions under the lisbon treaty and our expectations of the european union, such as the establishment of eu diplomacy, ambitious research projects, and on the other hand, the process of economic and financial crisis in individual member states, which is forcing savings. these two opposing processes also face the constraints of the multiannual financial perspective. the margins are running out, on behalf of the s&d group. today we have almost a year of work with two presidencies, fortunately under the same good leadership of mr marinescu, on a draft regulation which would really change the face of rail transport. i wanted to highlight two key things. firstly, we are concerned with competitive rail freight transport. secondly, we want the regulation to have some added value. my group sees this as an opportunity for added value in that we are going to start to create elements of a european railway area, something like the european single rail market, so that we can move from national rail systems to a european system. the basic provisions and solutions that led us to endorse it are, firstly, the one-stop shop as a convenient concept for the customer. secondly, we want to create nine corridors in the continental system, which for the first time is a chance to cross national borders, including all the countries concerned. and thirdly, we're talking about the opportunity to increase interoperability. what is the source of the railway disaster? very low interoperability. fourthly, we have created the conditions for identifying strategic investment needs within five years. finally, there should be a timetable, so that we do not put it off indefinitely, and there should be an institutionally unified way of managing each transport corridor. these are the points that have led us to support and perhaps they will be promising if these pessimistic assessments of mr grosch are not fulfilled, that is if the railway wants to be a business and an industry.
madam president! analysis of the european parliament and council regulation on a rail network for competitive freight transport shows how challenging it was to reach agreement on such a difficult and politically charged issue. unfortunately, however, there are still provisions in that regulation which are controversial to me, both in terms of the competitiveness of rail transport and the independence of the management of the railway infrastructure manager. i refer to those provisions, in particular the new paragraph of article 12, which confer the right to grant capacity to a corridor 'one-stop shop', thereby infringing the exclusive right of the manager in that regard and limiting his independence. i also find the proposal in paragraph 3 to have the manager inform the applicant of the allocation of other works to a 'full service point' which will reply to the applicant very controversial. the possibility of submitting a negative response via a 'full service' point will undoubtedly bureaucratize and delay the train route allocation process, while reducing the flexibility to respond to the changing needs of carriers. this can clearly undermine the competitiveness of rail transport. the provisions of paragraph 4 are also highly questionable, since they infringe the principle of commercial confidentiality, which, instead of ensuring transparency in the operation of the 'one stop shop', may become a tool for combating competition through the use of unfair practices.
