the harmonization of labelling and mutual recognition of foodstuffs is of great importance for the internal market. currently, additional national rules and different interpretations of existing community rules on food products by individual member states are a source of obstacles to trade, the flow of goods and competition problems. i am concerned about the provisions on the obligation to provide information on the country of origin of products of specific categories. in my view, this is an expression of the protectionist attitudes of the member states, which is contrary to the idea of a common market eliminating significant barriers and obstacles to the movement of goods. therefore, in the interests of consumers, i believe that information on the country of origin of products should be provided on a voluntary basis and in cases where the lack of such information could mislead the consumer as to the actual origin of the product. i believe that this approach is balanced between the interests of consumers and the interests of food producers. during the debate on the commission regulation and the rapporteur's report, the issue of a balanced diet and nutritional habits of the european union's population was raised on several occasions. in my view, food labelling is just one of many aspects of informing consumers about good nutrition. it can complement public knowledge on healthy lifestyles, for example through campaigns and educational activities, but it cannot replace it. i am therefore opposed to the introduction of colour labelling which could have a lasting impact on food habits. finally, it is not possible and not permitted in our social order to introduce rules under which citizens are not held accountable for their own conduct and choices.

mr. chairman, please! i would like to begin by thanking mrs hautala for her report, which is both detailed and comprehensive. i agree that the european union's position as the protector of human rights defenders in the world is closely linked to its internal principle of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. i therefore support the points made in the report on the appointment of local liaison officers in these european missions. i also agree with the recommendations on the assessment of the human rights situation in third countries. the human rights assessment is essential for countries that engage in trade relations with the european union. the importance of sanctions against third countries that commit serious human rights violations should be addressed with greater determination.
in writing. the protection and promotion of human rights is a priority for the european union. the situation is still far from perfect, but the community is not giving up in its fight to uphold human rights worldwide. the eu has a long history of supporting the development of the region. the list of countries with which the eu discusses human rights issues is unfortunately impressive. in 2007, the european instrument for democracy and human rights (eidhr) was established to fund projects led by civil society to promote the rule of law and democracy. for example, the eidhr has supported the reform of the electoral system in chad with €5 million. as you can imagine, eu action in this area is most effective with regard to the candidate countries. for example, many positive developments have been noted in croatia and turkey. the former has ratified the most important international conventions and cooperates with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. turkey, on the other hand, is beginning to put more emphasis on tackling its traditional problems, such as child labour. these actions should not obscure the fact that even greater efforts are needed to promote human rights. the current tragic situation in kyrgyzstan is a sad illustration of this.
in writing. the european union and its institutions are at every turn reminding people of their commitment to human rights around the world. the legal provisions in this area are present in all treaties and other strategic documents. i wholeheartedly support all the initiatives mentioned in mrs hautala's report. however, i would like to express my unequivocal opposition to the european parliament's lack of action in relation to the current situation of the polish minority in lithuania. first, it is a case of the lithuanian central commission for professional ethics, which opened an investigation against the lithuanian mp waldemar tomaszewski, who stood up in defense of poles living in lithuania and drew attention to the fact that the country does not comply with international conventions on the protection of the rights of national minorities, especially in the area of language rights. how long will parliament allow its members to keep their mouths shut? another issue is the current actions of the lithuanian parliament in the field of the education act, aimed at limiting the teaching of polish in polish schools in lithuania. will parliament wait until they are eliminated?
in writing. human rights defenders around the world play a vital role in protecting and promoting fundamental rights through their daily engagement, often at the risk of their own lives. support for human rights defenders has long been an element of the european union's human rights policy in its external relations. this issue is now becoming more relevant in the light of articles 3 and 21 of the lisbon treaty, which place the promotion and protection of human rights at the heart of the european union's external action. in this context, one of the priorities must be the promotion of human rights as a core value and objective of the union's foreign policy. the structure and human resources of the european external action service currently being established should reflect adequately the monitoring, promotion and support of human rights. i consider the support, protection and safety of human rights defenders to be a very important element of the eu's strategy in this regard. these issues should be prioritised in the eu's relations with third countries and taken into account at all levels and in all union foreign policy instruments in order to enhance the effectiveness and credibility of the eu's action in this area. i therefore ask the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy to implement the human rights clause effectively in international agreements and partnerships and to establish a genuine mechanism to enforce this clause.

member of the commission. − mr president, indeed the floods in central europe are a very dramatic reminder of our vulnerability to natural disasters, and actually, as we speak in this chamber tonight, flash floods in the south of france have so far taken the lives of 19 people. so disasters are not confined to the areas which are this evening’s subject matter (poland, the czech republic, slovakia and hungary). floods this year have also been hitting hard in the country where we are meeting tonight. we are all aware that natural disasters are on the rise as climate change leads to more extreme weather events, and when faced with disasters of this magnitude the national capacity to respond is simply overwhelmed. in such cases european solidarity makes a difference in saving and protecting both lives and critical infrastructure. these floods we are discussing this evening have underlined the added value of a coordinated eu response. let me take us back to the beginning of the floods in poland, hungary, the czech republic and slovakia. very heavy rainfall and severe flooding affected the basins of the vistula, oder and warta rivers in the first half of may. on thursday 19 may poland asked for assistance – specifically they asked for high-capacity pumps – through the eu civil protection mechanism, which i am responsible for. the eu response to this request was swift and generous, with eight member states providing exactly what was needed – germany, the czech republic, france, denmark, and the netherlands delivered within hours high-capacity pumps and technical expertise. an eu cofinanced multinational module developed by estonia, latvia and lithuania under the preparatory action for an eu rapid response capability, which this parliament promoted, was also deployed. in total over 55 pumps, 22 expert teams and 300 rescuers were deployed plus one liaison officer from the monitoring and information centre in the commission. six days later, hungary, which had also been hit by severe flooding, requested sand-bags to reinforce its flood containment capacity. the eu civil protection mechanism managed to secure more than three million sand-bags from slovenia, romania, the netherlands, bulgaria, germany, the czech republic, norway, slovakia and croatia. as we speak, floods and their consequences have not yet abated. rains continue to affect part of central europe. a flash flood hit france yesterday and today. we are waiting for a second-wave flood to affect the south of poland, where nine european teams are still on the ground. the situation in hungary is gradually improving. we are in daily contact with the member states, monitoring the situation constantly and ready upon request to mobilise extra eu expertise. beyond these emergency measures, the eu solidarity fund could also be mobilised to cover certain expenditures linked to repairs and recovery, and the commission is already cooperating with the affected countries, giving them guidance in preparing applications. the floods have proven the value of the civil protection mechanism as a platform for real-time information dissemination and response coordination. this mechanism, as you recall, was also triggered for haiti and for the oil spill in the gulf of mexico, and clearly shows the potential of this instrument. by the end of this year, the commission will adopt a communication on the reinforcement of the eu’s disaster response capacity. it will look at the response to various types of disasters within the eu as well as outside the eu. one key issue will be improving the mobilisation of the eu’s in-kind assistance. most – not all – but most of this assistance is already channelled through the commission’s monitoring and information centre (mic). the system ensures that real needs are being met and that duplication is avoided. but it is based on ad hoc offers, and because of this it is simply not possible to guarantee that the right assistance will be available. so disaster hits and we pray that it won’t hit in so many member states that we will be faced with inability to meet demands. we propose to address this by developing reference scenarios for major types of disasters so that we can anticipate the type of help that will be needed, and by mapping out the available assets in the member states for use when disaster strikes. and we will aim to find agreement with member states on a voluntary pool of key assets that can be put on stand-by for immediate deployment. to develop these ideas, we are engaging in a wide-ranging consultation and we will continue to do so with the parliament, member states and other stakeholders. the recent floods are also a reminder that the eu and its member states need to step up work on disaster prevention. this is a good moment for the affected countries to reinforce their knowledge of flood risks, to draw up risk assessments and maps, to prepare flood risk management plans, and to take all the steps necessary for effective implementation of the floods directive. the increased frequency and intensity of disasters in europe should also provide a further incentive for member states to invest in preparedness and build up their capacity. eu solidarity has to go hand in hand with national responsibility, and preparedness will be part of the proposals the commission will put forward. so let me conclude, mr president, by saying that we all recognise that emergency situations have massive human, economic and environmental cost. with the frequency and intensity of disasters on the rise, european citizens expect us to be effective in addressing them both inside and outside the eu. we have identified disaster management as a priority, and i am personally committed to bringing forward proposals to strengthen the european disaster-response capacity. i would like to thank parliament for its interest and support. you have been a very strong factor in developing the capacities i reported on, and i do hope you will continue to play this critical role of driving us towards a better response capacity in the future.

on behalf of the s&d group. the recent floods in central europe and the one in france have shown the immensity and unpredictability of natural disasters. the european parliament resolution, expressing its sympathy for the victims of the floods and all those affected, primarily obliges the european commission to provide assistance under the solidarity fund quickly and efficiently. the resolution also recalls the legal measures needed to limit the negative effects of flooding in the future. in simple terms, it is about the proper implementation of the so-called flood directive, which requires member states to set up a flood risk management system with a preliminary risk assessment and the identification of areas where there is a high or likely flood risk. the directive requires states to draw up flood hazard maps and flood risk management plans. as regards the situation in poland, i would like to point out that before this year's floods, environmental ngos repeatedly drew attention to the incorrect implementation of the flood directive in the polish legal order, and in particular to the lack of an appropriate flood inventory system and their unclear legal status. i would therefore like to draw the attention of the european commission to the need to enforce eu flood law effectively, so that poland and other community countries do not have to apply for eu funds from the solidarity fund in the future.

member of the commission. − mr president, on behalf of the commission, i thank you for the question that has been put to us. i am very pleased to engage in dialogue on this question with the european parliament. the commission is working at improving access to european judicial training, not only for judges and prosecutors, but also for all other legal professions. we consider contacts with all networks and representative organisations to be of the utmost importance. member states are also of major importance since they have the overall responsibility for training of judges, prosecutors and court staff. the commission is currently assessing what financial means would be necessary to implement european judicial training and exchanges on a larger scale and some proposals could be presented, or actually are going to be presented, for the new financial perspective. in the mean time it is important to do more and better with the available means, with what we have now. we have already taken steps to ensure that european judicial training is better taken into consideration in the 2011 financial programmes. however, i would like to underline that, for several years, stakeholders have been encouraged to present more training projects in response to calls for proposals, but results have been disappointing: only a limited number of good quality projects on judicial training were received and the commission regrets in particular that very few quality projects have been presented on training of court staff, bailiffs, notaries or legal interpreters. the commission services are already working on developing proof of concept projects for exchanges between legal practitioners. we are not developing any pilot project this year under article 49(6)a of the financial regulation. feasibility studies are necessary to help the commission define which features should be common to all legal professions and which ones should take into consideration organisational aspects specific to one particular legal profession. to develop a common judicial culture, the commission is keen to encourage european networks, stakeholders and member states to organise common activities on comparative law and approximation of law, which might eventually come under the umbrella of a european law institute, as indicated in the commission’s action plan. contacts with stakeholders have shown that there is a need to better structure european judicial training and they have framed a number of questions that the commission is focused on now. questions like the following: what type of activities are we talking about when we consider european judicial training? what tools do we have to assess the impact training has at european level? how do we assess the level of quality? how can we reuse good practices, and transfer know-how? how can we allow legal practioners to be trained not only in eu law or comparative law, but also in the skills necessary to work in a european area of justice, such as knowledge of other languages, understanding of cross-border banking and similar issues? how can we achieve a european training scheme which focuses on the needs of our citizens? we would like to use the feedback from european judicial training activities to assess the quality of eu legislation, in our ongoing efforts for better regulation. these are some of the aspects on which the commission is working and they will be the basis of the communication the commission will be presenting in 2011. and in this communication there will of course be a funding proposal and the commission has a higher level of ambition with regard to funding than we currently have available. we welcome opportunities to further discuss european judicial training and will engage with parliament on this important matter.

mr president, fiscal and financial reforms – pivotal as they are – are not a substitute for structural change and competitive growth policies. that is why, firstly, i would like to address briefly the role of cohesion policy in the delivery mechanism of the eu 2020. in its conclusions, the council sent us a clear message to integrate cohesion policy in the implementation of the eu 2020. after all, according to the recent march communication from the european commission, this policy area was the only truly successful strand in the delivery of the lisbon strategy. why? because, it sets out binding guidelines or conditions for the transfer of european resources to a member state, region or city. it also gives member states and regions the scope to translate common european objectives into their own reality. it is efficiently adapted to monitor and support the achievement of goals; and last but not least, it has an efficient sanctions mechanism. on economic governance, i strongly support the idea of going beyond fiscal surveillance towards the competitiveness-related factors which generate or contribute to imbalances. i also believe we should state today – clearly, urgently and loudly – why fiscal surveillance did not work and why the stability and growth pact did not deliver. continuing to rely exclusively on decentralised fiscal discipline might give us ‘better’ european governance but it will not give us ‘good’ european governance.

of areas of community activity. the report 'the european union strategy for the baltic sea region and the role of macro-regions in future cohesion policy' highlights the cooperation of the regions to achieve objectives across a range of policies, including transport, fisheries, energy, agriculture and research. this ambitious plan was made possible in 2004 when eight of the nine baltic states joined the european union. the priority areas for cooperation within the macro-region are transport policy and environmental protection. they are linked by the need to equalise infrastructure standards and by the fact that they perfectly reflect the structure of interdependence of the member states that is characteristic of this approach. in the baltic area, effective action to combat pollution and ecosystem damage cannot be achieved without integrated action by each of the countries bordering the region. secondly, cooperation within the macro-region is undoubtedly beneficial and macro-region. this in turn will be of vital importance for the development of the european union as a whole, for which a stronger position and a more stable economic situation are of undeniable strategic importance. thirdly, we must not forget the social objectives. the creation of conditions for the well-being of citizens, the integration of cultural, educational and tourist elements into promoted. the european union strategy for the pioneering pilot baltic sea macro-region is now an important reference point in the debate on the future of cohesion policy after 2013. currently, projects implemented under the strategy benefit from the funds under the said policy. however, given their multisectoral nature, today's debate should be directed towards the near future, with a view protection of existing activities. this will enable the medium-term analysis of the strategy's implementation to serve as a reference point for future such projects. the key questions to be answered developing. they all have the opportunity to focus across borders on issues of importance to territorial cohesion, i.e. to put into practice the idea of integration that the european union has promoted from the beginning. the creation of functional regions that share the same objectives also has the potential to increase the effectiveness of regional policy. ladies and gentlemen! the baltic in writing. at the beginning of my speech, i would like to thank mr olejniczak for his report on the strategy for the baltic sea region the first eu macro-region, which defines this multifunctional area of cooperation and focuses on common development goals and challenges or trends for future macro-regional policy. it also aims to develop a specific roadmap for the next macro-regional strategies. the baltic sea region is characterised by extensive, multi-level cooperation in the fields of economics, environmental protection and broadly defined social development. the countries in the area share many common challenges and, while remaining independent, they strengthen the implementation of the european union's strategy for the baltic sea region. despite its rather general tone, the report defines many common objectives and recommendations necessary for the successful implementation of the strategy, namely the establishment of a good platform for cooperation, effective coordination and a management system. however, financial resources are needed to successfully meet all these challenges. and those are missing. 8 eu countries and russia are beneficiaries of the strategy. let's not let the unresolved issue of funding the strategy stand in the way of developing and perfecting this ambitious, transnational initiative.
the union's primary objective is to overcome the economic crisis. this is primarily to tackle the structural problems created by the crisis, especially in terms of competitiveness and employment. the european commission has put forward the following proposals to bring about economic recovery at national and regional level: support for enterprises, increase knowledge and innovation, increase flexibility in cohesion programmes. therefore, investment should be accelerated and the implementation of cohesion policy programmes simplified and made more flexible. smart investment should be at the heart of cohesion policy programmes. the union as a whole must be further integrated, the solidarity of the union and its common market must be strengthened, and the action of individual states must not be limited to their own particular interests. the european union must focus on creating durable mechanisms that guarantee protection against the negative effects of the economic crisis.

in writing. the recently concluded spanish presidency of the council of the european union was, for at least a few reasons, one of the most important of the past decade. first, spain had to face the difficult task of 'testing' the changes introduced by the lisbon treaty. these changes were implemented efficiently, although the madrid government did not know until almost the beginning of the presidency on which treaty the eu's agenda would be based. second, spain has faced the worst financial crisis in the history of the euro. i would remind all those who are sceptical about the recently concluded presidency that the spanish government was one of the first to correctly assess the scale of the crisis and to call for effective measures to be taken, including sanctions for exceeding the budget deficit ceiling. thirdly, the spanish presidency should be commended for its enormous contribution to the work on the swift negotiations and the shape of the european external action service. thanks to madrid's seemingly unremarkable work, an agreement in both areas is now within reach. the balance of the spanish presidency of the council of the european union can certainly be considered positive. i hope that the belgian presidency, which has just begun, will maintain the pace of work and follow the path set by the madrid government.
in writing. - i congratulate the spanish presidency on the six months it has held the presidency of the union. it was a difficult and meaningful presidency. difficult, because it is the first since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon to appoint the president of the european council and the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. the presidency's programme was based on the old treaty, as the fate of the lisbon treaty was 'uncertain' during the preparatory phase. the greek crisis has slowed the implementation of the presidency's objectives. the delay in approving the new composition of the european commission (february 2010) and the consequent delay in adopting its legislative work programme was a hindrance. the presidency was significant: (a) institutionally, as it set out certain rules of conduct within the institutions with the adoption of the new treaty; (b) prospectively, as it set out the union's course of action for the next 10 years with the adoption of the 2020 strategy. the most important achievements of the socialist government of prime minister zapatero are: (a) the adoption of the action plan implementing the provisions of the stockholm programme (cooperation in the field of home affairs and justice); (b) the commitment of the presidency to combat violence against women; (c) the adoption by the council (3-4 june 2010) of the negotiating mandate for eu accession to the european convention on human rights and fundamental freedoms; (d) the launch of the committee on internal security (cosi); (e) the adoption of the draft regulation of the ep and the council laying down the procedures and conditions required for the submission of a citizens' initiative.
in writing. − very often in the ep we take action to defend fundamental rights and civil liberties around the world. the ep awards the sakharov prize to individuals who have made outstanding contributions to the defence of civil and minority rights. meanwhile, in the eu, these rights are also being violated. this is mainly the case for national minorities. some member states, i mean the lithuanian state, are making a mockery of the council of europe's framework convention on human rights. waldemar tomaszewski, mep, is being held accountable by the lithuanian parliament for defending the rights of minorities in lithuania in the ep. this is a shameful, unacceptable and scandalous situation. i call on the ep's human rights committee, on the european commission, to raise the level of the european union's standards on fundamental rights, freedoms and the rights of national minorities and to enforce them effectively.
in writing. - the case of deputy waldemar tomaszewski consists of two problems. the first is the situation of the polish minority in lithuania, whose rights are being raised by mr tomaszewski. the second is a causal consequence of the first, but only apparently. the central commission for professional ethics of the republic of lithuania imposed a 'public warning' on waldemar tomaszewski under the lithuanian code of conduct for state-level politicians. a situation in which a member is 'forgotten' by a public institution of a given country because of words he has spoken in the course of his mandate is unacceptable. the fact that it is a matter of public defence of a national minority does not change the situation. it only makes her more upsetting. that's why i decided to support waldemar tomaszewski's motion to invoke immunity and privilege.
in writing. - i congratulate the rapporteur on a very well-prepared report. i voted in favour of the report on the european union strategy for the baltic sea region and the role of the macro-regions in future cohesion policy. the document addresses several sensitive issues: the environment, energy and the external dimension. in my view, one of the most important challenges for the baltic sea region is to create an efficient network of different modes of transport. i am pleased that my amendment to the final version of the document, which emphasises the importance of the central european transport corridor, has been included. the development of transport networks and the provision of adequate access to infrastructure for all regions are the guarantee of the real cohesion of the european union.
in writing. − one of the eu institutions' tasks is to stand with citizens in their conflicts with profit-maximising business. this often goes against the rights of the disabled. they face frequent discrimination when they try to be mobile, when they want to use transport services. i consider the ban on discrimination on grounds of disability in bus and coach transport to be a major step forward in the fight for the right of disabled people to participate equally in society. compensation for cancelled or delayed flights, as they are known in the air transport sector, is also an important element of the regulation which is to regulate coach and bus services. they should be the standard for all types of transport services, as they show respect for passengers. i also feel the same way about legislation that forces transport companies to pay compensation to accident victims for both personal injury and damaged luggage. these are steps in the right direction, as they strengthen the position of citizens in their relations with transport companies. taking into account the above provisions, i have decided to vote in favour of the recommendation for second reading on the council's position at first reading on the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on passenger rights in bus and coach transport and amending regulation (ec) no 2006/2004.
in writing. - i voted for the final report. i have serious reservations about the outcome of the vote on amendment no 6 tabled by the ppe group. the essence of the original text was that unused cohesion fund funds could be invested for transport investment purposes. this is justified by the investment needs of the beneficiary countries, as is very well shown by the example of poland. in addition, we expected about eur 23 billion for ten-t, and we received three times less. amendment 6 does not provide for any additional transportation measures, it maintains the status of non-use in the intended uses. instead of a more flexible fund, we got a conservative one. i want to thank my colleagues who voted to reject amendment no. 6.
in writing. - i welcome the results of today's vote. the rapporteur, mathieu grosch, proposed very ambitious targets to be achieved by 2020. among other things, he advocated increased road safety, a 40% reduction in fatalities, a 20% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions from road transport, and a doubling of the number of passengers on buses, trams, and railways. i agree with the overall message of the document: it is necessary to create a balanced and coherent vision of the future of transport as a sector that forms the basis of the internal market, which would guarantee the free movement of people and goods and ensure territorial cohesion throughout the european union. however, i could not agree to one of the rapporteur's proposals. i was a little skeptical about the idea of a transportation fund. this could lead to a future departure from the current system of allocation of the structural funds and the cohesion fund.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the report by mr carlos iturgaiz on the deliberations of the committee on petitions during 2009. even though the report was mostly technical in nature, i believe it touched on some important issues that should be addressed in the future. according to the report, 46% of submitted petitions in 2009 were deemed inadmissible. this is far too high a number. as such, i strongly support the report’s recommendation for improving the information available to the citizens through the petitions web page on the ep portal. petitions are important because they give the european parliament a means to connect with its constituencies and vice versa. it is vital that citizens understand what specific issues petitions deal with and, subsequently, what courses of actions are available to them.
in writing. - the crisis has hit the new entrants to the labour market hardest. i have no doubt that youth unemployment is one of the eu's biggest problems today. even if young people do get a job, they very often work on the basis of so-called 'junk' employment contracts. there is also a lot of excitement about internships. on the one hand, they play a very positive role, enabling young people to acquire important practical skills. on the other hand, they often lead to a situation where work that should be done by a full-time employee is done for free by an intern. in some companies in poland, the rule is that each well-paid specialist can be replaced by a finite number of free trainees. this approach is not good for the labour market, much less for the position of workers. i welcome the fact that the ep has taken up this issue and has developed a number of solutions to improve the position of young workers. in supporting them, i decided to vote for the report on promoting access for young people to the labour market and improving the status of trainees and apprentices.

president of the commission. − mr president, i will try to respond to some of the concrete questions. first of all, to corien wortmann-kool, thank you for your support. in fact we believe this will enhance the credibility of our stability and growth pact, but also of the euro and of the european project as a whole, and we believe that parliament should be closely associated with all these efforts. at the last european council, when president buzek was there, i made a point that parliament should be kept fully informed of progress in the discussions on the future economic governance of europe. i think that some of the concerns expressed by mr hughes and mr bisky should be considered, but in fact i believe that our proposal does consider your concerns because in this proposal we are saying something new: that the stability and growth pact is not everything, that we are linking analysis of the implementation of the measures in the framework of the stability and growth pact with macroeconomic imbalances, with the problems of divergences in competitiveness. so, in fact, what we are proposing is a holistic approach that does not look only to the macroeconomic aspects but also to growth, as guy verhofstadt was suggesting, that looks also to innovation, to the reforms. that is precisely our goal with youth 2020. and yes, mr verhofstadt, as you rightly mention, we are concerned now with the internal market and we are working on this taking the report presented by mario monti – a report i have asked him to present – as a basis and commissioner barnier will come in the fall with some very important proposals, a single market act in fact to address this issue. so our proposal is not only about prudence in macroeconomic aspects. today we are discussing economic governance, so it is natural that we look at what did not go well, but i want to underline this point – this is not just about macroeconomic prudence: it is also about growth and about our reform agenda. what is new here is that now, for the first time – if, of course, this plan can in the end be agreed – we have this comprehensive approach, trying to look at all the aspects. you will remember that, when i presented the europe 2020 strategy some months ago, in some quarters in europe some people were saying ‘no, you cannot link it to the stability and growth pact because it may weaken the stability and growth pact’. i think that everybody agrees now that discussing the macroeconomic constraints without discussing structural reform, and without considering competitiveness, makes no sense. that is why i also do not agree with the idea that our approach is not balanced. in youth 2020 we were fighting for targets such as reduction of poverty, education, and employment to be included. so it is, in fact, a very balanced approach, one in which we try to combine all the economic policy instruments, to have a european dimension and a national dimension and to have, at the madam president, the current crisis has taught us that when a european bank runs into trouble its problems can spill across borders. an eu-wide system of financial supervision is being established to deal with the prevention of such situations; while an integrated european framework for cross-border crisis management will hopefully compliment the supervisory architecture as soon as possible. the last two years have proven that relying on national approaches to cope with crises is clearly a sub-optimal solution. the new system will have to be developed in such a way that a crisis can be handled cost-effectively, moral hazards eliminated and taxpayer finance bailouts excluded. asset transfers will have to be regulated in a manner that ensures a level playing field, especially for host countries. the cross-border crisis management system – based on 28 regime concepts – should be designed in a way that would eliminate the interdependence between banks and national budgets. it should also contribute to the emergence of a single banking market of the union. after all, if we had a single banking market in europe we would not have to talk about cross-border crisis management. last but not least, let me emphasise that all the elements of the european financial stability framework, as well as the resolution regime for cross-border institutions, should be adopted urgently to reduce uncertainty and fragilities in the banking sector. having a european mechanism in place would also allow europe to be more effective in ensuring that global solutions materialise quickly.

member of the commission. − accession of the european union to the european convention on the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms will not affect the manner in which a judgment of the european court of human rights against an eu member state is executed by that member state. that means that the accession agreement can only create obligations on the basis of the convention and, where applicable, of any additional protocol of the convention which the union might ratify insofar as it concerns acts and measures adopted by the institutions, bodies, officers or agencies of the union but not when it concerns acts and measures adopted by the member states. there are no plans to introduce any eu mechanism for monitoring the implementation of such rulings, since there is no legal basis for doing so. indeed protocol no 8 to the lisbon treaty states that accession will ‘not affect the competences of the union or the powers of its institutions’ or ‘the situation of member states in relation to the european convention’. this relates not only to the scope of the substantive obligations of member states, but also to the manner in which a judgment of the european court of human rights against an eu member state is executed.

member of the commission. − mr president, i will try to answer the question. where member states act in the scope of union law, they must respect fundamental rights as enshrined in the charter and in the general principles of union law. any violation of this obligation may lead to an infringement procedure before the european court of justice under article 258 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. however, this is the only procedural means that the european union has at its disposal to ensure the compliance of a member state with fundamental rights. conversely, where member states act outside the scope of union law, there is no general competence under the treaties in the area of fundamental rights. therefore the union is precluded not only from monitoring in general whether a member state respects fundamental rights, but also from monitoring whether a member state complies with the judgment of the european court of human rights.

mr. chairman, please! tighter rules on industrial gas emissions and meeting environmental obligations are the main objectives of the changes to the regulations for industrial installations in the european union. the draft directive on industrial emissions, which combines and updates eight existing directives, is crucial for improving the state of the environment and air quality in the european union. it introduces stricter emission standards for large combustion plants and regulates a much larger number of combustion plants. each country's energy sector has its own specificity and energy security policy, at least until we adopt a common, uniform energy policy. poland's energy sector is about 95% coal-based. the adoption of the initial requirements of the new directive would result in a serious threat to the energy security of poland and other countries in our part of europe, which are in a similar situation, have similar specificities of this sector. in this context, it is a good idea to enable member states to meet their environmental targets by establishing transitional national plans to allow for the periodic application of more lenient emission limits. the possibility of granting derogations whereby emission allowances may take into account local specificities, geographical conditions and economic considerations will also be relevant. however, legislative changes in the field of the environment should always be geared towards setting targets that can be achieved by all member states. the compromise text restored many of the council's original assumptions, which took into account the fact that many countries are unable to meet the environmental standards set by the council because of their dependence on coal or geographical conditions. i believe that this approach to reducing emissions and setting high standards is the right one, because it is rational and realistic to implement.

in writing. the legislative process for the ippc industrial emissions directive, which is of eu-wide relevance, is slowly coming to a close. however, it should be stressed that not all member states are able to implement it. from poland's point of view, a directive adopted in this form could have serious consequences for industry and heating plants. losses in the industry could reach as much as 50 billion. the implementation of the directive will also have a negative impact on thousands of polish enterprises. reducing pollution to the proposed level will mean that many old plants will have to be replaced by new ones, which is a bigger problem than reducing carbon emissions. however, for district heating plants, the directive provides for a transitional period to comply with union standards by 2019. that's four years less than poland expected. the extension of the transitional period would allow for a more gentle conversion of small heaters. the implementation of the directive will also have an impact on the lives of ordinary citizens. according to the polish ministry of the environment, the introduction of industrial emissions legislation will increase the price of heat by one fifth. the cost of electricity will also increase. consequently, the recommendations for the second reading of the abovementioned directive should be rejected.

vice-president of the commission and high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, i am delighted to be here to discuss one of the most important issues on the european agenda – the creation of the external action service. let me begin with a word of gratitude for the constructive engagement of parliament and the rapporteurs – in particular elmar brok, guy verhofstadt and roberto gualtieri – throughout this process, and to the committees – afet, development, constitutional affairs, budget and budgetary control, the juri committee – whose work has improved the text of the eas decision in many ways. thank you also to the president of parliament. we have achieved a lot together in recent weeks, building the necessary ground among all concerned. i pay tribute to the other members of the quadrilogue – maroš šefčovič and the commission and the spanish presidency led by miguel moratinos together with colleagues in the council. i am especially grateful to the legal services who have offered us good advice and support throughout. the time has come to decide. in recent months, there has been, rightly, a lot of attention on the institutional complexities and the administrative intricacies. laying the foundation is a critical task, but without losing sight of the reasons we are creating this service, reasons that have become more and more obvious as i have travelled, on your behalf, to visit governments, military missions, and our delegations and programmes across the world. before going into some of the detail, i would just like to say something about the vision for the service in the future. there is no better place than this house and no better moment than today to remind ourselves why the service is so important to the european union and why it marks a change in how we operate in a fast-changing geopolitical landscape. we cannot afford to act in a disparate manner in a world that is seeing fundamental power shifts and where problems are increasingly complex and interlinked. we need to defend europe’s interests and project europe’s values in a more coherent and effective way, and we should be ambitious in how we do it. the european union and the member states have an impressive array of instruments, resources, relationships and expertise to help build a better, more stable world. now we need to bring all this together, to forge joined-up strategies and maximise our impact on the ground, particularly in the troubled parts of the world where our actions matter the most. wherever i have travelled – from gaza to haiti to east africa and the balkans – this has been my key conclusion. eu external action will always involve different actors. it is right and proper that development policy operates differently from diplomacy, crisis management or humanitarian aid. andris piebalgs, stefan füle and kristilina georgieva, together with other commission colleagues, have clear, distinct roles and i pay tribute to the work they are doing, but under lisbon we have the opportunity to operate together under one shared comprehensive political strategy – an aspiration now becoming reality. my vision for the eeas is one which ensures that when we speak, our voice is heard and when we engage, our actions make the difference. our citizens know very well that in the face of big problems – fragile states, pandemics, energy security, climate change and illegal migration – we are much more effective together. that effectiveness requires us to mobilise all the means at our disposal – diplomacy, political engagement, development assistance, civil and military crisis management tools – in support of conflict prevention, peace-building, security and stability. this is important for the future of europe and important for the future of the world. i have seen myself what we are capable of when we work together. when i travelled to east africa i saw what our naval operation, atalanta, was doing very well offshore, but i also saw the important capacity-building and development work onshore. as those engaged in our military mission were quick to say, the solution to the problems at sea lies on the land. that is why, working with andris piebalgs, we are making sure our programmes work better together, and why i will be returning to meet again with the leaders of kenya, tanzania, mauritius, seychelles, south africa, mozambique, the regional organisations and the african union, to discuss how we can support african leadership to find political solutions on the ground, and how we can support the people of somalia to a better future. i know what we can do and what we are doing and i also know what we can achieve for the future. i am ambitious, i confess, for i believe it is time to move forward and to get the service up and running quickly. we have a good deal on the table: a draft decision and a set of declarations that form a coherent package. mr president, i am submitting them formally to the record of today’s proceedings. i will not dwell on each and every aspect, but let me highlight just a few specific points on how we have found the proper safeguards in areas that i know are important to this house. first and foremost, the text makes clear that we are safeguarding the community method in all areas where it exists today. the external action service will cooperate closely with the commission services as part of the eu system. second, i know how important political accountability is for this house. i am confident that a good framework has been found through the political declaration on political accountability. i am looking forward to the intense dialogue and exchange of information with the european parliament and will make sure that my collaborators give high priority to this aspect of their work. the many obligations inherent in my position do not allow me to be present as often as i would like in your debates, but i am happy that we have a system for my replacement in such cases, involving in particular colleagues from the commission and, from time to time, also members of the foreign affairs council, from the rotating presidency or the presidency trio. third, financial accountability. i am satisfied that we have clear language and guarantees regarding sound financial management, including appropriate solutions to issues such as discharge and subdelegation of budgetary powers to heads of delegation. as a sign of the importance i attach to this issue, i envisage a senior management team that not only has a chief executive officer in the executive secretary-general but also a chief operating officer in the senior director-general for budget and administration. fourth, we have agreed carefully balanced arrangements regarding development policy and instruments. i know there was some concern that we might lose sight of development policy in the new set-up. believe me, the opposite is the case. development is central to eu external action. it has given us a strong profile on the international stage as the world’s leading donor, so our cooperation programmes are a key tool in our bilateral and regional relationships. that remains the case in the new lisbon context, but development cannot be pursued on its own, separate from other strands of external relations. that is why we are creating a strong common platform, allowing us to work together – andris piebalgs, stefan füle and myself – to ensure that general development objectives and poverty reduction in particular are mainstreamed in our cooperation programmes. fifth, we have a balanced agreement on staff issues, between the wishes of member states to have at least one third of staff in the service coming from national diplomatic services – so we can draw on their expertise, language and historical ties – while at the same time ensuring at least 60% of permanent officials. in the same way, i am clear we need to ensure a proper gender and geographical balance, and not lose sight of wider diversity issues. i am personally committed to this. diversity is strength. a service that represents the eu should reflect that diversity. the wealth of experience, insights and languages that europe’s best diplomats will bring to the service will be one of our distinctive features and competitive advantage. sixth, you will have seen my declaration on the eas central administration. the idea is that we all have a shared understanding on how the service will look. it is important to try to get things right at the beginning, while giving ourselves the chance to review how things work in light of new priorities and developments. members of this house have asked a number of questions on the handling of crisis management and peace-building. i will ensure that the relevant units from the commission will deal with planning and programming of crisis response, conflict prevention and peace-building, and that the csdp structures work in close cooperation and synergy, both under my direct responsibility and authority within the appropriate structure. this is of course without prejudice to the specific nature, notably intergovernmental and communitarian, of the policies. effective coordination of the work of the various departments in the eas will be key. under my direct authority and responsibility, full coordination between all the services of the eas, in particular between the csdp structures and the other relevant services of the eas, will be ensured, respecting their specific nature. i will also ensure that the right coordination is established between the eu special representatives and the relevant departments in the service. finally, this house has also always paid great attention to human rights issues. it is a priority i fully share and i promise that, as high representative, i will give high priority to the promotion of human rights and good governance around the globe and make sure they are a silver thread that runs through everything that we do. there will be a human rights and democracy structure at headquarters level as well as focal points in all relevant union delegations with the task of monitoring the human rights situation and promoting an effective realisation of eu human rights policy goals. honourable members, europe needs the external action service to build a stronger foreign policy. we need an integrated platform to project european values and interests around the world. it is time to give ourselves the means to realise the ambition. it is time to get the right people in place to start doing the necessary work. i agree with the amendments that have been proposed and will support them in the council. it is important now that we move rapidly also with the amendments for the staff and financial regulations and an amending budget for 2010. as i began, i thank you for your cooperation and i count on your support. the vote you will make tomorrow, i hope, is an historic step in the development of the european union and, although it is not our final destination, it is a key staging post in realising our shared vision for the future.

we are all aware of the scale and magnitude of the environmental disaster that has occurred in the gulf of mexico. it's been almost two months since our last debate on offshore drilling platform safety. in the meantime, there was also a debate in the environment committee. millions of gallons of oil have been pouring into the gulf for three months now, devastating the entire ecosystem in the region. the stain has already reached the coast of florida, threatening cuba and mexico. the cost of repairing the damage was also enormous. bp has reported that the cost of fighting the tragic oil spill in the gulf has already exceeded $3 billion. in the light of the above, i would like to express my support for the proposals for the creation of a special fund and insurance against oil spills in european waters. i believe that the fuel companies, while minimizing the risk, should be prepared to assume financial responsibility in the event of a disaster. the creation of such a fund would provide a form of security and would be an expression of environmental and social responsibility for the company's own investments. i also believe that a uniform system of technical inspection of platforms in the territorial waters of the european union and a periodic and publicly available assessment of their security status should be introduced.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − madam president, honourable members, i welcome the opportunity to participate in this session on human rights and hiv/aids. it is a timely debate, as we are only 11 days from the opening of the 18th world aids conference, which will take place in vienna. the spread of hiv continues to cause considerable suffering. the impact of hiv is worse in situations where human rights are not respected, and we know that conflict situations can lead to an increase in hiv infections, especially when sexual abuse against women and children is common. in the absence of proper anti-discrimination laws, people living with hiv are often too frightened to come forward for help because of fear of stigma. in countries where homosexuality is criminalised, some face the additional fear of imprisonment and, in extreme cases, even the death penalty. human rights should empower individuals, including people affected with hiv. the right of everyone to enjoy the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health implies that those who are affected by hiv must have access to information as well as effective prevention and treatment options. affected people should not be discriminated against because of that status. honourable members, we know that hiv infection is used in some countries as a reason to exclude asylum seekers from their right to seek protection. infected persons may lose their right to work; infected children are sometimes excluded from school. the european union has been at the forefront of the defence of the rights of hiv-affected and infected people. the european council adopted conclusions in november 2009, with an eu programme for action to confront hiv/aids through external action, including the need to address the human rights aspect. the european union has been very active in promoting freedom of travel for people living with hiv. our stance is that hiv-specific restrictions on entry, stay and residence based on that status are discriminatory and do not protect public health. we therefore welcome the recent modifications of the regulations in the us and in china as positive signs. in the last months eu representatives, both in brussels and in partner countries, have made several démarches on this issue, including voicing eu concerns about the criminalisation of sexual behaviour among consenting adults – uganda, burundi, malawi – or harassment of aids activists by police and judicial authorities in senegal. the recent adoption of an eu tool kit to help promote and protect the respect of human rights by lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people will further consolidate eu action in this area.
on behalf of the ppe group. - mr president! - i have to go. i want to thank baroness ashton very much for the fact that while everyone is watching the game outside, we are here to debate the rights of people with aids. we're debating because it's a very painful issue for all of us. despite progress in treatment and prevention in recent years, we are less than five years away from meeting the millennium development goals, under which un members committed to curbing the spread of hiv/aids and reducing the number of new infections. but the truth is, the number of people infected with the virus is increasing. this is particularly true in certain regions and for certain social groups of women and girls. that is why in our resolution we declare and strongly support three types of action. first, legal action to encourage countries particularly vulnerable to aids to make the fight against aids a priority and to prepare plans to combat the disease, including the preparation and implementation of anti-discrimination laws to protect vulnerable groups. second, we put a lot of emphasis on educational activities. it is particularly important to ensure access to hiv education and information in order to transform discrimination into understanding and acceptance. this is not only important in developing, underdeveloped countries, but also in european countries, and it's still a painful and important issue. in addition to the educational activities, we emphasize the importance of access to certain medicines. for example, a free trade agreement with india will be signed this fall. one of the fundamental problems we encountered during our visit to india was the emphasis that this country produces very cheap drugs that are supposed to prevent and fight aids. when this treaty is signed with the european union, this will be limited and therefore this issue must also be taken into account.

in writing. ladies and gentlemen, the future of the common agricultural policy after 2013 is of the utmost importance to us. the cap is a key element in many important decisions - the shape of the eu budget, the future of agriculture, farmers and rural areas. the whole european parliament should be aware of the importance of the cap for the future of the eu. the key is, of course, direct payments, but also to achieve a level playing field between countries. today, the differences between the levels of subsidies in the member states are too great. it undermines the sense of solidarity, equality and community. what farmers need most is income stability, even over longer periods of time. without this, it is very difficult to modernise farms and to maintain the positive environmental and cultural impact of agriculture. let us therefore try to ensure that future changes to the cap lead to a stabilisation of european farmers' incomes. thank you very much. thank you.
in writing. in reforming the cap, we must not forget the principles of integration, solidarity and community. direct payments have a significant impact on food security. they not only help to stabilise farmers' incomes, but also compensate for the costs of meeting the increasing demands placed on agriculture. if we do not equalize the level of direct support, this main cap financial instrument will continue to divide the european union into old and new member states. the abandonment of the historical division criteria would not only be a symbolic gesture towards more complete integration, but would also contribute to ensuring a level playing field in the single community market. moreover, it is necessary that the rural development strategy remains a key component of the cap, supporting broad economic and social development. the key is to continue restructuring and modernising farms and to pursue any innovation aimed at increasing productivity and improving competitiveness in the enlarged union. a strong second pillar is the opportunity to facilitate the start-up of young farmers, improve the quality of life, activate the society and improve the situation of women in rural areas.

in writing. −hiv/aids infections are global and do not affect so-called risk groups or specific regions. now it's not just a problem for drug addicts or homosexuals, it's a problem for everyone. the greatest risk is to young, educated, white, working in large corporations. nearly half of all people living with hiv are women. they are more susceptible to infection, since the virus is much more easily transmitted from a man to a woman than vice versa. the 18th international aids conference (vienna, 18-23 july) stressed the need to intensify information campaigns targeting women and young people. women must have universal, easy access to information on sexual and reproductive health and health services. free distribution of anti-hiv medicines to pregnant women is essential to prevent transmission of the disease from mother to child. school-based sexual and reproductive rights education programmes are key to hiv/aids prevention. the most visible consequences of a lack of sex education in schools are the infection of young people with hiv and other sexually transmitted diseases and the early, unplanned pregnancies of young women. the hiv/aids epidemic, due to its reach, the risk of death and the high rate of infection among young people, should be a sufficient reason to introduce sound sex education in schools. that is why i voted for the adoption of the resolution on aids/hiv in the context of the 18th international aids conference.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - what are you doing? the brussels 1 regulation lays down detailed rules governing the jurisdiction of courts in civil and commercial matters and the recognition and enforcement of judgments from other member states. it was rightly considered a great success. it has facilitated the free flow of judgments, increased legal certainty and avoided parallel proceedings, although it has been criticised in some quarters for causing adverse or anti-commercial effects. the quality of the court's case-law is also perceived as uneven. the european parliament was merely consulted when the brussels 1 regulation was adopted. parliament will now deal with all future proposals to amend this regulation in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure. it is therefore good that we are already involved in the commission's green paper phase. the issues raised in the green paper include the possible abolition of the exequatur procedure, the functioning of the regulation in the wider international order, the functioning of the choice of court clauses, the functioning of the regulation in industrial and intellectual property disputes, and the possible reform of the rules on lis pendens. i tried to make a balanced, forward-looking report. i was moved by the reaction to two working papers in which i supported the idea of abolishing the exequatur procedure, which should bring concrete benefits to the citizens of the european union. at the same time, i am convinced that this step must be compensated by a special procedure, combined with appropriate safeguards for debtors. irrespective of the abolition of the exequatur procedure, i am convinced that authentic instruments should not be directly enforceable in the executing state without being verified by the competent judicial authorities of that state, and that the existing principle that the enforceability clause may be refused or modified only if the judgment is contrary to the public policy of the executing state should be changed. in certain circumstances, an authentic instrument may be incompatible with previous judgments of the courts of the state of enforcement. i maintain my objection to the removal of the arbitration exemption from the scope of the regulation. however, i believe that the relationship between arbitration and judicial proceedings should be given much more thought and that, pending a full review and thorough consultation, the concept of primary jurisdiction should not be pursued in judicial proceedings in support of arbitration. in the future, i find the idea of giving full retroactivity to the provisions of the regulation attractive. it's too soon for that now. i urge that there be extensive consultation and political debate before any action is taken on this matter beyond the suggestions made in this draft report. i also support the idea of resuming negotiations on a convention on international judgments at the hague conference. the report deals with very complex problems in the field of private international law. although defamation issues are not addressed in the european commission's green paper, the forum shopping problem of choosing the most favourable jurisdiction in order to obtain the highest possible damages in defamation cases does exist. freedom of speech and the media must therefore be balanced against the rights of the individual who has been defamed or whose right to privacy has been violated. i am therefore opposed to the exclusion of defamation from the general rules of the brussels 1 regulation. of course, i wonder whether an instrument such as brussels 1 is appropriate for regulating the rules of private international law. perhaps another legal instrument is needed to regulate the conflict between media freedom and fundamental rights of the individual. the brussels 1 regulation was not designed to refer to the qualitative assessment of the courts of the member states. the european court of justice in the lugano opinion clearly stated that the brussels 1 legal instrument is based on mutual trust. i would like to thank my colleagues on the legal affairs committee, and in particular mrs wallis and mrs regner.
we have repeatedly spoken in our reports about the difficult situation of women in the european union and we have tried to improve their situation by giving them equal opportunities. how much more difficult it is for women who are ethnic minorities, and who are also part of our society. we should therefore also help them to access the labour market, education and training. we should protect them from social exclusion and multiple discrimination, and strive to involve them in political and social activities in all their dimensions. it's the only way to avoid stereotypes, stigma, ethnic segregation, and just plain violence and aggression. such people should be given opportunities and opportunities so that differences in culture and tradition do not hinder their working together but rather add value. the events of the past few days show that instead of facing the difficulties that come with being a multicultural society, some people try to get rid of them, only to cause more outrage and social disapproval.
the ageing of the population is a phenomenon that requires our particular attention. among the problems we face, the problem of poverty, although multifaceted, is largely due to high unemployment. a significant decline in employment is already being recorded in the over-50 age group and is particularly affecting women. because of their age, they do not feel attractive to employers. some of them choose to retire early, and their low pensions sometimes leave them in extreme poverty. in order to increase employment in this age group, legal solutions should be applied at governmental level in each country. entrepreneurs need incentives to hire people over 50. this may take the form of tax exemptions, special arrangements within the healthcare system and a range of free training to adapt such workers to the needs of employers. such ideas will not only improve the living standards of these people, but also bring tangible benefits to national budgets.
in writing. it is good that the ep report focuses on the situation of women over 50 in the context of the demographic changes taking place in europe. previous reports have indicated a slow improvement in the situation of women in the labour market and in public life. the situation of women in this group may change markedly in the coming years, especially in countries with poor or inadequate social and health care systems. in these countries, the aging of the population will place a special burden on women to care for aging parents and relatives. women are already burdened with such responsibilities today, and they will be especially burdened in the future. in many respects, they will replace and supplement inefficient institutions. and we need to prepare today for the demographic bomb, which this time will be the huge number of elderly and disabled people. the adaptation of institutions will be long and difficult, and we need to think now about how to help families in an ageing society. the european commission and parliament must start monitoring today how member states' institutions are adapting to the needs of an ageing population. the report rightly emphasises the need to facilitate access to public and private services, in particular healthcare. it is important that these records are reflected in everyday life and not just a dead letter in eu documents.
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the report of the committee on women's rights and equality on the role of women in an ageing society rightly noted that women of retirement age are more likely to live in poverty. the reason for this phenomenon is very often the lower accumulation of pension benefits, which is a consequence of lower wages for women and periodic reductions in wages, for example during childcare. the project lists a number of elements that could improve the quality of life of women over 50 - including taking on additional part-time work. but the first thing to consider is how to ensure that women approaching retirement age do not have to fear losing their jobs and thus their financial resources. the european union should place particular emphasis on equal pay for men and women. according to the charter of fundamental rights and the lisbon treaty, discrimination on grounds of sex is prohibited in the workplace. therefore, there must be points in the report that would ensure that women receive the same pay as men. in addition, it is important that public opinion highlights all issues related to discrimination against women in the workplace.
