forecast. the unemployment rate, whilst still much too high, has stopped increasing. clearly, uncertainties and risks remain, not least outside the european union. we should be under no illusions. our work is far from finished. there is no room for complacency. the unemployment problem is an extremely serious one. budgetary expansion played its role to counter the decline in economic activity. but it is now time to exit. without structural reforms, we will not create sustainable growth. we must use the next 12 months to accelerate our reform agenda. now is the time to modernise our social market economy so that it can compete globally and respond to the challenge of demography. now is the time to make the right investments for our future. this is europe's moment of truth. europe must show that it is more than 27 different national solutions. we either swim together or sink separately. we will only succeed if, whether acting nationally, regionally or locally, we think european. today, i will set out what i see as the priorities for our work together over the coming year. i cannot cover here every issue of european policy or initiative we will take. through president buzek, i will send you a more complete programme document. essentially, i see five major challenges for the union over the next year: dealing with the economic crisis and governance; restoring growth for jobs by accelerating the europe 2020 reform agenda; building an area of freedom, justice and security; launching negotiations for a modern eu budget; and pulling our weight on the global stage. let me start with the economic crisis and governance. earlier this year, we acted decisively when euro area members and the euro itself needed our help. we have learned hard lessons. now we are making important progress on economic governance. the commission put its ideas on the table in may and in june. they have been well received by this parliament and in the task force chaired by the president of the european council. they are the basis around which a consensus is being developed. we will present the most urgent legislative proposals on 29 september so as not to lose momentum. unsustainable budgets make us vulnerable. debt and deficit lead to boom and bust and they unravel the social safety net. money that is spent on servicing debt is money that cannot be spent on the social good nor to prepare ourselves for the costs of an ageing population. a debt generation makes an unsustainable nation. our proposals will strengthen the stability and growth pact through increased surveillance and enforcement. we need to tackle severe macro-economic imbalances, especially in the euro area. that is why we made proposals early on to detect asset bubbles, lack of competitiveness and other sources of imbalances. i now see a willingness on the part of governments to accept stronger monitoring, backed up by incentives for compliance and earlier sanctions. the commission will strengthen its role as an independent referee and enforcer of the new rules. we will match monetary union with true economic union. if implemented as we propose, these reforms will also guarantee the long-term stability of the euro. it is key to our economic success. for the economy to grow, we also need a strong and sound financial sector –a sector that serves the real economy and that prides itself on proper regulation and proper supervision. we took action to increase bank transparency. today the situation is better than it was a year ago. with the publication of the stress test results, banks should now be able to lend to each other so that credit can flow to europe's citizens and companies. we have proposed protecting people's savings up to eur 100 000. we will propose to ban abusive naked short selling. we will tackle credit default swaps. the days of betting on someone else's house burning down are over. we continue to insist that banks, not taxpayers, must pay up front to cover the costs of their own risks of failure. we are legislating to outlaw bonuses for quick wins today that become big losses tomorrow. as part of this approach, i am also defending taxes on financial activities and we will come forward with proposals this autumn. the political deal on the financial supervision package just concluded is very good news. the commission proposals, based on the de larosière report, will give us an effective european supervision system. i want to thank parliament for the constructive role it has played and i hope it will give its final agreement this month. we will also go further on regulation. initiatives on derivatives, further measures on credit rating agencies and a framework for bank resolution and crisis management will soon be before you. our goal is to have a reformed financial sector in place by the end of 2011. sound government finances and responsible financial markets give us the confidence and economic strength for sustainable growth. we need to move beyond the debate between fiscal consolidation and growth. we can have both. honourable members, sound public finances are a means to an end: growth for jobs. our goal is growth – sustainable and inclusive growth. this is our overarching priority. this is where we need to invest. europe 2020 starts now. we must frontload and accelerate the most growth-promoting reforms of our agenda. this could raise growth levels by over a third by 2020. this means concentrating on three priorities: getting more people into jobs, boosting our companies' competitiveness and deepening the single market. let me start with people and jobs. over 6.3 million people have lost their jobs since 2008. each one of them should have the chance to get back into employment. europe's employment rates are at 69% on average for those aged between 20 and 64. we have agreed that these should rise to 75% by 2020, bringing in particular more women and older workers into the workforce. most of the competences for employment policy remain with member states. we know that. but we will not stand on the sidelines. i want a european union that helps its people to seize new opportunities and that is social and inclusive. this is the europe we will build if member states, the european institutions and the social partners move ahead on our common reform agenda. it should be centred on skills and jobs and investment in lifelong learning. it should focus on unlocking the growth potential of the single market, to build a stronger single market for jobs. the opportunities exist. we have very high levels of unemployment, but europe now has four million job vacancies. later this year the commission will propose a 'european vacancy monitor' which will show people where the jobs are in europe and which skills are needed. we will also put forward plans for a european skills passport. we must also tackle problems of poverty and exclusion. we must make sure that the most vulnerable are not left behind. this is the focus of our 'platform against poverty'. it will bring together european action for vulnerable groups such as children and old people. as more and more people travel, study or work abroad, we will also strengthen citizens' rights as they move across borders. the commission will address persistent obstacles as early as this autumn. growth must be based on our companies' competitiveness. we should continue to make life easier for our small and medium-sized enterprises. they provide two out of every three private-sector jobs. among their main concerns are innovation and red tape. we are working on both. just before the summer the commission announced the biggest ever package from the seventh research framework programme, worth eur 6.4 billion. this money will go to smes as well as to scientists. investing in innovation also means promoting world-class universities in europe. i want to see them attracting the brightest and the best, from europe and the rest of the world. we will take an initiative on the modernisation of european universities. i want to see a europe that is strong in science, education and culture. we need to improve europe's innovation performance not only in universities but along the whole chain, from research to retail, notably through innovation partnerships. we need an innovation union. next month, the commission will set out how to achieve this. another key test will be whether member states are ready to make a breakthrough on a patent valid across the whole european union. our innovators often pay ten times the price faced by their competitors in the united states or in japan. our proposal is on the table. it would substantially reduce the cost and double the coverage. after decades of discussion, it is time to decide. we will also act further on red tape. smes are being strangled in regulatory knots. 71% of ceos say that the biggest barrier to their success is bureaucracy. the commission has put proposals on the table to generate annual savings of eur 38 billion for european companies. stimulating innovation, cutting red tape and developing a highly-skilled workforce: these are ways to ensure that european manufacturing continues to be world class. we want a strong, but modern, industrial base in europe. a thriving industrial base in europe is of paramount importance for our future. next month, the commission will present a new industrial policy for the globalisation era. we have the people and we have the companies. what they both need is an open and modern single market. the internal market is europe's greatest asset, and we are not using it enough. we urgently need to deepen it. only 8% of europe's 20 million smes engage in cross-border trade, still fewer in investment. even with the internet, over a third of consumers lack the confidence to make cross-border purchases. at my request, mario monti presented an excellent report and has identified 150 missing links and bottlenecks in the internal market. next month we will set out how to deepen the single market in a comprehensive and ambitious single market act. energy is a key driver for growth and a central priority for action. we need to complete the internal market for energy, build and interconnect energy grids, and ensure energy security and solidarity. we need to do for energy what we have done for mobile phones: give real choice for consumers in one european marketplace. this will give us a real energy community in europe. we need to make frontiers irrelevant for pipelines or power cables, to have the infrastructure for solar and wind energy, and to ensure that across the whole of europe we have a common standard so that charging electric car batteries becomes as natural as filling up the tank. over the next year, we will bring forward an energy action plan, an infrastructure package and an energy efficiency action plan to put this vision in place. i myself will travel to the caspian region later this year to promote the southern corridor as a means of enhancing our security of supply. to build a resource-efficient europe, we need to look beyond energy. in the 20th century the world enjoyed phenomenal resource-intensive growth. in the 20th century we saw, globally, a four-fold growth in population, accompanied by a 40-fold growth in economic output. but in the same period we also increased our use of fossil fuels 16 times, our fishing catches 35 times and our water use 9 times. our carbon emissions increased 17 times. that means we have to deliver on our climate and energy package, as a core driver for change. this means integrating the different strands of policy on climate change, energy, transport and environment into a coherent approach on resource efficiency and a low carbon future. a forward-looking agricultural sector will play a major role in european measures to address some of the biggest challenges ahead, such as global food security, biodiversity loss and the sustainable management of natural resources. so will our maritime policy. all of this will not only strengthen our economy tomorrow, but will provide new openings today. jobs in the eco-industry have been increasing by 7% a year since 2000. i want to see three million 'green jobs' by 2020 – three million green collar workers that complement our blue and white collar workers. we need sustainable growth, and we also need smart growth. half of european productivity growth over the last 15 years was driven by information and communication technologies. this trend is set to intensify. our european digital agenda will deliver a single digital market worth 4% of eu gdp by 2020. mr president, everything we do is for the citizens of europe. a fundamental dimension of our european project is building an area of freedom, security and justice. we are working hard to implement the stockholm action plan. we will make a real push on asylum and migration. legal migrants will find europe a place where human values are respected and enforced. at the same time, we will crack down on the exploitation of illegal immigrants within europe and at our borders. the commission will make new proposals on policing our external borders. we will bring forward an internal security strategy to tackle threats of organised crime and terrorism. europeans will find that their fundamental rights and obligations exist wherever they go. everyone in europe must respect the law and governments must respect human rights, including those of minorities. racism and xenophobia have no place in europe. (applause) on such sensitive issues, and when a problem arises, we must all act with responsibility. i make a strong appeal not to re-awaken the ghosts of europe's past. an area of freedom, liberty and security will create a place where europeans can prosper. honourable members, another challenge for next year is sorting out the future budget of the european union. next month we will put forward the commission's first ideas for the budget review. it will launch an open debate without taboos to prepare our legislative proposals that will be presented in the second quarter of next year. we need to spend our money where we get most value for it. we should invest it where it leverages growth and delivers our european agenda. the quality of spending should be the yardstick for us all. it is important to discuss not only the quantity, but also the quality, of the spending and investment. i believe that europe offers real added value. that is why i will be pushing for an ambitious post-2013 budget for europe. i believe we should pool our means to back our policy priorities. the issue is not about spending more or less, but spending more intelligently by looking at european and national budgets together. the eu budget is not for brussels. it is for the people that you represent – for the unemployed workers being retrained by the social fund, for the students that participate in the erasmus programme, and for the regions that benefit from the cohesion fund. energy interconnections, research, and development aid are obvious examples where a euro spent at european level gets you more than a euro spent at national level. as you know, some member states are seeing this logic even in areas of core national competence, like defence. they recognise that huge savings could be made if they pooled some of their means and activities. pooling money at european level allows member states to cut their costs, avoid overlaps and get a better return on their investment. that is why we should also explore new sources of financing for major european infrastructure projects. for instance, i will propose the establishment of european union project bonds, together with the european investment bank. (applause) we will also further develop public-private partnerships. as this parliament has made clear, we must also address the issue of own resources. the present system is stretched to its limits – propped up by a byzantine set of corrections. our citizens deserve a fairer and more efficient and more transparent system. some will not agree with all the ideas we will raise. indeed, i find it extraordinary that some are already rejecting them, without even knowing what they will be. (applause)i know that one issue of interest to this parliament is the duration of the next budget. various options exist. i would like to look at a 10-year framework, with a mid-term review of the financial dimension after five years. let us call it a 'five plus five' option. this will give us longer-term planning and a clearer link with the mandates of both our institutions. of course, part of a credible european budget is the rigorous pursuit of savings. i am looking at the administrative costs within the commission and other community bodies like agencies. we need to eliminate all pockets of inefficiency. we will build on recommendations from the court of auditors to improve financial management. honourable members, the final challenge i want to address today is how we pull our weight on the global stage. when we deal with our everyday problems, we sometimes lose perspective and forget europe's achievements: a peaceful and successful transition to a european union that has doubled in size and is negotiating further accessions; a sound currency – the euro – that is a major world currency; and a strong partnership with our neighbourhood that strengthens us all. if we act decisively we have nothing to fear from the 21st century. as the strategic partnerships of the 21st century emerge, europe should seize the chance to define its future. i am impatient to see the union play a role in global affairs that matches its economic weight. our partners are watching and are expecting us to engage as europe, not just as 27 individual countries. if we do not act together, europe will not be a force in the world and they will move on without us – without the european union but also without its member states. this is why, in my political guidelines, i called for europe to be a global player and a global leader – a key task and test for our generation. together with high representative and vice-president ashton, i will present our vision of how we can maximise europe's role in the world. with the european external action service, we have the means to match our aspirations. in our globalised world, the relationships we build with strategic partners determine our prosperity. to be effective on the international stage, we need the weight of the european union. size matters, now more than ever. a good example is the fight against climate change. copenhagen showed that, while others did not match our ambition, we did not help ourselves by not speaking with one voice. negotiations may have stalled but climate change has not. i want us to intensify our engagement with international partners to turn their press releases into credible commitments to cut emissions and push forward with fast-start funding. the next two months will see crucial summits with strategic partners. the more we are able to establish a common agenda, with a clearly defined european interest, the more we will achieve. for example, i see huge potential in developing a transatlantic agenda for growth and jobs. where we are already punching our weight is the g20, the forum where the key economic global players address common challenges. when president van rompuy and i go to seoul in november, representing the european union, we want to see concrete results – further progress in global economic coordination, more stable and responsible financial markets and agreement on reform of international financial institutions, more effective global financial safety nets, and more progress on a g20 development agenda. we will continue to show leadership in this forum and work closely with the french g8/g20 presidency next year. we also want to see support for the doha round. trade boosts growth and prosperity. we will also pursue bilateral and regional free trade agreements. in october, the commission will present a renewed trade policy to drive new benefits for europe. being open to the world also means standing side by side with developing countries, especially with africa. when i go to the millennium development goals high-level event in new york in two weeks' time, i intend to commit – with your support and on behalf of the european union – an extra eur 1 billion to the millennium development goals. being a global player also means standing up for our values. human rights are not negotiable. i am shocked at how the rights of women are being infringed in many countries. i am appalled when i hear that sakineh mohammadi ashtiani has been sentenced to death by stoning. this is barbaric beyond words. (applause) in europe we condemn such acts, which have no justification under any moral or religious code. our values also mean that we must come to the aid of those facing a crisis situation, anywhere around the world. our humanitarian aid to pakistan is the latest example of europe's solidarity in action. it is a striking example of the need to present the different contributions of the commission and the member states as a truly european aid package. the member states have the helicopters and the civil protection teams. we now need to pool them to create a real european crisis response capacity. this is what the commission will propose in october. i urge the member states to show they are serious about the union punching its weight in this area. we are also making progress on a common foreign policy, but let us be under no illusions. we will not have the weight we need in the world without a common defence policy. i believe now is the moment to address this challenge. (applause)honourable members, we are still bedding down the new institutional set-up of europe created by the lisbon treaty. what really matters is what the institutions deliver to the people. what matters is the difference europe makes in their daily lives. the secret of europe's success is its unique community model. more than ever, the commission must drive the political agenda with its vision and proposals. i have called for a special relationship between the commission and parliament, the two community institutions par excellence. i am intensifying my political cooperation with you. europe is not only brussels or strasbourg. it is also our regions. it is the cities, towns and villages you come from. when you walk round your constituencies, you can point to the european projects that are so important for their prosperity. at the end of the day, we are all in the same boat – the european institutions, member states and regions. the union will not achieve its objectives in europe without the member states and the member states will not achieve their objectives in the world without the european union. the citizens of europe expect us to take the action needed to get out of this crisis. we must show them that the common efforts we are making today will lead to new jobs, new investments, and a europe fit for the future. i am confident that europe has what it takes. we will get the results we are reaching for. one thing is certain – it is not through pessimism and constantly promoting defeat that we will win this battle; it is with confidence and with a strong common will. today, i have outlined how i see the european union doing that. i have committed myself to delivering the proposals to build our economic union. i have made the case to fast-track our reform agenda. i have set out how to modernise our social market economy to deliver growth and jobs in a smart, sustainable and inclusive economy through our europe 2020 flagship initiatives. i have set out how to achieve a common energy policy in europe. i have defended the need for an area of freedom, security and justice, where europeans will find that their fundamental rights and obligations exist wherever they go. i have made clear that the commission will strive for an ambitious budget. i have proposed developing eu project bonds to finance major european projects. i have announced our reinforced commitment to the millennium development goals. i have made the case clear as to why we need a common crisis response capacity, a common foreign policy and a common defence policy. i have urged european leaders to act together if they want europe to be a global player and defend the european interest. it is indeed a transformational, ambitious and challenging agenda. for europe to succeed, the commission needs your support for a stronger, fairer europe for the benefit of our citizens. president of the republic of mali. - mr president of the european parliament, mr president of the european commission, madam high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, mr commissioner for development, honourable members of the european parliament, honourable members from mali, i would first of all like to congratulate you, mr president, on your election as president of the european parliament, but i would also like to thank the chairmen of the political groups and all the members of the european parliament for the privilege of coming here today to share with you, first of all, my vision of some of the major challenges facing my country and even africa, and above all, to stress the efforts it is making every day to find suitable solutions. ladies and gentlemen, mali covers an area of 1 240 000 km2 and is situated in the heart of west africa, with seven countries and 7 000 km of borders. a land of ancient civilizations with a rich and varied cultural heritage, mali's prestigious history could be told through a few facts, landmarks and symbols. among them i would like to mention the charter of kouroukan fouga. adopted 776 years ago, at the founding of the mali empire by soundjata keita in 1236, the charter of "kouroukan fouga" had all the attributes of a constitution. it codified the organisation of power, limits and obligations, the defence of human rights and public freedoms, the protection of professional activities, persons and their property. one of its articles was worded as follows: 'the human person is sacred and inviolable', thus proclaiming, a few centuries in advance, what was to become a key principle of modern democratic constitutions. in the high place of the expression of democracy that is the european parliament, this reference seemed important to me. the history of mali is also timbuktu: the mysterious city, the city of the 333 saints, which already had in the 16th century 25,000 students from many countries to listen to the scholars in the shadow of the venerable mosque of sankoré and its university complex. mahmoud kaati, author of the "tarikh-el-fetach", testifies to the time in these words: "timbuktu was known for the solidity of its institutions, political freedoms, the security of persons and property, for its leniency and compassion towards the poor and foreigners, for its courtesy and assistance to students and scientists". in 2006, timbuktu was declared the capital of islamic culture. mali is also the dogon country, known throughout the world for its exceptional natural site and cultural wealth, which make it the number one tourist destination in our country. mali's history is also one of an ancient relationship with europe. as a reminder, emperor mansa moussa, better known as kankou moussa, established diplomatic relations with portugal as early as the 14th century. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, before you, the elected representatives of europe, i would like to express the deep appreciation of the malian people for the quality and the volume of cooperation between the european union and mali. the european union is mali's main development partner. we are the second largest recipient of european development fund (edf) aid in sub-saharan africa. i would like to congratulate the commission on the success of our cooperation. for example, the 9th edf was committed at 100% and, for almost two years, the 10th edf has been running on very good foundations. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the results of our cooperation have a direct impact on the quality of life of the people. they also strengthen the foundations of our democratic system. the process of democratization in mali, which began following the events leading to the coup d'état of 26 march 1991, was marked by a number of key milestones, including the democratic transition from 26 march 1991 to 8 june 1992, which was completed on time and in accordance with the commitments entered into. after 14 months of transition, free and democratic elections were held in 1992. ten years later, in 2002, i was elected after a presidential election which marked the first democratic alternation in peace in mali. ladies and gentlemen, after my election, i proposed to the malian political class a consensual management of power whose philosophy was essentially this: to govern together, with respect for our differences. the uniqueness of the malian experience lies in the fact that it was not the result of any post-electoral crisis. it is a conscious and voluntary approach to the need to pool the efforts of political, social and associative forces in the service of mali's development. in my view, power should be more a factor of cohesion than of division, and this in respect of all fundamental freedoms. it should be stressed that the political consensus we have adopted or that i have proposed does not mean unanimity. consensus implies rather the notion of compromise. the political consensus in mali is an advanced attempt to build this new political system that is emerging in africa, namely the broad government coalitions. the malian experience has brought together all political forces around the vision of an independent elected president. the political consensus has strengthened the basis for reconciliation between the significant components of the political class and the institutions of the republic, on the one hand, and reconciliation between politicians themselves, on the other. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is in the same spirit of consensus that we have started to reflect on the consolidation of democracy in mali, after 20 years of practice. the expert committee responsible for conducting this mission met with the political class, civil society, religious denominations, trade unions and traditional legitimacies. the reforms proposed following these consultations are primarily aimed at correcting the gaps and shortcomings identified by institutional practice, achieving high voter turnout and reducing the cost of electoral consultations, strengthening the capacity of political parties and developing a statute for the opposition and the leader of the opposition. they will, of course, be the subject of a constitutional referendum after their adoption by the national assembly of mali. it is appropriate for me to greet here, before you, the malian deputies with whom i have the best relations, whether they are in the presidential majority or in the opposition. i would like to express my sincere thanks to these members for agreeing to be present with me here in strasbourg. (applause) i would like to thank mr president, ladies and gentlemen, decentralisation will always play a prominent role in mali's political and institutional development. i would like to remind you that our great empires -- and we've had many since the 10th century -- all of these empires were decentralized. so, in our country, decentralization is a fact. the original decentralisation approaches devised and implemented by mali are based on the following factors: first, the basis of a political will in harmony with the conviction that decentralisation cannot be achieved without decentralisation, and this in successive stages. it cannot be achieved without the development and implementation of substantial reforms to improve economic and social governance, especially at local level. it cannot succeed without the continuing support of the european union in the financial and, above all, in the technical field. the administrative reform support project (parad) and the institutional development programme (idp) have both benefited from european support. they contribute to better organisation of the state and to the modernisation of its administration by strengthening its capacity. mali has 703 urban and rural communes, 49 circles, 8 regions and 1 district, which are administered by communal councils, circle councils and regional assemblies. a high council of local and regional authorities ensures the national representation of our decentralised entities. the creation of a senate is envisaged in the proposed political reforms to deepen our process of decentralisation. to support local development, an original financial instrument called the national agency for investment in local and regional authorities (anict) has made it possible to build many public facilities and, above all, to provide basic social services to our populations. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, before this august assembly i also wished to raise the subject of immigration. the issues of migration concern us all because they have a multifaceted dimension for each of us, for each of our countries, which brings together demographic and economic issues, social and humanitarian considerations and identity and security concerns in the same problematic. today we need to find areas of shared interest and incentives that will make migration a contribution to the overall growth and well-being of our two continents. that is the challenge we face. brain drain is the most significant cost of migration for african countries, given the limited supply of skilled personnel in many fields, including education, but especially health. according to the international organisation for migration (iom), 40% of african countries have 35% or more of their university graduates living abroad. but, make no mistake, the migration of africans is first and foremost and above all in africa. of the estimated 1 billion africans, only 2 million are from sub-saharan africa and live in europe. the tragedy of these young men, women and girls, trying to cross deserts, seas and oceans to the european paradise, at the mercy of all dangers - unscrupulous smugglers, excuse me for the word - is still vivid in our memory: how many died of thirst, how many drowned and disappeared. no statistics can tell. (applause) to take my country, mali, as an example, which is a great country of immigration and emigration, of the 4 million malians around the world, 3 and a half million of them live on the african continent and about 200,000 throughout europe and the rest of the world. in economic terms, the income transfers of the malian diaspora are estimated at €456 million per year, or 11% of gross domestic product, according to a study by the african development bank which was prepared in 2005. according to the same sources, these transfers would be equivalent to 85% of the official development potential migrants and returning migrants, to provide information on the legal conditions of migration and to raise public awareness of the prevention of illegal migration, as well as to develop human, financial and technical capital and malians from abroad. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, security is an important aspect of our relations with the european union. it is therefore appropriate to discuss the sahel-saharan strip, which is now a collective threat, including to europe. covering an area of 8 million km2, a quarter of the african continent, and stretching from mauritania to sudan, mali, burkina faso, niger, algeria, libya and chad, the sahel strip has a population density of almost zero per km2, a very difficult terrain, mountain ranges for hundreds of kilometres and sand dunes covering hundreds of thousands of km2. it is a very hostile area with a particularly harsh climate. it can be barely 1 degree in december and 50 degrees in the shade from february onwards. the only activity is intensive livestock farming in the most inhospitable environments. the drought this year, for example, has caused us to lose 50% of the herd in the sahel-saharan strip. the people there live in precarious conditions and their young people have no alternative but to provide fighters for criminal groups of all kinds. the young remain a key issue. mali is situated in the central-western part of the sahel-saharan strip, which covers an area of 650 000 km2, or 70% of the total area of our country. mali is a transit zone and, as i say emphatically today, my country is also a hostage and at the same time a victim of cross-border threats that come from elsewhere and are mainly aimed at other regions and other continents. the threats are first of all the smuggling of cigarettes, the smuggling of illegal immigrants to europe, drugs from the south american continent and salafist groups from the maghreb. they are manifested in the form of hostage-taking, assassinations, but their main characteristic is extreme mobility on the border bands between countries. none of the threats i have just mentioned originated in our country, none of them are directed at us. mali is a secular country with a large muslim majority, of course. islam has been practiced since the 9th century. our practice of islam has always been peaceful, and above all respectful of the human person. this is our misunderstanding of the islamist ideology preached in the sahel-saharan strip. (applause) its religious impact is still small, but for how long? that is the question we are faced with. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the countries of the sahel-saharan region, including mali, have been making efforts for a long time, both human, material and financial, to stem the phenomenon of insecurity, whose transnational character is taking on increasingly worrying proportions. the essentially, firstly, on the management of the population to ensure the ownership of security policy, on the assistance to vulnerable populations by meeting basic needs and, above all, on sustainable repressive measures. honourable members, ladies and gentlemen, in accordance with the strategic lines of the programme to combat insecurity and terrorism, mali has launched an emergency programme to thank you, chairman. given that the globalisation adjustment fund was set up to reduce the threat of unemployment and to increase the chances of finding new jobs for those who have suffered from globalisation, it is nevertheless worrying that the 500 million a year that is earmarked for the globalisation adjustment fund is still very little used and that there are nine countries that have not submitted any applications at all. this seems to be a positive initiative, since the commission decided to ease and simplify and also to improve the mechanism for allocating funds after the crisis, but this work must continue. i think this is particularly true of the new member states, where there are many small and mediumsized enterprises, where not many people lose their jobs in one enterprise, but many people lose their jobs in many enterprises. and it is this aspect that needs to be further developed in order to make the globalisation adjustment fund truly available to countries with a gdp below the eu average. thank you.
today we adopted an important report on fair incomes for farmers and improving the functioning of the food supply chain in europe. the functioning of the food chain is not only due to the length of the journey of agricultural products from the field through processing, wholesale and retail trade, to the consumer's table, but also to its specificity and complexity. agricultural production is highly dependent on natural and climatic conditions over which the farmer has very little influence. the processing industry imposes prices on farmers, and trade behaves similarly towards the processing industry and the consumer. it is therefore important to analyse price relationships and monitor their transparency. this does not mean that market laws are violated, but only that the monopolistic activities of intermediaries in trade are limited. supervisory and monitoring bodies are now being introduced into financial markets. some want to remove supervision and monitoring from the agricultural market. it doesn't take into account that producers are fragmented, unbundled and will lose to a powerful trade, incurring huge losses.
in today's world, older people are too often mistakenly considered to be under-productive and unfit for work, even though eu law prohibits age discrimination. what is forgotten is the added value they bring to national economies, thanks to their long experience. in this context, women are particularly disadvantaged in the labour market because of the persistence of gender discrimination. in addition, women live longer than men statistically, which makes them more vulnerable to poverty and to lower pension benefits due to lower wages than men in the same positions. all these problems are particularly evident in rural areas. in this context, i am pleased that resolutions are being passed which remind us of the problem and mobilise us to continue to work to improve the situation.

in writing. - i welcome the results of today's vote. voluntary forms of producer organisations are the most economically efficient social forms of farmer activity. they increase their bargaining power on the market, level the playing field in negotiations with the processing industry and allow production optimisation without the need for excessive external resources. to compete, farmers need to cooperate more. cooperation and coordination at producer organisation level allows a number of initiatives to be taken, such as the promotion of regional products or the implementation of consumer information campaigns, thus ensuring the diversity of production on the community market. in addition, the group is best placed to identify the need for strategic planning, cost rationalisation, improvement of efficiency of management and organisation of sales of agricultural products. the measures for producer groups will have a positive impact on the use of human and investment potential and thus on the increase of income and the improvement of the market position of farms.
in writing. - i supported the resolution on the financing and operation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf). the rules for the functioning of the egf need to be improved in order to make effective use of it. i hope that the commission will take advantage of parliament's proposals, which will make it possible to reduce the procedure for granting aid by as much as half. the crisis-induced increase in unemployment has given the egf a special importance, as it provides individual support for redundant workers and their professional activation. the rigorous criteria for granting aid and the length of the procedures mean that member states do not make full use of the possibility of receiving aid from the egf. for example, from my country, poland, only three applications for financial support under the egf were submitted. the main reason for the lack of interest is the long-term nature of the procedures. in addition to improving the functioning of the fund, the criterion of supporting workers made redundant as a result of the current crisis should be extended, at least until the end of the current financial perspective, and the co-financing rate of costs should be maintained at 65%. the impact of the labour market crisis will be felt for many years to come, and this is why such help is and will be needed. i also draw the attention of the commission and the member states to the coordination of the exchange of best practices at european level, which will allow for rapid and effective intervention by the egf in the event of mass redundancies.

in writing. - i support the report by ms pietikäinen, because it puts the ageing of society in a new light. usually, this process is misrepresented in a negative way. discussions focus on costs and burdens. the consequence is discrimination against older people, and especially women, who live longer, are more at risk of poverty, receive lower pension benefits, and have difficulty accessing public and private services. according to statistics, the proportion of the population aged 65 and over in the european union will increase from 17.1% in 2008 to 30% in 2060, and the proportion of people aged 80 and over from 4.4% to 12.1%. in poland, according to gus, in 2030 there will be as many as 26% of elderly people, or 10 million. it's time to change the way we treat the elderly. it's a huge potential to exploit. it includes, among other things, a vast experience, intellectual capital, knowledge, social competence. the sooner we realise these benefits and start to use them, the better for us, our economies and eu strategies. i therefore welcome the commission's initiative to designate 2012 as the year of active ageing in solidarity between generations. let's promote the so-called silver economy, invest in older people, fight stereotypes. it's our job to make sure that older people want to work. the level, the social culture and the wisdom of a society can be judged by its attitude towards the elderly.

the agenda includes a statement by the council and the commission on the situation of the roma in europe. i would like to welcome to our meeting the representative of the council, mr olivier chastel, vice-president of the european commission vivian reding and commissioner lászló andor. mr olivier chastel will be the first to speak on behalf of the council.
in writing. the roma, or gypsies as they used to be called, are as worthy of respect as any other ethnic group. they are a people who have been present in europe for centuries. the roma also brought a rich culture to europe. and that's how they should be seen, with their poetry, their song, their music, their craftsmanship, their love of travel, their eternal wanderings. attempts have been made to exterminate them, to forcibly settle them, to teach them their customs and to force them to renounce their traditions and values. they didn't give up, they're still with us. but the world is changing. today, their world is dramatically different from the world around them, from the world of career at any cost, consumption, getting rich and success. this situation is a challenge for all of us, for all of europe. the eu must develop an effective support programme for this community, so that, while respecting its tradition, it can break out of its isolation and exclusion. the european union was not created just to live in peace and to get rich. it is also responsible for meeting the most difficult challenges. i also do not believe that any eu country is incapable of bringing the real perpetrators of crime to justice, rather than simply being satisfied with the general suspicion of any group of criminal predisposition.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank you for putting pakistan on the agenda. more importantly i would also like to thank parliament for its active contribution so far to the eu response by organising very useful meetings at committee level and for having exercised your right of scrutiny very rapidly, in fact in one day, this summer. that allowed us to adopt financing decisions swiftly to ensure help could be on its way. my aim today is to convey the impressions gained from my recent mission to pakistan, identify the next steps in our efforts, and conclude with some lessons we can draw for the european union. so let me start with my impressions of pakistan, which were dominated by the fact that this is an incredibly complex situation which is actually two disasters in one. up in the north there are 3 million internally displaced people and refugees, who have had to flee from armed conflicts only to see their camps and their newly-built houses washed away and their newly-built lives destroyed. downstream, in the fertile plains of south pakistan, rural communities have lost not only their homes, but also their livelihoods and a large part of the economy of pakistan on which the country relies. since i briefed the development committee, the numbers indicating the impact of this disaster have actually gone up. all in all, more than 20 million pakistanis have been affected by the floods across the whole country. more than 12 million people are in need of immediate assistance. (the president asked some members to be quiet). i know that the issue that was discussed before is a very important one for european values. as indeed is the one i am addressing now, so thank you. in terms of numbers, just a week ago we were talking about 8 million people being in need of immediate assistance. now the numbers have been revised upwards to 12 million. more than 1.8 million houses have been destroyed or damaged; this number has been revised up from 1.2 million. more than 3.4 million hectares of agricultural land are under water. there are reports of diarrhoea and cholera outbreaks. in these conditions our aid is focusing on the obvious immediate priorities: food, clean water, sanitation, health assistance and shelter. in the face of a disaster of such massive proportions, massive international relief assistance is necessary. so let me move straight to the next point. what has the eu done, and what do we intend to do next? our humanitarian response has been significant. the eu, that is the member states and the commission, has contributed so far a total of eur 231 million for immediate relief assistance, with eur 70 million coming from the commission and the remaining eur 161 million from the member states. twelve member states have also mobilised in-kind assistance through the union’s civil protection mechanism. this makes us the largest donor. our contribution should be measured against the un call for usd 460 million for immediately relief, but i must also stress that this call is going to be revised upwards and we will probably get a new appeal from the un within a week. our assistance was also swift. on 30 july, it became clear that the floods were going to be devastating and our first financial decision for eur 30 million was taken on the next day, 31 july. we activated the european civil protection mechanism, on receiving a request from the pakistani authorities, immediately on 6 august and we deployed a team of 18 experts to coordinate our assistance with the un and the pakistani authorities so it could be most effective. this is the fist time that in-kind aid from member states has been delivered using civil strategic airlift capacity in coordination with the eu military staff. it allowed us to provide much-needed water purification units, mobile hospitals, medicine, shelter and tents. but i am not going to hide the fact that, despite this tremendous effort, there are big challenges ahead of us. so let me highlight four main challenges. first, the humanitarian crisis is far from over. we may not yet have even reached the peak of this crisis. we know from relief workers that, as of today, they expect in the month of september to have reached 6 million people out of the 12 million who are in need of assistance. so in a way the crisis is expanding faster than help can be mobilised to catch up with it. the situation may get worse before it gets better, especially in terms of epidemics. secondly, it is critically important, as we strive to reach as many people as possible, to target those that are most vulnerable. these include poor communities, women, especially women-led households, children, the elderly and the handicapped, because they are likely to be left out if they are not targeted consciously. so this is exactly what the commission aims to do, working with our 26 partners. thirdly, bringing aid speedily is not only a matter of people’s survival. it is also a matter of preserving the stability of a country which faces significant security challenges. popular discontent can easily grow out of desperation and therefore we have to be absolutely determined to try to help people as quickly as possible, as much as possible. fourthly, important as it is to save lives today, we also need to think of recovery starting now. in terms of early recovery there are two very important tasks. to ensure agricultural recovery when the water recedes, we have to be ready with tools and seeds and with help to farmers so they can catch up this planting season. at the same time there is a need to rebuild the critical infrastructure that connects farmers to markets and also allows us to reach out to remote communities. in the long term, obviously, the country is facing a major challenge of recovery. an assessment led by the world bank and the asian development bank, with the commission and the undp, is currently ongoing to determine the long-term recovery needs. we have been working throughout very closely with high representative and vice-president ashton, commissioner piebalgs and commissioner de gucht so that the european union can come up with a comprehensive and holistic proposal as to how we can support the country's development. pakistan will be on the agenda in the next gymnich meeting and at the friends of democratic pakistan meeting in brussels on 14 and15 october. so let me draw some lessons for the eu. i see three. first, the pakistani floods are only one of many reminders that the impact of climate change is profound. looking at the resulting cost, it is very important to focus on disaster preparedness and also on rebuilding a highly vulnerable country devastated by a disaster in a way that is resilient to the risk of climate change. taking a cautious approach, i cannot claim that these floods are caused by climate change. i certainly know, however, that scientific opinion is very clear that the increased frequency and intensity of disasters is due to climate change. secondly, in a year which saw an earthquake in haiti, a drought in the sahel, conflict in sudan and now floods of major proportions in pakistan, once again our budgetary situation is precarious, as our own budget and the emergency aid reserve are almost depleted. yet it is still only the beginning of september. because of the upward trend in the number and intensity of disasters, there is a widening gap in our humanitarian budget which must be taken into account as we prepare for the next financial perspective so we can match our resources to our citizens’ commitment to helping people in need. my third point is that the eu has been on the front line since the outset of the crisis, and yet in the early days our presence was not widely reported in the media. we have to focus very strongly, therefore, on improving not only the efficiency but also the visibility of eu disaster response instruments, as was indicated this morning in the session that you had with president barroso. we will come up with a proposal in the next month. let me conclude by stating with pride, on behalf of our citizens, that pakistan has shown that eu solidarity is not just words; it is deeds and action. we can take pride in that, because our work is not only saving lives but also upholding principles and values that are at the heart of the european project.

the single market and the freedom to work are among the greatest benefits of european integration. we are discussing the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states for the europe 2020 strategy in the midst of the crisis that has hit european economies and labour markets. the fight against unemployment should therefore become one of the priorities of union policy, for which the common budget must provide funds. in this regard, close cooperation at union level and the establishment of current crisis-related objectives as well as strategic objectives are necessary. europe faces long-term challenges such as demographic change and globalisation. both at european level and within member states, we need to ensure the potential for job creation and help with integration into labour markets. however, these priorities cannot be pursued at the expense of increased administrative and regulatory burdens. we must ensure that the member states' actions in areas such as the economy, employment and social affairs are consistent. however, guidelines and common objectives at union level may in no case undermine the competences of the member states.
mr president, there is a high risk of ‘jobless recovery’ or ‘jobless growth’ and europe cannot afford that to happen. firstly, we must focus our employment strategy on the union’s comparative advantages – which are education, research and green technology. secondly, we must avoid a trade-off between innovation and job creation; such a trade-off can be avoided if innovation is inclusive. thirdly, we must strike a sustainable balance between support for existing jobs and the creation of new ones. investing in a highly-skilled labour force will go hand in hand with innovation. of course there will be jobs that are not sufficiently rewarded by the markets, and we must have policy instruments to cope with this. fourthly, there is a need to activate both labour demand and supply policy measures. there are plenty of employment policy instruments available, but they must be put together in a good and comprehensive policy framework. fifthly, we must successfully orchestrate efforts and responsibilities and policy instruments between all levels of governance – european, national, regional and local. last but not least, the internal market must provide for full mobility of the labour force, particularly in terms of career and lifelong learning; and it must do so horizontally geography-wise.
mr. chairman, please! in the european employment policy debate, we talk more about fighting unemployment and providing adequate social protection, but unfortunately we spend much less time on issues such as increasing labour force participation and supporting entrepreneurs who create new jobs. the priority of promoting vocational activity is included in the guidelines. but remember, along with priorities, it's also incredibly important to implement them. the european commission's communication is worrying, as it shows that 70% of the social fund for increasing employment has been used by beneficiaries who are educated and employed, and only 30% by those who are looking for work. i hope that the implementation of the 2020 strategy will reverse this, and indeed increase the effectiveness of the social fund, while at the same time contributing to an increase in the labour force participation rate, and thus finally becoming competitive in the global labour market.
i would like to start by congratulating my colleague csaba öry for a great opinion. the guidelines should be clear and simple, and the reduction in the number of guidelines is a step in the right direction. increasing the level of labour force participation is a key challenge. it is not enough to reduce structural unemployment. it is important to anticipate and prevent, to educate and develop entrepreneurship and flexibility. it is not enough to increase the number of people entering higher education. higher education institutions must provide training at the appropriate level and in areas where there is a need for staff. the best way out of poverty is to get a job. however, individual support programmes are often needed. it is also necessary to measure the effectiveness of actions in this area. the success of the europe 2020 strategy depends on its close link with cohesion policy. the simplified and de-bureaucratized structural funds should serve the objectives of the strategy.
in writing. the union economy is slowly recovering from the crisis that began in 2008. however, employment levels in most eu countries remain worryingly low below pre-crisis levels. young people are one of the groups most affected by the problem of rising unemployment during the economic crisis. since 2008, the number of young people out of work has increased dramatically and the unemployment rate for those aged 15 to 25 is now higher than the overall unemployment rate in many member states. these figures are worrying, especially in the context of the ageing of the european union's populations, which means that the number of people of working age is decreasing in relation to those who are retired. it is therefore particularly important to support young people in taking up their first job and finding stable employment. the report on the guidelines for employment policies under the europe 2020 strategy is a positive step towards improving the situation of young people in the labour market. however, additional measures at member state level are needed to ensure a significant improvement. particular emphasis should be placed on supporting young people in finding their first job and on combating unemployment among graduates. providing a skilled workforce with skills that meet market demand and preparing graduates for entry into the labour market are just some of the tasks that should be undertaken at school level.

the rapporteur. - ladies and gentlemen, the 2011 budget is not only the first budget implemented under the lisbon treaty, as my predecessors have rightly pointed out, but it is also the first budget on the basis of which the new political ideas that the lisbon treaty brings will be implemented. this is also the fifth budget drawn up on the basis of the 2007-13 multiannual financial perspective, so we should already know a lot about its weaknesses and strengths in the fifth budget i appreciate the efforts of the belgian presidency in preparing the council reading, but i am very concerned that as many as seven member states voted against the council reading. i sometimes get the irresistible and unpleasant impression that when the finance ministers of the individual member states look at their national budgets and see the item 'contribution to the budget of the european union', they think about how to reduce it, how to get rid of it, without thinking about what is really happening with this contribution, what is being financed by it, without thinking and debating about the consequences of reducing it. i very much regret that such a debate is lacking and was lacking, in my view, when the council's draft was adopted. i also feel that the council's proposal lacks the necessary justification in terms of detail. why have these budget lines been reduced and not others? why were they reduced to this dimension and not another? i hope that as we continue our work, we will be able to clarify and clarify the missing information. we have a greater responsibility to ensure that the next budgetary process for 2011 is detailed and accurate and that we consider each budget line responsibly, that is, not just thinking about percentages but also about what is important, what we want to finance and what we can sacrifice in order to save. i would like to emphasize the priority of the european parliament, which is no longer surprising to anyone, it is not the only one. this is a priority for youth, mobility and education. if the council proposes to cut the main line of this priority, namely the line relating to lifelong learning, by eur 25 million, it is difficult to talk about dialogue here. i hope, however, that we will return to a serious dialogue during the consent procedure, because we have made our priorities clear enough to take them into account more than by proposing such cuts. we are currently in the process of preparing the reading in the european parliament. we are very far along, and i hope that our reading will be adopted by the committee on budgets by the end of the month and that we will be able to show at the plenary session at the beginning of october that a good and constructive budget can be adopted under the lisbon treaty. i look forward to good cooperation with both the belgian presidency and the commission.
on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. there can be no free and democratic society without free and pluralistic media guaranteeing the transmission of reliable information and different points of view and opinions to the people. media for democracy is like the circulatory system for the body. this metaphor from the medical world seems to be more relevant here than anywhere else. if the circulation fails, the flow of blood is impeded, and the body inevitably weakens and begins to get sick. it's no different with the relationship between media pluralism and democracy. if the flow of information fails and is blocked, democracy is in trouble. it seems obvious to us, but it is not, contrary to what we think, because we do not give it the attention it deserves, even in the european union. it is high time that the institutions of the european union started to pay much more attention to this fundamental - i emphasise what the commissioner said: 'fundamental problem'. the question is whether we are doing enough and whether the eu institutions are doing enough to ensure that the bulk of media coverage is not concentrated in the hands of a few. the aim is also to prevent the concentration of different media in different areas, i.e. television, press, internet and radio, by individual operators. it seems that the european union should do much more to introduce legislation to ensure decentralisation in each of these areas of the media market, not just in television. often, it should be emphasized, the limits of expression in commercial media are determined by the interests of their owners, the interests of advertisers. the danger is also that media owners who are sympathetic to certain political groups may prefer their viewpoints. in poland, there is a problem of a closed media system, as some commentators call it. all the major media outlets speak with one voice. journalists who go outside of this mainstream, who present a different point of view, are met with negative coverage, sometimes with infamy actions, or even attempts to discredit. so there's a problem of a great asymmetry in the transmission of information and opinion, which is the foundation of a democratic society. i can name journalists - editor sakiewicz, pospieszalski, editor stankiewicz, jankowska, who have been meeting with harassment in poland recently, you could say that, although it's a strong word. these people have a beautiful tradition in the struggle for a free and independent poland, for a free and democratic society, for a free and democratic media. now in europe we have to remember this and do everything we can to bring about a real pluralism in the media market.
i am very pleased that the issue of freedom of expression is the subject of today's debate, because in june of this year i initiated, together with other members of the european parliament, the creation of a reflection group on this issue. invited journalists in strasbourg spoke about the forms of ostracism used against media representatives. the participants of this meeting presented ways to restrict freedom of speech by imposing huge financial penalties by the courts for raising awkward historical topics and defending traditional values, blocking the distribution of films presenting awkward topics, such as the causes of the smolensk disaster, harassing the constant controls of catholic radio stations that do not sympathize with the rulers. but i would like to mention a very spectacular case of an investigative journalist in poland being bullied into breaking his psyche with false accusations. in desperation, he tried to commit suicide. in his farewell letter to his children, he wrote that they should not believe the slanderous things they write about him. this is just one of the many cases we've seen during the june meeting. the next meeting of the reflection group on the defence of the right to freedom of expression will take place on 22 september in strasbourg.

president of the council. − on the basis of the commission communication entitled 'possible options for post-2010 with regard to the european union's biodiversity perspective and objectives', the council adopted on 15 march 2010 conclusions entitled 'biodiversity: post-2010 vision and objectives at eu and global level, and international access and benefit-sharing regime'. in its conclusions, the council expressed its serious concern that the 2010 biodiversity targets have not been met at eu and global level, that biodiversity loss is continuing at an unacceptable rate and that it has very serious ecological, economic and social consequences. however, he stressed that these objectives played an essential role in enabling useful measures to be put in place to promote biodiversity. it set out a long-term vision that by 2050 biodiversity in the european union and the ecosystem services it provides, its natural capital, will be protected, valued and restored in an appropriate manner, taking into account the intrinsic value of biodiversity and its essential contribution to human well-being and economic prosperity, in such a way that catastrophic changes caused by biodiversity loss are avoided. it also set a headline target of halting biodiversity loss and the degradation of ecosystem services in the european union by 2020, ensuring their restoration as far as possible, while enhancing the eu's contribution to preventing biodiversity loss globally. in the context of the eu's priorities for the protection and enhancement of biodiversity, the council noted that the destruction, fragmentation and degradation of habitats are the main threats to biodiversity. as regards the origin of this habitat situation, the council highlighted the harmful change in land use, the over-exploitation and unsustainable use of natural resources, invasive alien species, the illicit trade in endangered species, ocean acidification and, of course, pollution. climate change could also, increasingly, even exacerbate some of the effects, for example, on the number of species threatened with extinction. with regard to the europe 2020 strategy, the council's broad economic policy guidelines call on the member states and the union to put measures in place, to turn environmental challenges into growth opportunities and to use natural resources more efficiently, thus also contributing to ensuring biodiversity. the role of biodiversity was also clearly underlined by the european council in its conclusions of march 2010, when it stated that there is an urgent need to reverse the persistent trend of biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation. the european council endorses the long-term vision for biodiversity by 2050 and the 2020 target set out in the council conclusions of 15 march 2010 referred to above.

president of the council. − the objective of our policy towards the western balkans region is to contribute to the stability of the region and to help the countries of the region to establish lasting peace, democracy, stability and prosperity. in 1999, the union decided to implement the stabilisation and association process - the framework for the accession process until the possible accession of these countries - to better align the european perspective of these countries. this perspective remains essential for stability, reconciliation and the future of the region. it is being developed and implemented in accordance with the thessaloniki agenda and the renewed consensus on enlargement, which establishes fair and rigorous conditionality. the council has therefore repeatedly reaffirmed the european union's unequivocal commitment to the european perspective of the western balkan countries, including most recently at the foreign affairs council on 14 june following the meeting in sarajevo on 2 june. over the years, the union has signed six stabilisation and association agreements with the countries of the region, four of which have already entered into force. in october 2009, the commission proposed to open accession negotiations with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. the accession negotiations with croatia, which have been ongoing since october 2005, are in their final stages. politically, the union remains committed with all its instruments - three common security and defence policy missions, two in bosnia and herzegovina and one in kosovo, and three special representatives in the region, in skopje, pristina and sarajevo. the financial assistance will amount to over eur 900 million in 2010 and will reach eur 1 billion in 2013. in total, the european union's financial assistance to the countries of the region has exceeded 13 billion since 1991. as regards the dates of accession, they are entirely dependent on compliance with the copenhagen criteria for accession and the conditions set by the stabilisation and association process. this process has established a clear sequence: stability and association agreement, commission opinion on the application for accession, candidate status, accession negotiations and finally accession. the council looks forward to the next steps in the process, but it is up to the governments of the countries in the region to respect the conditions set, to continue - or even to step up - the pace of necessary reforms and to address the major challenges. the states of the region should increase their efforts in the fight against corruption and organised crime, in strengthening administrative capacity and in resolving outstanding issues. the objectives of the stabilisation and association process can only be achieved if the peoples and governments of the region take an active, responsible and determined part in it. the future of the region ultimately depends on its peoples and governments themselves. regional cooperation and the good neighbour policy contribute to reconciliation and the settlement of bilateral disputes. these policies are at the heart of the union's approach to the region and have been systematically promoted by the union since 1995. in this context, on 14 june the council called on the countries concerned to settle outstanding issues with neighbouring countries. i would like to conclude by recalling that in november 2009 the council decided to liberalize visas for citizens of three countries in the region and is preparing an identical decision for citizens of albania and bosnia and herzegovina. i hope that the european parliament and the council will take this decision again this year. finally, as regards the impact of enlargement on the union's budget in the current period and over the period 2014-2020, the council cannot comment at this stage, as it is still awaiting the commission's proposal on the next financial perspective.
