the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, we create community law where it is needed. this law must be correctly implemented in the legal systems of the member states, and it must be clear, transparent and understandable to citizens. but in practice, it doesn't seem that simple. european law is often described as confusing, imprecise and leaving too much room for interpretation. the widespread delays in transposing legislation have led to the creation of article 260 of the lisbon treaty, a provision that makes it easier for the european commission to punish countries for failing to implement community law properly and in a timely manner. in this context, i welcomed with great interest the idea of smart regulation put forward by president barroso, the political guidelines a year ago. in encouraging the commission to pursue the smart regulation agenda and taking advantage of the presence of its representatives here today, i would like to ask what is happening in this regard? how has the commission implemented it? i hope that wasn't just a fancy technocratic slogan. another thing that president barroso has promised is an ex post evaluation. i agree that we should pay more attention to what happens to eu law once it has been adopted. is it being implemented correctly and, if not, why are there delays? is it understandable to the public? if european law does not have a positive impact on the economy, the environment and society, then all our work is meaningless. hence the question to the commission: what happens to the ex post evaluation? how does it differ from the enforcement mechanisms used so far? another issue is the impact assessment that accompanies every new law proposal. parliament has repeatedly pointed out that the commission, when proposing new legislation, must carry out a detailed analysis of its implementation based on reliable data. in my report i looked at the problem of impact assessment from two perspectives: firstly, the content, i.e. what consequences the commission should examine from the proposed legal acts. i would urge the commission to pay particular attention to the social impact of its initiatives. answers to questions such as the impact of a given legislative proposal on the european labour market, on employment in particular age groups and sectors, are particularly important in the context of the economic crisis. i think that, up to now, this aspect has not been sufficiently analysed. on the other hand, i would like to address the issue of the independence of impact assessments, which is closely linked to the issue of better lawmaking. in the report i stress the need to ensure full independence and adequate resources for the body which monitors the quality of impact assessments, and which, i would remind you, was set up in response to parliament's requests. i am referring to the impact assessment board, which is composed of the highest officials of the commission and reports to its president. at the same time, i am very cautious about hiring external experts to assess the impact, because parliament is not really in a position to control their independence. i also refer to the programme for reducing administrative burdens in the report. the european union is too often associated with complex and unnecessary bureaucracy. i am therefore pleased that the commission is planning to reduce these charges by up to 33% by 2012. however, i have also been receiving signals that in some cases the exemption of companies from administrative duties leads to lower standards, for example in relation to occupational safety. i therefore urge the commission to look at the problem in a global way. reducing administrative costs cannot be at the expense of lowering social standards in the european union. i also refer to the work of the high level group on administrative burdens, chaired by mr stauber. i am positive about the work of the group so far and welcomed the extension of its mandate until 2013. i hope that parliament will be informed of how the group assesses the implementation of the programme to reduce administrative burdens at european union level. finally, i would like to refer to the issues related to the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, and specifically to the practical aspects of deepening contacts with national parliaments and implementing the citizens' initiative. i hope that interparliamentary cooperation will not only cover issues relating to the control of the subsidiarity principle, but will also contribute to a better transposition of european law. as for the citizens' initiative, i think there are millions of citizens waiting for parliament's position on this issue. i understand that the committee on constitutional affairs is working intensively on this issue and i hope that the first reading of the document will take place later this year. i'm hoping for a productive discussion now.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, allow me to start by thanking mrs geringer de oedenberg for an excellent report. she will see from my introductory remarks that the commission fully agrees with most of it. we very much like the effort and strong emphasis the european parliament puts on smart regulation because this is clearly the way forward. i am very glad to announce to you today that on tuesday the commission took the final steps to withdraw 59 pending proposals listed in the 2010 work programmes which we will not pursue any more because we see that they are outdated or have outlived their initial purpose. this is also how we are honouring the commitment we undertook in our framework agreement negotiations. i would also like to confirm to you that the commission will adopt a communication on smart regulation on 6 october, as well as the annual report on better lawmaking where we will be dealing in a detailed manner with subsidiarity issues. i believe that these documents will address in detail the issues raised by mrs geringer de oedenberg in her report, so i will just limit myself to some key points. the first point on which i think we all agree, and the financial crisis is clear proof of that, is that regulation has a positive and necessary role in assuring that markets deliver sustainable prosperity for all. at the same time, i totally agree with mrs geringer de oedenberg that we need to be very careful how we legislate because we do not want to overburden businesses, and especially smes, with unnecessary administrative burdens. we are doing our utmost to reduce the administrative burden in existing legislation and also in the legislation we are preparing. we are going to work very hard to pursue the four main activities related to smart regulation. we are going to continue with impact assessments. we are going to do our utmost to further improve quality. we are going to simplify legislation which is already on the books. we will continue our efforts to reduce administrative burdens for businesses, and we are also going to evaluate regulations which are already in place to see how efficient this legislation is. i have to say that we have some disagreements and shall limit myself to two issues. the first relates to the independent body accountable to parliament. we are pleased at how the impact assessments are being done within the commission. the commission, as you know very well, is accountable to the european parliament, so parliament as a legislator is the body which in the end controls the quality of legislation. the second issue is recasting. you know we have exchanges of opinions between the commission and parliament reflected in the exchange of letters between our presidents, where we see that the current situation which arose after the changes to the european parliament rules of procedure raised questions about the use of the recasting technique. ultimately, if this situation persists, the use of recasting for simplification initiatives and for amending existing legislation will no longer make sense. otherwise, i think we have very strong agreement on other matters and our mutual goal is to legislate smartly, efficiently and in a way that is very good for our citizens and our businesses.
author of the draft opinion of the committee on constitutional affairs. - mr president! - what are you doing? first of all, i would like to congratulate and thank the rapporteur for the very good cooperation she has shown in the preparation of this report. i am also pleased that my opinion, which was prepared in the afco committee, was very widely taken into account in the final form of this document. over the years of the communities and then the european union, we have come to realise that a single community regulation for all member states is more effective in a world of free movement of goods, services and people than complex, and very often extremely complex, legislation at the level of 27 member states. however, new and existing rules should not create further barriers for those who benefit from them. they should regulate life, not prevent it. the basic idea is to simplify eu law and create a friendly legal environment that will make it easier for citizens to function in this tangle of european regulations. however, this should in no way lead to a lowering of the existing standards in this area, but on the contrary, should lead to their raising. this year's report highlights a number of changes brought into force by the lisbon treaty for the union that will have a significant impact on the whole eu legislative process. the increased role of the european parliament, the european legislative initiative and the further reduction of administrative burdens for smes will naturally draw the attention of union citizens to the process itself, its quality and efficiency. the greater involvement of the parliament in the eu legislative process naturally brings with it greater responsibility. citizens will thus see parliament as an institution with a real impact on the law it creates and will therefore look more closely at our parliamentary work. therefore, another important issue is to ensure an independent, comprehensive impact assessment. the rapporteur and i differ on this point in the commission's view of the matter. but we all want to have an objective and reliable basis on which to set our course and to make decisions on future regulation. we must also remember that good law is one of the safeguards for the effective implementation and subsequent application of eu law in the member states, which unfortunately is still a rather serious problem throughout the european union.
mr. chairman, congratulations on the report. it rightly stresses the need to make the law simple, transparent and understandable to citizens. but we ourselves, here in the european parliament, are calling for this, and we are preparing reports, declarations and resolutions in language which is very complex and difficult for ordinary citizens to understand. many of the documents prepared are written in illegible legal language. the resolutions in which we inform third countries of our values and speak about human rights violations are also drafted in this language. i therefore think that parliament should join the commission's clear writing campaign. this action provides information on how to prepare documents so that they are legible.
the rapporteur. - in conclusion, i would like to thank all my colleagues and the commissioner for a fruitful discussion. i am delighted to have had the opportunity to work on the better regulation report this year, the first year after the entry into force of the lisbon treaty and the year of the adoption by the council of the european strategy eu 2020. both documents will have an impact on many aspects of better lawmaking, and the report was a good opportunity to address them. in preparing this report, i met with a wide range of stakeholders, seeking to hear from business and labour, trade unions and organisations such as the etuc. i think that the absolute unanimity in the vote in the legal affairs committee shows that we have managed to find a reasonable compromise between the expectations of all the political groups. i would like to thank all my colleagues for their excellent cooperation and i would like to add that this was an exceptional cooperation, because it was above political level, which is rare in this house. i also hope that the vote in plenary today will be a success.

in writing. intellectual property is a broad concept covering both patent law, the right to use designs and trademarks (logos) and copyright law. the report is limited to piracy by exploitation of copyright, and mainly of another's trademark. the aim is to enforce the control rules by: 1. setting up an observatory; 2. applying administrative procedures; 3. appropriate intergovernmental agreements. a trade mark serves to distinguish the goods or services of one trader from the same goods of another trader. unfair competition may seek to exploit the reputation of a product or service in the marketplace. all the proposed methods of fighting piracy are the expansion of a kind of "police" at the expense of the taxpayer. rather, the need to strengthen customs offices is mainly to better detect the threat of harmful plant protection products, counterfeit medicines, harmful food and feed. liberals on the one hand want to weaken the state, which is supposed to be cheap, and on the other hand they want to make it a monopoly, and this can be solved by associations representing industries. the state should be the only party to settle any disputes. to this end, the following community laws should be developed and enforced: - patent law, - law on registered designs and trademarks, - copyright law. there is also a need to better monitor the community customs border and the excessive, competitive flow of goods from third countries and their quality.

author of the draft opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety. the citizens of europe expect the european union to take actions and decisions that will clearly and concretely express our will to manage transnational infrastructure together. this regulation meets those expectations. this is particularly the case for transport, i.e. the ability to move quickly anywhere in europe (high-speed rail, road and air links) and for security, including energy security. for several years now we have been calling in this parliament for energy supply to be treated as a strategic political issue. europe cannot be dependent on a single supplier, as is the case for central and eastern europe, which gets most of its supplies from russia. gazprom has repeatedly stated that it views gas as a strategic weapon to increase moscow's political influence by making it more difficult to supply blue fuel. we, as poles, polish meps, have pointed out the selfish nature of the northern gas pipeline, an investment undertaken without consulting the member states of the european union. today's gas solidarity regulation is an expression of europe's awareness that only together can we build an effective solidarity-based gas supply and distribution system. a system that will not leave any gas-deprived country on its own. however, the implementation of the regulation requires the political will of governments and the financial effort of the european union.

in writing. the adoption of the regulation on security of gas supply opens the way to the future creation of a common gas market at eu level. important provisions in this document include the introduction of an obligation to prepare prevention and crisis plans in each country, the obligation to declare a state of emergency at eu level when two countries declare a state of crisis, the application of the geopolitical risk criterion in the overall risk assessment of the eu gas security. the two-way transmission of energy will enable a country in energy distress to receive the necessary help from another country that has the resources at its disposal. this is undoubtedly the beginning of the application of solutions based on the idea of cooperation and solidarity. referring to the issue of energy diversification will allow member states to step up their efforts in this area and will support projects already under way such as nabucco. in conclusion, thanks to the solutions proposed in the regulation and increased investment in infrastructure, we are able to protect ourselves, or better protect ourselves, from the situation that occurred in 2008 in ukraine. it is an illusion to be completely independent of russia in terms of gas supplies, but we can at least strengthen our position in negotiations with it. i would like to thank all those who have helped to reach a compromise on an issue of such importance to the union as a whole.

we have adopted an important report on the security of gas supply. the solutions it proposes are a step in the right direction, but they do not provide a full sense of security for society and the economy. the experience of recent years has shown that the actions of a number of member states have been directed towards their own interests rather than towards the construction of a genuine, coordinated and solidary european policy in this field. we must separate the so-called extraction from the transmission, eliminate the monopoly, separate the gas issues from the international policy. diversification of gas production sources and supply routes, infrastructure development, cooperation between gas operators and their joint transnational activities are necessary actions to be implemented. this document is, in my view, the beginning of the construction of a common energy policy.

in writing. statistics show that up to half of patients take medicines not as prescribed by their doctors, and about three quarters of patients would like to have easy access to reliable information on the effects of medicines and their possible side effects the proposal for pharmacovigilance will enhance patient safety and ensure their right to better information on the uses and effects of medicines. the creation of information portals at both european and national level is an important step towards transparency in medicines information. the national portals will be linked to the european portal and will have to contain a description of each product, a leaflet and an impact assessment. the european medicines agency, in cooperation with the member states and the commission, will supervise this database where information will be collected and compared as part of pharmacovigilance. i think this is an important step towards ensuring that patients have the right to better, reliable and objective information about pharmaceutical products.

in a constant state of concern for the economic and social development of areas with special needs, such as mountainous regions, islands or sparsely populated areas. the treaty of lisbon reinforces the importance of territorial cohesion. this is one of the objectives of the union as set out in article 174. this is why the commission has launched a comprehensive discussion process with the green paper on territorial cohesion. one of the key outcomes of this consultation was not necessarily to create new and additional financial resources, but instead to highlight the importance of integrated territorial development approaches and better consideration of the strengths of different regions. the regional characteristics are, in my view, basically strengths of the respective regions. therefore, regional characteristics - whether it is the island location, the mountainous area or sparsely populated areas - do not automatically create a problem or a higher need for support, especially since these areas are by no means uniform. there is therefore no one-size-fits-all solution for these seemingly interconnected regions. the commission attaches the utmost importance to ensuring the harmonious and joint growth of the regions. i therefore want to work together to implement the europe 2020 strategy in all regions, rather than jeopardising rather than promoting the joint work of different strategies for differently structured areas. we therefore believe that there is no need for a specific policy for areas with special circumstances, but that on the contrary we must also strengthen the integrated approach of our policy together with other policies and encourage the regions even more to create programmes tailored to their particular needs. we need to strengthen the territorial dimension in all policy areas, both in design and implementation. this gives rise to four priority areas of action. firstly, to bring regional policy closer to the citizens and to the regions. in the interests of territorial cohesion, we must strengthen the consistency of policies at the various levels. this also means taking the multi-level governance approach seriously and integrating all relevant stakeholders into the design and implementation of our policies. but this also means making greater use of existing opportunities for interregional, multiregional and multinational cooperation to better take account of the common challenges of certain areas, such as large mountain regions such as the alps or the pyrenees. secondly, better coordination of regional policies. territorial cohesion also means taking better account of the complementarity and coherence between regional and sectoral policies. we need to be clear about the impact of policies on the regions. the commission has therefore set up the inter-service group on territorial cohesion, which brings together representatives of the different directorates-general. the main task is to analyse the individual sectoral policies and their impact on the regions, and in particular on those with particular geographical challenges. thirdly, territorial cooperation to strengthen european integration. cooperation is particularly important for areas with particular geographical challenges. it is about solving common challenges across borders, whether in the form of macro-regional strategies such as the baltic sea strategy, interregional networks or the exchange of good practice. fourthly, and finally, we must make better use of regional expertise. in order to deliver a targeted and subsidiary regional development policy and thus support the europe 2020 objectives, we need to know even more about the situation of the regions and the impact of policies. we need an even better monitoring system, which can process the existing data even better, and we need targeted indicators to ensure appropriate policy. this will only be possible in conjunction with the regions, the regional economic operators and the citizens. ladies and gentlemen, we need a strong regional policy for all regions, which takes account of the different needs and specificities of all regions. i am pleased to be able to discuss with the european parliament very soon the future of regional policy and also of the special areas on the basis of the fifth cohesion report.

member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, trademarks are of real importance in modern commerce. they help to identify the origin of products and services, to guarantee a constant level of quality, to convey the image of the company. access to the community trade mark is a challenge for the development of our businesses and also for the fight against counterfeiting. you have expressed concern about the decisions taken by certain national trade mark offices. those decisions seek to restrict the use of the community trade mark by invoking a requirement that the use of a community trade mark in a single member state does not constitute genuine use of the mark. i would like to thank the members who have drawn the attention and the vigilance of the commission to this situation, which we are following very closely. the great merit of the community trade mark is that it offers all businesses, including small and medium-sized enterprises, an effective tool for protecting trade marks at european level. until now, the rule that any genuine use of a community trade mark by the proprietor is sufficient, irrespective of where it is used in the community, has always been regarded by users as one of its main advantages. this rule is consistent with the unitary character of the community trade mark. it is also consistent with the very principle of the single market. any further restriction on the use of the community trade mark could therefore have serious consequences for the fight against counterfeiting, which will be the subject - i repeat this to parliament - of the commission's commitment to an action plan against piracy and counterfeiting, in particular in the draft single market act. what are these consequences? firstly, the introduction of a new requirement could slow down the fight against trademark infringement. the community trade mark is an effective tool in the fight against counterfeiting, as i have just said, because it provides unfailing protection throughout the european union and at all its external borders. it is essential for counterfeit products, which are currently being imported in large quantities from third countries, to be seized at the external borders of our union under community customs regulations. and then, the introduction of such a requirement could make access to the community trade mark more difficult for small and mediumsized enterprises, for start-ups. these companies often operate at the national level and only start exporting, expanding their business beyond borders, after their business has proved successful. the growth of these companies could therefore be made more difficult if they were no longer able to obtain and use a community trade mark before expanding their business. and it would also be in contradiction with many of our policies which are aimed precisely at promoting the development of small and mediumsized enterprises, which - i remind you - represent more than 95% of european enterprises. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, i want to confirm or assure you that my services will be following very closely these developments in the member states. at this stage we are confident that the national courts will not confirm these decisions which we consider to be inconsistent with the unitary character of the community trade mark and the principles of the single market, as i have already said.

and that we need to make better use of eu positions and the projections of eu powers in foreign policy. we can achieve this by making better use of foreign policy synergy and we need to work on member states and the european institutions singing from one hymn sheet with one voice. i therefore appreciate highly the importance president van rompuy placed on ownership of eu foreign policy, not only by the institutions, but also by the leaders of the member states, because only in that way, when we speak with one voice, not only multilaterally but also in our bilateral contacts, will we achieve the necessary results. a couple of words on economic governance. here again i see strong support in parliament for maintaining the momentum of the change we started this spring. there is very clear support for building up a new and better system and i would like to assure the honourable members of this parliament that we are not going to look critically only at budget deficit. we are also going to take a very close look at the issue of debt – how to manage it better and how to monitor it better in the future. parliament will have the chance to discuss this issue annually because commissioners will be coming every january for the annual growth survey which will start the so-called european semester, and where you will see the complex picture of the european economy and the economic state of the different member states. this will be a very welcome opportunity to have a deeper debate on this issue at the beginning of every year. at the same time, i would like to assure you that we have not forgotten the importance of growth and employment. for that we need to use the eu 2020 strategy tools, because we would like to set the european economy on new bases, on new wheels, and we want to pursue the smart inclusive green – meaning healthy – growth of the european economy. therefore, we need to focus more on employment, on better education, on high quality youth policies and, of course, on the reduction of poverty. these two strengths – better surveillance and smarter economic policies – must go hand in hand, because only in that way will we achieve the necessary results. so if the commission is for something, it is for smart consolidation. turning to the external action service, i think that baroness ashton made it very clear that she is fully committed to building a professional european external action service which will reflect european values, strength and also the european landscape. therefore, geographic and gender balance, as well as an agreed balance among the sources for the european external action service from our institutions and member states, as has been agreed, are very important in building up the new professional staff of the european external action service. cathy ashton undertook to inform you regularly about progress in building up the service. i believe that the progress achieved in the transitional period to 2013 will answer present concerns, which i fully understand. for my last point, let me thank you all for your insistence on respecting european law, cherishing european values and undertaking to look for better ways to alleviate the plight of the roma people and for their integration. more than eur 17.5 billion have been allocated to measures benefiting roma and other vulnerable groups by the commission and 12 member states, mostly from the european social fund. however, we have to look at how we use our means and the instruments which are at our disposal. i would call for these to be used more efficiently. for that we will need to take a new fresh look at how to do this in the future. if we do this together it will definitely be much more efficient, and will bring much better results than in the past.
president of the european council. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank all those who have spoken in the debate. i know that it is a difficult task to answer, but i know that it is also a very difficult task to summarize, in one minute, the points of view that we want to develop. and so, i won't be able to respond to all the comments. only on two important chapters, a few remarks. chapter one: foreign policy, foreign policy. we've come a long way from here. there was mr. solana's important work. we forget that too often. i have listed the common positions we have been able to reach with the european union on iran, the middle east and certain trade issues. but we also took a step forward, particularly in our position at the g20, which is the world's largest annual conference. and when i joined the european council as prime minister, there were still, a year ago, separate meetings of all the member states that are part of the g20. they were establishing a common position. i asked, demanded and have since demanded that there be a common position of the 27. even though not all countries are present at the g20, mr barroso and i represent the union as a union, and so we have a common position. i can assure you that at the g8 and g20 meetings the member states and the union representatives are delivering the same message. there are also positive developments and progress, and i should like to stress that there has been some progress in this respect. and this is the biggest international world conference, which is the g20. are there any more problems? of course you are! and we are still reeling from the trauma of copenhagen. we had a common position. we had a common message. but we have failed to impose, to make others accept our position. the result: everyone loses, because the results are totally unsatisfactory. so there has been progress in various areas, but more work needs to be done in the right direction. i was asked what your message will be at the summit with china. i would ask you to read carefully, not superficially, but carefully, what has been written in the european council conclusions. i suggest you do. of course, we are not going to indicate in the conclusions of the european council the strategy we are going to develop, the balances we are going to present to our strategic partners, such as the chinese partners. but if you read the text, you will notice that there are, in fact, new accents and that the notion of reciprocity is going to be introduced. it's not just us who react to the message of others. we have become claimants to a number of partners. and we need this concept of reciprocity. the european parliament is involved, and even more so since the treaty of lisbon, in trade agreements, in complete co-legislation when it comes to international agreements and international trade agreements. and so there is progress, but more needs to be done. the summit with the american president will be prepared at the october council. we will agree on the messages that mr barroso and i will give to the american president. we shall agree to speak on behalf of the union, on behalf of the 27. so again, step by step, we're going to go in the right direction. the second point is economic policy. we have had a very clever economic policy in the last two years, much cleverer than in the past. we lost ten years. we could have acted in time on budgetary and competitiveness issues, but we did not. and that's exactly why we have problems today. what have we done since the financial crisis? beyond the bailouts of banks and others, a very risky expansionary policy was pursued in 2008 and, for the most part, in 2009. a risky policy because it increased budget deficits. but as soon as there was a recovery in growth - which was thought to be slow at the beginning of the year - a policy of fiscal consolidation was initiated, of gradual reduction of budget deficits, not in a brutal way, but gradually. even for this year, we still have a slightly expansionary effect. we have been conducting a smart monetary policy. the markets have always been liquid, so there has not been, as in the 1930s, a liquidity breakdown. the policy of low interest rates has been implemented so that recovery can take place and the budgets of the member states are not affected by very high interest rates. we have pursued a prudent, wise and gradual policy on the budgetary and monetary front. why would you do that? not for the sake of making serious budget cuts, as we are going to do now, not for the sake of reducing debt, but to have sustainable economic growth, to have a fruitful employment policy. all these efforts are in the service of employment, to reduce unemployment. there is a great social purpose in every effort we make. we're not doing this for the pleasure of reducing debts and deficits. it is only a tool: the objective, of course, is employment and the reduction of unemployment. and as the vice-president of the commission has just said, to put this in an even more social context, we have included the poverty target in our 2020 objectives. we had to fight to get it. we have integrated an education policy and we are maintaining a cohesion policy. the structural funds are being maintained, and i hope they will be maintained in the financial perspectives that are to be drawn up, so that living standards are the most balanced in the european union. the aim of all our action is therefore a highly social aim, the rest are only instruments. i wanted to tell you that at the end of this debate.
president van rompuy, thank you very much for your report from the european council and for the discussions with us. we look forward to your next important discussions with the european parliament. the next european council will be in october, so there will not be a big break between now and then.
i fully support parliament's position on mountain regions, islands and sparsely populated areas. these are usually areas of special natural value and care should be taken to combine support for them with the protection of natural assets. we should support these regions in such a way that they can make good use of what they have to offer in an innovative way, but also that they take care to protect this wealth in an appropriate way. i would also like to draw attention to the plight of farmers in those areas where farming may be the only or one of the very few means of subsistence. they need special care. this solidarity does not have to be limited to financial support, but also to supporting the education of young people and supporting innovative technologies.
in writing. - the most important thing from the point of view of poland, but also of the whole union, is that we have uniform regulations. today, a number of regulations have been incorporated into the legal order as part of the financial supervision package. the financial crisis has exposed a number of weaknesses in the global financial system, including the lack of proper supervision of financial institutions in europe. in response to these shortcomings, we have adopted proposals to strengthen the supervision of financial markets in the eu. poland has been in favour of the establishment of strong and independent supervisory authorities with the ability to issue binding decisions at supranational level from the outset. we wanted the supervisory bodies, which will be european in nature, to be very strong and have a very wide range of competences. this objective has been largely achieved. it must be considered that a satisfactory solution has been found. one that reconciles the national interests of 27 countries. this is largely due to the european parliament. for the first time, meps spoke with one voice on financial matters and agreed on the merits of the decisions taken.
in writing. − the crisis has highlighted the weakness of the eu's supervisory framework divided along national borders and the need for better supervision of cross-border financial institutions. european policymakers have recognised the need to establish a single system of financial supervision. the european commission has been working hard for a year to establish a european framework for this supervision. from the outset, parliament pushed for strong eu control of financial markets, convincing the council and the commission to adopt its position. three new supervisory bodies will be established, whose powers will go far beyond the advisory nature of the current supervisory committees. the fourth body, the european systemic risk board (esrb), will be tasked with closely monitoring the market situation and warning of emerging risks in the european economy. economic and monetary union requires the establishment of a well-functioning european system of financial supervision and today's vote is an important step in that direction.
in writing. - as a strong supporter of the protection of authors, i believe that their rights are often protected in an illusory way, on paper, and that technical means make it easy to circumvent copyright. i am also against the criminalization of internet users sharing files for private use i believe, as do consumer organizations, that this is the result of the lack of a clear, legal offer that users could easily take advantage of. it would be better if we facilitated legal access to protected goods online, for example on eu-wide platforms offering such goods for free or for a nominal fee, with advertisers covering the licence fees. thinking creatively, you have to adapt the law to the realities of the 21st century! in our resolution, which was unfortunately rejected, we proposed the promotion of new economic models that would allow for real funding and a clear distribution of income for creators. the marielle gallo report takes a restrictive approach to the phenomenon of downloading files from the internet, penalising it on an equal footing with the production of counterfeit medicines or car parts, which is grossly disproportionate. the proposed 'non-legislative measures' to improve law enforcement raise concerns for me about fundamental rights. i think that by adopting the marielle gallo resolution, parliament has sent a very bad signal to the public about how it understands the balance between intellectual property law and fundamental rights. i hope that common sense will return when we discuss the draft specific legislation.
in writing. − marielle gallo, in her report on improving the enforcement of intellectual property rights in the internal market, highlights the role and importance of intellectual property rights, patent law, the fight against counterfeiting in health and safety sensitive sectors, the creation and promotion of formats accessible to disabled people, the creation of a single market in the digital environment, industrial espionage online and the theft of industrial property data. these are all extremely important issues that require concrete solutions. gallo stresses the importance of adapting the european regulatory framework for imps to current trends in society as well as to technical developments. the commission is proposing the creation of a european observatory on counterfeiting and piracy. the most controversial were the ipr infringement and the sale of counterfeit products online. gallo calls on all actors to adopt specific warning and information measures on the value of copyright and the impact of ipr infringements and counterfeiting on employment and growth, and stresses the importance of educating young people in this regard. i have therefore decided to support this report as it contributes to better protection of intellectual property rights in the internal market.

on behalf of the ppe group. the democratic republic of congo is experiencing one of the most serious humanitarian crises in recent years. the rapes in late july and early august, while horrifying in themselves, are just one episode in a series of tragic events. in the congo, more than a thousand women are raped every month, and tens of thousands of children are soldiers. sexual violence is a method to terrorize and punish congolese people who support the wrong side of the conflict. sexual violence is so widespread that doctors without borders says that 75 percent of all rapes in the world take place in eastern congo. the problem is also that the world's largest peacekeeping force, the un, monusco, is doing little to stop this. the debate over when monusco learned of these latest rapes, whether five days, two weeks, or a week after, is embarrassing. the monusco base was 10 miles from where these rapes took place, and the main method the un uses to stop sexual violence is to put signs on houses that say rape is inhuman. we're not gonna be able to eliminate this thing with this method. to make matters worse, un soldiers themselves were involved in a sex scandal a few years ago, accused of forcing girls into prostitution. perhaps the problem is even deeper and there is really no will in monusco to fight this pathological phenomenon. the european union must be decisive on this issue. she needs to be focused on helping the victims. the matter is urgent because we are going to have the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly in kinshasa at the beginning of december and this culture of impunity, of helplessness - i agree with the belgian presidency - must be ended, because we will have to face ourselves.
this is another debate about the situation in the democratic republic of congo and what, as someone said, is largely in the name of democracy where human rights are violated every day. we are talking today about violence against the most vulnerable, especially women who are raped, children who are drawn into the army, among other things, this illegal army. we're talking about rape, torture, murder, this violence that is mostly carried out with impunity, a violence that is so pervasive that it's hard to even talk about any kind of cultural or other kind of tolerance. we're talking about violence that is committed by guerrillas, but also by soldiers of the army and civilians. we're talking about women who have no one to defend them. we must not forget that we are - paradoxically - discussing one of the poorest, yet most resource-rich, regions of the world and africa. these resources should be sufficient to meet the needs of all its inhabitants. we must not forget that this is another manifestation of a disaster that has cost tens of thousands of lives and resulted in some 200,000 rapes in the last ten years. how many cases are unreported, we can only guess. the situation is a matter of deep concern, also in the deliberations of the human rights committee of our parliament. the question arises of the effectiveness of the united nations forces, of the impunity for crimes committed by both the guerrillas and others crimes that must be judged. i think that the meeting between the acp countries and the european parliament is also a great opportunity to put an end to this inhuman situation. with the crisis in the congo, the international community must take the initiative. it is also our task - the european parliament's - to speak out.

fifty years after its independence, congo is still a country in a state of war, in a state of constant conflict, a country that is being called, in a macabre way, the rape capital of the world. the shocking events of the past two months, hundreds of women and children (boys and girls) raped, show that kinshasa is not coping with the systematic pogroms organized by the rebels. rape has become a common weapon of war in the congo. the latest crimes by militias have been committed in the vicinity of the un international forces, which are in fact the only effective stabilizing force in the country. kinshasa must put an end to impunity, guarantee the safety of the civilian population, effectively combat the widespread corruption and finally create a real army with properly trained soldiers. congo is rich in mineral resources, but unfortunately it is a victim of its own wealth. in this country of ten million, three quarters of the population live on less than a dollar a day. this country has become an african territory of plunder of natural resources. the illegal race for raw materials is driving them into poverty, chaos and humanitarian disaster. the international community must bring about a dramatic resolution of the conflict, and the international companies must guarantee the legal origin of the raw materials. only a stable congo can guarantee peace in the region.
today's debate on the democratic republic of congo is a stark reminder of the seriousness of human rights violations in that country. for years, the world's media have been reporting on the crimes that are being committed there. the democratic republic of congo is the scene of the worst crimes against basic human rights. it is estimated that some four million people have already died in the congo conflict. about 3.5 million have been forced to flee and abandon their homes. murder, rape, kidnapping of children and forcing them into armed militias are the horrifying daily realities faced by the people of this country. it is therefore the duty of the entire international community, and above all of the european union, to fight to force the congolese authorities to take effective action to put an immediate end to the killings and persecution. we can't leave the victims to fend for themselves. it is high time for europe to wake up and act effectively.

on behalf of the ecr group. after these few years of experience, one thing can be said crossborder cooperation under the neighbourhood policy does not work. that's not a success. we certainly need to clarify the responsibilities of the various managing authorities in the context of regional development, in the context of neighbourhood, in the context of crossborder cooperation. we certainly need to do something about the procedures, because they are now deterring the regions, both european and neighbouring, from cooperating with dg relex. we need to bring these institutions together. there's another problem. in addition to these procedural changes that are needed, we need to do something to make the policy on neighbourhood policy more clear. we can clearly see that morocco is not happy with the fact that it has to operate in the same political and financial framework as the countries of eastern europe. we see clearly that russia, on the one hand, wants privileged rights within the neighbourhood, and on the other hand, treats the neighbourhood as an element of european imperialism. we encourage it to do so, and we continue to offer it a very privileged status, for example in the context of the partnership for modernisation. so we have two problems to solve: first, procedural changes, and second, policy changes so that everyone knows what this neighborhood is. is this a substitute for membership? is this a step towards membership or, on the contrary, a step towards weakening the political relations between europe and its neighbours?
the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument, together with its crossborder cooperation programme, is a major eu initiative combining international and interregional cooperation. it deserves further support as it brings together regions on the european union's external border. however, the condition is that the instrument's procedures are streamlined and that clear and understandable rules for its operation are laid down. it is good that a large part of the funds provided under the instrument is allocated to cooperation with countries in europe, i.e. ukraine and belarus. in this context, we should continue to put pressure on the belarusian authorities to finally start listening to the citizens' demands for pluralism and democracy. positive signals from the regime of readiness to undertake reforms will allow the full use of the eur 228 million allocated under the instrument and will also allow belarus to participate fully in all dimensions of cooperation within the eastern partnership. however, if the lukashenka regime is not ready to cooperate, consideration should be given to transferring these funds to regional cooperation with ukraine.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i will start by remarks in english, and then i will switch to portuguese, and then back to english. i would be able to address you in five of the european languages, but i will not do that because i will get confused myself, so i will stick to two: english and portuguese. i am grateful for the privilege to address this august institution, the embodiment of europe’s rich cultural diversity and its democratic political culture and institutions. my admiration for europe and for the institutions you have created, for the road you have walked from disunity, rivalries and wars to unity, partnership and peace, democracy, inclusion and prosperity, as well as for your deep belief in solidarity among peoples, led me as a nobel peace prize laureate in 2008 to nominate the european union and the european commission for the nobel peace prize. at one end of the globe, there is the overwhelming influence and shadow of the only surviving superpower. at the other end, there is asia with the shadow of two emerging asian giants looming over the rest of the region. in between, there can be the european bridge – a bridge that could connect all in a new partnership for peace and prosperity. this europe of inclusion extends from the beautiful atlantic coast that bathes portugal to the edges of the old continent where asia begins. as i speak here, i am particularly grateful to this august institution, to many of its esteemed members, to the european commission and in particular to its president, our friend josé manuel durão barroso, who has stood behind us for over three decades in our long quest for freedom. as a young politician and diplomat, first as secretary of state, then as foreign minister and later as prime minister of portugal, he was a wise and passionate advocate for timor leste, as he was also for africa, asia and latin america. but i would fail in my duty if i were not to thank the many other members of the european parliament, some of whom are no longer here because of the irreversible ageing process from which none of us can escape. what we found in this institution from all spectrums, from left and from right, was that you gave us a forum when nowhere else gave us a voice to speak. it was, for instance, the portuguese members of the european parliament from all parties who, in the 1990s, gave a portion of their own salaries to the person who is today our foreign minister, dr zacarias da costa. he was here for five years as a representative of the timorese resistance, and it was the portuguese members of the european parliament from left and right who every month would give us some financial assistance to keep an office going here in brussels. it was also this institution that gave us for the first time anywhere in the world a pass, an identity card, representing timor leste in parliament to advocate the cause of timor leste. so, in coming back here, i come with an immense sense of gratitude to all of you. allow me to turn now to portuguese, and i will address the issue of the millennium development goals, how we are doing in my country, and what we expect the international community to do to assist us and others. timor-leste não era um país independente em 2000 e só na apresentação do nosso primeiro relatório sobre os odm em 2004 que estabelecemos as primeiras metas a atingir. durante os últimos três anos, timor-leste tem vindo a viver uma verdadeira paz, que possibilitou um crescimento económico robusto de mais de 12%/ano, a redução dos níveis de pobreza de 9% durante os últimos dois anos, a redução da mortalidade infantil e da mortalidade de crianças com menos de 5 anos de idade, atingindo mesmo já as metas estabelecidas para o ano 2015, a inscrição escolar cresceu de 65% em 2007 para 83% em 2009-2010, o analfabetismo das pessoas adultas tem sido gradualmente eliminado graças a um programa conjunto entre timor leste e cuba. antecipamos, desde já, a erradicação do analfabetismo em timor-leste dentro de dois a três anos. por volta de 30% do orçamento geral do estado está a ser afectado à saúde pública e à educação. esta reviravolta foi graças a um financiamento público agressivo em programas sociais tais como a transferência directa em dinheiro para idosos, viúvas, deficientes e veteranos, bem como em esforços determinados na expansão de áreas cultivadas e no incremento da produção de bens alimentares. estamos a finalizar o roadmap do nosso plano de desenvolvimento estratégico de 2010-2030, que possibilitará a libertação do nosso povo de séculos de pobreza e elevar o nível de vida do nosso povo para a classe média-alta em 2030. relativamente à gestão dos nossos recursos petrolíferos é uma satisfação poder notar que a iniciativa de transparência nas indústrias extractivas, ou seja extractive industries transparency initiative (eiti), classificou timor-leste, no seu relatório de 1 de julho de 2010, como o primeiro na ásia e terceiro no mundo no que diz respeito à solidez, transparência e efectividade na gestão dos lucros provenientes do gás e do petróleo. por volta de 30% dos deputados no nosso parlamento nacional são mulheres. no executivo, os ministérios-chave como finanças, justiça, solidariedade social, procuradoria-geral da república, etc., são liderados por mulheres. temos um parlamento permanente da juventude com 130 membros, acabado de ser eleito em todo o país. os jovens eleitos para esse parlamento da juventude têm idades compreendidas entre 12 e 17 anos. foi sempre nosso desejo que houvesse equilíbrio do género no parlamento da juventude. no entanto, a nossa expectativa foi ultrapassada. o parlamento jovem é constituído por 68 jovens deputadas do sexo feminino e 62 rapazes deputados. timor-leste tem o orgulho de ter adoptado uma das constituições mais humanistas do mundo, onde a pena de morte é proibida, sendo a sentença de prisão máxima de 25 anos, não temos prisão perpétua. ratificámos todos os principais tratados internacionais de direitos humanos. já apresentámos dois relatórios dos tratados às instituições relevantes e continuaremos a investir os nossos esforços no sentido de reforçar ainda mais o respeito pelos direitos humanos, pela liberdade e pela dignidade para todos. a nossa constituição reconhece o primado do direito internacional sobre as leis nacionais, isto é, todas as nossas leis devem conformar-se com o direito internacional. e agora, com permissão, mudo para inglês. i will now address the issue of climate change – obviously very superficially because of the time constraints here. while it is a fact that the rich and powerful contributed most to the deteriorating world environment, we acknowledge that the advance of science, technology and industries in the last 200 years has brought enormous benefits to all, even if those benefits have been distributed in an unequal manner. but we in the developing world should not put all the blame on the rich and powerful for the harm done to the planet. we must acknowledge our share of responsibility in the destruction of our forests, lakes, rivers and seas. asia has no less responsibility than the us and europe to reverse the climate calamity. we are almost half of the planet’s inhabitants. this alone means that we put enormous pressure on the land, minerals, forests and water. to modernise our economies and improve the lives of hundreds of millions of the poor in asia, we are using increasingly more energy extracted from planet earth. many of the emerging powers of asia are also now crossing oceans, searching for energy elsewhere – in africa and latin america. therefore timor leste – working together with the maldives, two of the smallest countries in asia – calls for an asian common agenda on sustainable development anchored on environmental protection and recovery, on land and water management, health and education for all, and on the elimination of poverty and illiteracy. i have an appeal to the rich and the powerful. the rich and the powerful should ask themselves whether they have delivered on the pledges made in front of tv cameras and whether past policies have been effective in addressing under-development and extreme poverty. all too often, leaders of the developing countries are blamed for the lack of improvements in the lives of our people, in spite of the generous development assistance we supposedly have received from the rich. but donors should also make an honest and critical analysis of the policies. we know there is a genuine sentiment of solidarity from men and women in the streets – in the us, europe and japan – towards their fellow human beings in poorer regions of the world, but donors must also streamline the lengthy, onerous, superfluous, wasteful, redundant and bureaucratic paperwork that drowns and discourages anyone in our countries. (applause) donors must invest more of every dollar they pledge in rural development, agriculture, food security, water and sanitation, roads, health and education. to strengthen national institutions and the democratically elected leaders, donors must provide more direct sectoral budget support to enable them to deliver services and development to the people. it is disheartening that only a handful of rich countries have met the target of 0.7% of gross national product for development assistance. at the same time, generous pledges made in the spotlight of international conferences – side by side with movie stars and rock singers – are largely forgotten the moment the hollywood curtains fall and the floodlights are turned off. it is even more disheartening to see how quickly tens of billions of dollars are easily found to rescue failed banks, insurance companies, fraudulent real estate agencies and obsolete auto industries, and how tens of millions of dollars in bonuses are paid to incompetents and crooks responsible for the financial debacle – and yet decades of appeals to the rich to increase foreign development assistance have been met with much resistance. we believe that one wise and fair way to assist countries suffering from the consequences of the financial meltdown is to write off the debt owed by the ldcs and small island developing states and to restructure the debt of the debtor countries that are facing enormous internal and external challenges – such as instability, climate change and extremism – in many parts of the world, particularly in south asia and the region of the great lakes of africa. timor leste is privileged in that we do not have a single cent in foreign debt, so our appeal to you is not motivated by self-interest. actually if you open the economies yearbook of 2010 – the pocketbook version – you will find some interesting data there. timor leste today has the highest surplus in the world as a percentage of its gdp and not a single cent in foreign debt. nevertheless, we feel in solidarity with those countries that for decades have incurred debt which they are today unable to pay and which entraps hundreds of millions of people in the world. if it has been possible to mobilise billions of dollars almost overnight to rescue failed banks and insurance companies, then there must also be the moral obligation and political wisdom to find the much smaller amount to meet the obligations of the developed countries towards the poor in the third world, to ratify some of the imbalances that are pervasive in the world today. as i speak here today with a deep sense of gratitude to you – to the european parliament, to european leaders and to all our development partners – i wish with humility also to acknowledge our own failings and our limitations. we in timor leste, and in much of the developing world, should not reverse roles by lecturing the west – in retribution for the west having lectured us for decades – but should also look at ourselves in the mirror and answer our own questions from our conscience. what have we ourselves done to lift the hundreds of millions of our people from extreme poverty? we can do that. we can all do better, in timor leste and elsewhere. we have made tremendous progress in the last three years. our country has only been independent for eight years. i have shared some of the figures with you, but there are many other areas of achievement that are not quantifiable. they are not measurable, but they are equally important. we have been able to heal the wounds of our society, reconcile separate communities and heal the wounds between us and indonesia with which we share a tragic history of 24 years. today timor leste and indonesia enjoy the best possible relationship of any two neighbours. we have been able to build bridges with the entire region. we have established diplomatic relations with more than 100 countries. these are non-quantifiable, non-measurable achievements. our people, in spite of the profound wounds of 24 years of occupation, do not harbour resentment towards anyone. these are our beliefs and our convictions. we are determined to live up to the expectations of our people and lead them towards a peaceful and prosperous future. may god, the almighty and the merciful, bless us all. in writing. the use of the death penalty is based on the mistaken belief that the severity of the sentence is a deterrent to crime. in fact, the inevitability of punishment is the decisive preventive factor, not its severity. that's why it's important to have an effective criminal justice system. those who break the law must know that they will be caught and punished. in 2009, the highest executions were in china, iran, saudi arabia, north korea and the united states. the use of the death penalty has not been shown to reduce the number of the most serious crimes. thus, as civilized nations developed, they abandoned the death penalty, and earlier, they abandoned such forms of punishment as crushing a wheel, tearing horses apart, burning at the stake, or nailing people to a stake. these are practices that trigger the lowest instincts and result in the brutalization of social life. in poland, right-wing conservative parties are pushing for the reintroduction of the death penalty, for whom governing is tantamount to intimidating the public. such actions create social fear, uncertainty about the future, and in turn lead to even more violence and crime. the death penalty therefore produces the opposite of the intended effect. therefore, there is a need for proper education and awareness among the public that the death penalty does not solve the problem of the most serious crimes.
in writing. unfortunately, man is not a beautiful animal, to quote the great polish philosopher barbara skarga. many of us, citizens of free and democratic countries in the european union, are in favour of the death penalty. it's scary, but it's true. fortunately, the death penalty is not part of eu law and no eu government, even the most populist, can introduce it. but the european union should and wants to be a beacon for other countries by its values and by its respect for them. that's why it's important that we operate globally. perhaps the day against the death penalty proposed by the belgian presidency is a step in that direction. i hope it will focus our attention on this important issue and reinforce respect for every human being and our responsibility for human rights standards in the european union, but also in those parts of the world where the death penalty is used.
in writing. the european union has introduced a ban on the use of the death penalty. this is a summary of the process that has taken place in european countries, although there are still many supporters of this punishment in europe. it does not seem to be the role of the european parliament to take a position on the deterrent effect of the death penalty, especially since numerous studies, conducted recently mainly in us universities, show that the death penalty is deterrent. our role is to make sure that our communities are safe. given the current law in the european union, we should remember that just as we demand respect for our decision, we should respect the views of other democratic societies and not impose our vision of justice on them. the people of the united states, japan, or south korea have the right to make laws as they see fit. we in europe should remember that the abolition of the death penalty cannot be seen as condoning the most heinous of crimes, the crime of murder. in such cases we need severe, deterrent and isolating punishments, such as life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. because if we want to live in a safe society, we need to have strict laws against those who violate the basic human right - the right to life - and are often willing to violate it again against innocent people.
in writing. – as we move forward with our efforts to fully abolish the practice of capital punishment, it is important to recognise that there are 58 countries worldwide that still utilise capital punishment when sentencing in criminal cases and a handful of others that use it in particular situations such as wartime sentencing. the european union has worked diligently as a whole to abolish this inhumane practice and our continued efforts will pay great dividends. there is however work to be done; we have european neighbours that have not fully abolished this practice and it should remain our focus to continue our efforts toward complete abolition. it is my belief that through continued communication and resolve we will be successful. although it is clear that this practice violates fundamental human rights, many cultures around the world have laws that are based on other factors such as religion, tradition and control. these factors make the abolition of capital punishment increasingly difficult, but it is our duty not only as members of the parliament but as members of the human race to continue our tireless efforts to bring this practice to an end.
madam president! disasters like this, very spectacular events like the gulf of mexico spill, very often are the impetus for policy changes, for big regulatory reform projects. but acting on emotion is not always rational, and that is why i would urge that we take very, very, very careful steps to impose new obligations on companies, whether it be insurance, whether it be environmental standards, whether it be safety standards, because those standards in the european union are already the highest in the world. we're at a different stage of development on this part of the regulation. the only consequence of such hyperregulation could be to weaken europe's competitiveness and to give the mining industry an edge anywhere outside the european union. the same is true of a moratorium on offshore drilling: such a moratorium is likely to have the opposite effect. the moratorium means more ships coming to european shores, and therefore more threats to the environment. so i would urge both regulation and moratorium to be very, very careful.
madam president! this is the third debate in the european parliament and shows how much importance we attach to the safety of oil exploitation in european seas. we do not want the disaster that occurred in the gulf of mexico to be repeated on the coast of our continent. in the first three months of this year alone, there were 175 north sea rig failures, eight of which were classified as very serious. in 32 cases, these plants were shut down. and then there's the issue of platform wear. of the 103 platforms that were launched in the north sea in the early 1970s, 44 are due to reach the so-called technical death in five years, and 26 have already exceeded their permitted operating period, but have received renewed oil rights. the plants have also changed owners over the last 30 years; the new managers do not necessarily share the same safety culture. the pressure to maximize production is not matched by safety measures or a proper risk assessment. we therefore support commissioner oettinger's efforts to review the legal framework for oil exploitation on european seas and, if necessary, to introduce the new rules needed to address the risks of offshore oil production and to strengthen the liability rules for oil pollution accidents. it is necessary to establish the highest safety standards for deep-sea drilling in european seas and to apply them to all operators operating in european waters. this must also apply to companies from outside the european union. we cannot allow, for example, that if norway and russia exploit cereals in the arctic, one of those countries will use technology that does not meet the highest safety standards of european union companies.
madam president! the safety of extraction and transport of natural resources should be monitored by the european commission. in addition to optimal safety standards, the preparation of natural resource extraction and transport companies for emergencies that may cause large-scale environmental pollution should also be a key issue. we must not forget the necessary financial resources which should be provided for companies engaged in this type of economic activity. a pipeline will soon be put into operation to pump huge amounts of gas from the bottom of the baltic sea. i think this is a perfect opportunity to ask whether the european commission has done anything to safeguard the interests of the millions of europeans living on the baltic who could be victims of an ecological disaster of unprecedented scale as a result of the explosion or the opening of this pipeline. it is worth recalling that the european parliament's resolution on this matter two years ago, on the preparation of the environmental impact of this investment, has been completely ignored and this investment is already underway. what will the european commission do to ensure that we do not regret the time we have lost when disaster strikes?
madam president! the unprecedented environmental disaster in the gulf of mexico should prompt the eu countries to monitor rigs in the waters where oil is extracted. there are even proposals to impose a moratorium on new drilling until the risk of environmental danger is eliminated. they are based on the assumption that the oceans have no boundaries and that an ecological disaster is threatening them all. this is in line with the european parliament's resolution on the environmental threat to the baltic sea posed by the nordstream project two years ago. we hope that the european commission will take a similarly firm and sensible approach to monitoring gas investment in the baltic sea using all possible instruments. it is also worth considering whether alternative technologies such as shale gas extraction should not be supported at the same time.
madam president! in view of the events of the past few months and the complex situation on the fuel market following the disaster in the gulf of mexico, we should take certain and decisive steps to protect the environment and, above all, to prevent similar disasters in the future. efforts should be made to increase the safety of oil extraction. with proper precautions, experts tell us that oil companies have a relatively low accident rate. yes, that's true. but the circumvention of procedures, the pursuit of cost-saving at the expense of safety, means that disasters like the one in the gulf of mexico could happen in the future in europe as well. there are about 1,600 rigs operating worldwide, and the number is growing. new oil wells are being built, drilling rigs of ever-larger, ever-more powerful sizes. the mining reaches deeper and deeper into the sea. this is why the importance of conventional shafts is decreasing and the importance of rigs is increasing. the debate on safety is inevitable, and the reality may come as a surprise. it is necessary to subject oil companies to additional restrictions and to introduce new regulations that can improve safety. i know some countries have already taken control of the rigs on their own. the first inspections revealed some breaches of safety standards. it has been found that many north sea platforms have operated in violation of basic safety rules. i believe that preventive measures should be taken immediately to ensure that drilling platforms and all extraction sites for seabed resources are subject to appropriate regulation and supervision. it is necessary to introduce new safety standards and rules that will apply to all operators involved in and jointly responsible for oil extraction. the possession of valid certificates is a key requirement.
