in writing. - i voted in favour of a resolution on human rights, social and environmental standards in international trade agreements. the european union is founded on principles that include respect for human rights. that is why it attaches such great importance to respecting human rights worldwide. the treaty of lisbon reaffirms that the external action of the european union, of which trade is an integral part, should be conducted according to the same principles that underpinned the union's creation. i therefore fully support the practice of including legally binding human rights clauses in the european union's international agreements. i would point out, however, that they must be implemented and that economic consequences must be drawn from them for countries which do not comply with the rules. in accordance with paragraph 15 of the resolution, i consider it essential to include in all free trade agreements negotiated social and environmental standards, including: a list of minimum standards to be respected by all eu trading partners, and a list of additional conventions to be implemented gradually and flexibly, taking into account the development of the economic situation, social and environmental issues of the partner concerned. in particular, i am in favour of including a ban on child labour in all future trade agreements. i also support the strengthening of cooperation on human rights between the wto and the main un institutions.
in writing. - by adopting the resolution on the situation in the beekeeping sector, we are taking another step towards strengthening and improving the beekeeping sector. the problems of this important and still underappreciated industry are global. bees are of economic and environmental importance. the high mortality of bee colonies currently observed has a negative impact on agricultural production. new funding mechanisms are therefore needed in the future financial perspective beyond 2013 to allow more scientific research into the causes of the decline in bee populations and to take appropriate measures to reverse this negative trend. support should also be provided for information and training campaigns to encourage young beekeepers to take up activities in the sector.
in writing. − energy policy is a particularly important area of european union activity at the moment. addressing energy crises in neighbouring countries and ensuring energy security in member states should be a priority for the institutions of the european union. it is of the utmost importance to strike a balance between energy policy and environmental protection. that is why we must promote the use of renewable energy sources as much as possible. this will not only reduce emissions of harmful substances, but can also effectively reduce the dependence of the european union market on foreign supplies of energy raw materials. to ensure energy security, which is so important for all citizens of the member states, it is essential to promote good relations between the european union and third countries, especially those that supply europe. diversifying oil and gas supplies is also important to make the eu less vulnerable to energy crises in neighbouring countries.
in writing. the report by ms kolarska-bobińska draws attention to a number of important problems, such as the lack of a unified energy policy that takes account of the specificities of individual eu countries and the need to import energy from third countries. the forecasts indicate that oil dependence will further increase in the future, and therefore the energy strategy must have a multi-faceted and international dimension, going beyond the framework of the european union. given the close geographical proximity of the community countries to russia, the european union should seek to strengthen cooperation with our eastern neighbours on appropriate terms. our efforts should also focus on meeting the objectives of the lisbon treaty, and thus on creating a single energy market while ensuring security of energy supply. the achievement of these objectives requires investment in network infrastructure, which would foster the integration of regional energy markets, as well as the modernisation of pan-european energy networks. as the honourable member rightly suggests, the installation of new terminals that could transport gas from anywhere in the world would allow for the discovery of new sources of gas imports, especially from regions rich in this raw material, such as central asia. the president of the european parliament, jerzy buzek, and former european commission president jacques delors also suggested financial assistance for infrastructure development, as a modernised and expanded energy network is the basis for building a coherent energy policy.

member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, i will address all the questions. thank you for placing this very important debate on the agenda. let me start by thanking mrs griesbeck for her support and her work in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs on the eu-georgia agreement with the adoption of a favourable opinion. following the crisis in georgia in the summer of 2008, it was decided at an extraordinary meeting of the council of the european union to step up relations with georgia, including visa facilitation measures. as you mention, mrs griesbeck, it is standard eu policy that a visa facilitation agreement cannot be offered to a third country without a readmission agreement, so the european council’s decision implied that the two should be negotiated and concluded in parallel. i am very grateful to mrs griesbeck for having also noted the important step forward in relations between georgia and the eu that these two agreements represent. the agreement is very much along the lines of a standard eu readmission agreement, covering nationals as well as third country nationals, and also safeguarding – as was said – respect for human rights through a ‘non-effective’ clause and an article on data protection. the agreement also provides for the establishment of a joint readmission committee, tasked with monitoring implementation of the agreement. this is an important step towards smoother mobility between the people of georgia and the european union. georgia has already waived the visa requirement for eu citizens, and this agreement will facilitate mobility for georgian citizens. the agreement will indeed make it easier, cheaper and quicker for georgian citizens – more than 60 000 per year – to obtain a schengen visa. it will bring other concrete benefits: a 10-day deadline will be set for the processing of applications and the visa fee will be reduced from eur 60 to eur 35. there will be certain categories of applicants who will be free of charge: students, journalists, children, pensioners, the disabled, etc. they can also benefit from a simplified supporting documents requirement and a multi-entry visa if they need to travel. also, holders of diplomatic passports will be entirely exempted from visa obligations, which will further strengthen official contacts between the eu and georgia. mrs griesbeck mentioned the evaluation. this has been slightly delayed, but i will present it by the beginning of next year – i hope no later than february. i will be happy to discuss it with the civil liberties committee and parliament. you also made reference to the programme for pakistan. this has only been operational for 13 days so it is a little early to evaluate it, but we will of course be happy to keep you updated. concerning the issue raised by mrs ojuland of the visa facilitation agreement between the eu and russia, this has been in force since 1 january 2007. it is one of the eight visa facilitation agreements that we have concluded. particularly important elements are that it applies on a reciprocal basis to eu citizens also, as they are currently under a visa obligation for travelling to russia. it is also an important agreement in quantitative terms. according to statistics provided by russia, more than 1.5 million visas were issued to eu citizens in 2008 and the same year member state consulates issued 3.5 million visas to russian citizens. that is more than a quarter of all schengen visas issued worldwide. all eu and russian citizens benefit from the general facilitation provided by this facilitation agreement, such as a reduced fee of eur 35. certain categories are also exempted under specific facilitation; there is a visa-free waiver and also a multi-entry visa. the commission has evaluated this facilitation and has found that it works quite well. however, there are some shortcomings, as were referred to. to address these, we adopted a month ago a recommendation for directives for the renegotiation of the visa facilitation with russia. this relates entirely to further facilitation with regard to documentary evidence and the length of the visa application procedure, the extension of the provisions for the issuing of multiple-entry visas and a visa-free waiver for a number of well-defined categories of applicants. as regards the specific issue of the implementation of article 10 of the visa facilitation agreement, which provides for the simplification of the registration procedure, we noted in our evaluation that russia had adopted some simplification; it is now possible to register by post, for example. the registration fee will be abolished by next year, but some of the other measures, such as the translation of the registrations into english and the possibility to register online, have not yet materialised. we are raising this issue with our russian counterparts and in different fora, and we hope that this will take place very soon. concerning the other eastern partnership countries, there have been other steps as well. this was also in your question. we have visa facilitation with moldova and ukraine as from 1 january 2008, but we are also renegotiating these agreements. regarding belarus, draft negotiating directives for visa facilitation were adopted by the commission a month ago, and we will recommend multiple-entry visas with a long period of validity for bona fide travellers and set deadlines for processing visa applications, as well as possible exemptions for visa obligations for holders of diplomatic passports. we will also adopt draft negotiating directives for a visa facilitation agreement with azerbaijan and armenia next year. on the correct application of the visa liberalisation scheme that mr weber referred to, namely that applicable to serbia and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, the council decided, as was also said, to grant visa-free travel to the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, montenegro and serbia in 2009. the decision came following incentive dialogue and substantial progress by these countries on the main matters covered by the visa liberalisation dialogues. the dialogues have proved effective in implementing a lot of important reforms but, as was also pointed out, the visa-free regime comes with responsibilities and the countries concerned should take the appropriate measures to make sure that there is no abuse of the visa waiver. some member states have experienced an increased number of asylum applications from these countries – notably serbia and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. these have to be assessed on an individual basis according to our legislation. we have taken a number of steps to address this situation: we have had high-level meetings with the ministers of the interior on the two questions, and there was a high-level visit to the two capitals by the belgian presidency and the commission. the authorities of these two countries have taken some steps. there have been new information campaigns organised to inform the citizens. there are instructions to the border police to deliver and to perform increased controls on people exiting the country and to inform travellers about the risk of unfounded applications for asylum. when, earlier this autumn, we proposed lifting the visa requirement for the citizens of albania and bosnia-herzegovina, both countries committed themselves to setting up information campaigns for their citizens on the rights and obligations arising from the visa waiver, and this has been done. these are very ambitious campaigns. in addition, after approval by the european parliament and the council, the commission made a commitment to intensify post-visa liberalisation monitoring for all the western balkan countries. there will be two parts to this. on the one hand we will continue to assess the sustainable implementation of reforms by the countries concerned through the stabilisation and association process – in particular in the area of justice, freedom and security. on the other hand, we will also act as a prevention mechanism against new situations of high in-flow of persons from the region. the collection of the necessary operational information that could help to prevent these situations was done early this year, and we will have active participation from frontex, europol, immigration liaison officers, western balkan police liaison officers and the secretariat of the police corporation convention for south-east europe, supported by the incoming presidencies – hungary and poland. all the information exchanged and collected will be shared by eu member states and, of course, when appropriate, with the countries of the western balkans. such information will also feed into the commission assessment to be carried out in the first semester of next year on post-visa liberalisation monitoring. i consider that these measures should contribute to avoiding the misuse of the visa-free travel regime, and i am confident that close cooperation between the countries of origin and eu destination countries, supported by the commission, offers an effective response. we will, of course, continue to report regularly to the european parliament and to the council on the results of this monitoring mechanism, for the first time in june 2011.
author of the draft opinion of the committee on foreign affairs. − as the permanent rapporteur of the european parliament's report on european union cooperation with georgia, and as the author of the opinion of the committee on foreign affairs on the reports of ms griesbeck, i would like to say a few words about these two agreements - the readmission agreement and the visa facilitation agreement between the european union and georgia. i feel obliged to say that these agreements were passed by the committee on foreign affairs by an overwhelming majority. i would like to add that at the last session of the european parliament, here in strasbourg, we heard a speech by president saakashvili, a speech which even in the eyes of those who are not his fans was described as substantive, balanced, rational. the president then not only declared the non-use of force or openness to talks with russia on difficult issues, but also declared what is the main goal of georgia's foreign policy and of course it is european integration and membership in the north atlantic treaty. i think we must remember, without mentioning any deadlines, because only a madman would be talking about deadlines today, that georgia and georgians are today the most pro-european country and nation of the countries that we include in the eastern partnership programme. the european union should give a positive, substantive response to these aspirations of the georgians. we should be open to working with georgia. the agreements we are discussing today are not a revolution, of course, but we all see them as a step in the right direction. the point is to implement them as soon as possible, because in my view it should not happen that today residents of abkhazia or south ossetia, which are regions separated from georgia, who hold russian passports, have an easier visa situation than georgians.
on behalf of the ecr group. georgia is a country today which, despite many problems, is in the process of very dynamic changes both socially and economically. any signals to the georgian people that the strength of these changes is reflected in our responses as an institution of the european union should be welcomed. also, when it comes to russia, we have to think about the context in which we see the visa regime with russia. i have the impression that this cannot be treated as an element of the prestige of the authorities, that if we abolish visas, that is, that the authorities in russia are negotiating well with the european union. we have to look at it in a different way, in the context of ensuring modernization, in the context of our relationship with ordinary russians. and so it's important to say clearly that the process of lifting visas, of opening up based on the conditions that have been set, is a very positive process that serves our relations with the societies in the east well. we must dispel the myth that visas are somehow an essential element of our security and we must say, perhaps in the european parliament, particularly clearly and repeat it at every opportunity: visas build walls, unnecessary walls. in the framework of the commission for cooperation with ukraine, which i chair, we have prepared a special report with ngos, in which we have examined this problem. it is clear from this report that visas are not really an important security instrument, visas are an instrument of separation between the societies of the european union and those of the east, and we should always be open to it. it is our duty as parliamentarians.
we have to talk about visas, we have to talk about visas from the standpoint of statistics, what the european union has done. this room is a pleasure. i would like all those who spoke with such satisfaction and contentment today to try to imagine a situation where, in order to get a visa, they have to stand in line for several hours, endure humiliation, inconvenience, stand in the rain in terrible conditions. they have to be able to afford, they have to pay one-third of their salary to get this visa. they have to hear, by the way, that diplomats in their country are exempt from the visa requirement, and then finally they applied for a multiple entry visa because they need it, and they get a single entry visa, they wanted a schengen visa, and they get a visa to the country. the visa process must be a matter of conscience for us. the visa process is really a humiliation for millions of people. people who stand in these lines. and let us remember that by expressing the satisfaction that is in this room today. i understand that we use the visa process as a stick and a carrot, but the government and the people who are in line deserve normal sympathy. madam commissioner, you are from sweden. as you know, in the 1970s, your country, with austria, was one of only two countries where there was a no-visa regime for the communist countries. as a citizen of poland, i visited your country in 1976. why? why? because travelling to sweden was visa-free. of course i love your king, swedish freedom and the economy, but please remember that, as long as we have visas, we shouldn't feel comfortable.
by liberalizing the visa regime, we should be sending signals about our values as well. it's not just about opening the doors, because we should open them as wide as possible, but also about promoting democracy in the countries that are neighbours of the european union. we should therefore support those countries which are genuinely committed to democracy, the rule of law and respect for european values. however, it seems that we should first of all liberalize the visa regime for these post-soviet countries first, and then for russia. and here i agree with those voices that said that if we do visa liberalization for russia before we do it for the people of ukraine and other post-soviet countries, that would be a very bad signal. in georgia, it may be that in the areas now occupied by the russians, many people will want to get russian citizenship and settle there, because it will be a pass for russia. let's also consider the visa regime as a promotion of democracy.
in writing. any visa liberalisation is a response to the expectations of the citizens of the countries concerned. i would like to stress that the visa agreement between the eu and georgia cannot be seen in isolation from the agreement on the readmission of persons residing illegally. we have been talking about this for a long time on the european stage, because visa policy is particularly important for the eu. visa liberalisation opens up eu countries to citizens of balkan countries and thus opens up opportunities for them to participate in eu dialogue and learn about democracy. however, with liberalisation we must also take into account the fact that more free movement of people across borders can be a boon for illegal immigrants and criminal groups. member states should apply uniform visa issuing procedures in this respect, as albania and bosnia and herzegovina are next in line. the european commission must respect the conditions for visa liberalisation and monitor the situation so that good solutions do not become a cause of trouble within eu countries. in addition, cooperation between countries and the use of existing experience in the visa procedure is important.
few european policies have generated so much excitement and controversy. cohesion policy, which some consider to be socialist policy par excellence, will be regarded by others as capitalist policy. it will be considered by some as a fair policy, by others as an unfair policy. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european network of national and regional authorities. there is really no contradiction in this policy, and it is really intended to promote greater cohesion in the european union, not only for reasons of social justice but also for equal opportunities in terms of competitiveness. in other words, it's cohesion for competitiveness. both reports speak to this, pointing out some elements that are important not only in the current situation but in the debate on the future of cohesion policy. i would point out that both of them pay particular attention to the principle of partnership. i would ask the commissioner to seriously consider whether the proposed development contract should include a requirement for member states. requirement that the member state agrees with the local and regional partners on any directions, priorities and principles before signing the contract. this should be mandatory in order to allow the european commission to clearly define the responsibility of the member state for implementing its part of the cohesion policy.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop this. i would like to begin by saying that i consider this report to be particularly important and to congratulate the rapporteur, mr petru luhan, on his excellent work. i believe that cohesion policy should be the leading policy of the european union and its importance should increase in the coming years. treated as a horizontal policy, it should set the direction of sectoral policies and contribute to increasing the competitiveness of european regions and strengthening the european union on global markets. the system for implementing cohesion policy must be modern and flexible, based on a multi-level governance model, as has been mentioned on many occasions. it should also promote coordination of the structural funds with other european instruments and with national measures. i managed a region of 2 200 000 inhabitants for two terms and was responsible for the implementation of cohesion policy instruments both on the basis of a centralised model between 2004 and 2006 and a decentralised model regional operational programme between 2007 and 2013. these experiences allow me to say with full responsibility that a decentralised model allows for a better use of local potential to implement strategic solutions and achieve positive change, and i am therefore convinced that the objectives should be agreed at european level, but the means of achieving them should be defined in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity at the level most appropriate for their achievement, which in the case of cohesion policy means precisely the regional and local levels. this requires linking spending to achieving measurable goals and outcomes: growth and higher levels of employment and social inclusion.
in writing. europe is going through a difficult period. the financial crisis of 2008-2009 is still strongly affecting the economy. this is exacerbating the gap between the rich regions of western europe and the poorer regions of central and southern europe. this situation creates the need to strengthen effective mechanisms to combat the crisis. the most important at union level are cohesion policy and regional funds. by co-financing investments at local level, they have become an effective symbol of european cooperation over national interests. they also made a significant contribution to the expansion of the economic growth zone between 2004 and 2007 and to the reduction of disparities between the countries of old and new europe. this is why it is so important to increase the eu's cohesion policy funding for the 2013-2020 financial perspective, to maintain convergence as the overarching objective and to maintain the current mechanism for selecting beneficiaries based on the value of gdp in each region. the possibility of increasing co-financing of investments from 75% to 80% while reducing funding for the so-called outermost regions also seems important. from the point of view of the eastern european countries, it is also important to continue financing infrastructure investments, especially in the vertical belt linking north and south of europe.
on behalf of the ecr group. with the entry into force of the charter of fundamental rights in europe, we are faced with two somewhat competing systems of human rights protection. one based on the charter of rights and the case law of the court of justice, the other based on the european convention and the case law of the tribunal. i think the main challenge that the kingi gál report sees is to ensure that these systems are coherent, both in terms of content and in terms of institutional arrangements. the charter of fundamental rights cannot be interpreted in such a way as to create a presumption of new competences for the european union. article 51 is very clear on this, but i think it is worth recalling, particularly in this house, that matters of matrimonial law, criminal law, the legal protection of unborn life cannot be regulated at eu level, either directly or through the judicial activism of this or that tribunal. such politicization of human rights instruments can only have one effect: a decline in confidence in international justice.
the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into union law does not extend the scope of its competences and is in line with the principle of subsidiarity. the charter is an integral part of the union's policy. i therefore once again call on the polish authorities to fulfil their obligations and adopt the charter of fundamental rights. there is no substantive justification for the polish opt-out of the charter. it's a political decision that compromises my country and hurts its citizens. the adoption of the charter is particularly important in the context of the forthcoming polish presidency. all europeans must have equal rights, regardless of where they live or how clerical their state is. unfortunately, in poland, even the constitutional court doesn't always understand this. i think it is particularly important to respect the rights of women, who are the only discriminated majority. i therefore once again call for a european directive on combating violence against women, including sexual and reproductive violence, which is being applied by some member states in the full force of their domestic law.
given the proposed changes, it is easy to see that this directive is one of the first initiatives to achieve these important objectives. not only must victims of violence be prevented from suffering harm at the hands of the perpetrator in their own country, but they must also be covered by such protective measures throughout the european union. the position of the rapporteurs should therefore be supported. it should also be noted that the scope of the initiative is broad, deliberately broad. although most protection orders in force concern women who are victims of gender-based violence, the initiative can cover all victims of violence children and adults of both sexes, provided the perpetrator has been identified. in this context, the stockholm programme concluded that victims of crime, including terrorism, who are in the most difficult situation or are particularly vulnerable, such as those exposed to repeated acts of violence in close relationships, victims of gender-based violence or those who are victims of other types of crime in a member state of which they are not nationals or residents, need specific legal support and protection. the european protection order should therefore apply to all victims of crime, including trafficking in human beings, female genital mutilation, forced marriage, honour killings, incest and other such cases. this initiative should therefore be supported and i fully support the rapporteur.
i am very enthusiastic about the report we are discussing today. the protection granted to a victim in one country is guaranteed to be valid in other eu countries, where the victim has to go for fear of his or her perpetrator, and this is a chance for the victim to live a normal life. it is thanks to the european protection order that protection measures adopted in one member state of the union can be recognised, applied and enforced by the courts of another member state. moreover, extending the application of the directive to victims of all types of violence, not just victims of gender-based violence, is another milestone. all victims deserve respect and expect that those responsible for their suffering will be justly punished. only the mechanism of protection of the victim's continuation seems to be fully effective and can prevent the same crime from being repeated, can actually protect the victim. i am very pleased that poland is among the countries that have joined this initiative.
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. fellow workers! in today's debate, i would like to address the issue of child trafficking. every effort should be made to improve and improve the legal and institutional system and childcare system in each member state. the scope of activities included in trafficking in human beings should be reviewed and extended. only in this way will we be able to prevent such phenomena as: 1) commercial adoption adoption with referral and waiver of the right to a child before the family court, usually for a fee; 2) leaving the country by pregnant mothers and returning to the country without a child; 3) disappearance of children whose parents have died in countries affected by armed conflicts. in times when a large number of crimes are committed via the internet, it is worthwhile to set up special interdisciplinary teams specialised in combating this type of crime. they would not only be engaged in surveillance of criminal circles, but also in gathering evidence by monitoring the financial situation of those involved in the trafficking of children. public officials should be trained and made aware of the situation of a child in a family where child trafficking may have occurred. this is particularly true of services working with families who are in need of state care because of their difficult financial situation. only through multilateral and harmonised action at the level of the 27 member states can we have a chance to eliminate or at least reduce trafficking in human beings, with a particular focus on child trafficking.
we cannot allow the huge amount of money we spend on cohesion policy to be squandered or wasted. it is therefore important to improve their management, but also their effective use. in this case, the local authorities, which are the most aware of the needs of the region, play a major role. attention should also be paid to cross-border areas to facilitate their integration. in order to ensure that vertical and horizontal cooperation runs smoothly, it is necessary to simplify procedures, including increased expenditure on training of specialists from the implementing entities in each member state. support is also needed for the modernisation and development of the it system, which will ensure easy and equal access to information for all beneficiaries.
many eu citizens still do not realise the importance of cohesion policy for the development not just of individual regions but of entire countries. its main task is to make up for the disparities between the regions of the community. this allows people in less-favoured regions with difficult economic conditions and limited access to transport to have the same access to social services, education, transport or energy as those in more socio-economically advantaged areas. the importance of the idea of cohesion cannot be overstated. we must therefore support all efforts to make better use of the structural funds and to make more effective use of their integrating role, especially as the effects of cohesion policy are felt most strongly at local level and thus largely in rural areas. these are the reasons why i supported this report.

member of the commission. − mr president, i shall be brief as i have already used up my time slot. in answer to mr belder, who may have already disappeared, the commission’s proposal on how to cooperate between the institutions was in direct implementation of articles 312, 324 and, specifically, article 311 of the lisbon treaty, for the specific procedure on the own resources decision in full respect of the fiscal sovereignty of the member states. as for the own resources, this was clearly and explicitly within the mandate given to the commission in december 2005, which was confirmed by parliament, to start not only the expenditure but also the revenue side of the budget, including the british rebate. we were delicate enough not to touch the issue of the british rebate in our budgetary review and our eventual choice for the future is not to increase the expenditure but to change the proportions between the national direct payment and own resources, in line with the vision of the treaty and the founding fathers of the european union. finally, a more general remark: hopefully if we vote tomorrow our test of lisbon, in budgetary terms, will be over and we will have to draw conclusions. it sends a good message to european citizens to have a budget without any deficits or debt and to show that we are not to be taken as a scapegoat for the failed policies in some member states. therefore, now having the budget in place, we should continue our discussion on the modalities of interinstitutional cooperation in much improved circumstances.

author of the draft opinion of the committee on regional development. - mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. energy efficiency is one of the major challenges facing the european union in the next ten years. it's also a key element of our energy strategy. the most important thing now is that the commission's good report and energy strategy are implemented by the member states. to make them a reality, a few problems need to be solved. at eu level, we are still faced with the problem of measuring this energy efficiency. we currently use 2020 projections for this purpose, but it would be unreasonable to adopt binding legal targets based on such projections. we're not psychics when it comes to the future. so it is necessary, and we have already discussed this in today's discussion, to develop a new, better technology. because she's the one who's gonna make it happen. it is also crucial to take account of regional differences. the way energy is used in copenhagen is different from that in eastern poland. there is no one-size-fits-all action plan, and we need to ensure that those plans are aligned with reality. regional and local authorities will be responsible for implementing energy efficiency policy. the european commission and the member states therefore need to coordinate their actions with local authorities. otherwise, it will be seen as a bureaucracy with huge costs for regions and citizens. without multi-level management and the allocation of funds, the whole project will be doomed to failure.
on behalf of the ecr group. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur very much for the very constructive and open cooperation in the preparation of this report. i'd like to focus on one thing in my speech. the introduction of binding energy efficiency targets into the european system will be unacceptable to our political group. first of all, we don't have a common methodology for measuring efficiency, too many indicators are not comparable. the targets should be set for each country individually to take account of the very different saving potential and take into account the achievements to date. i'll give you an example of my country. poland has improved its energy efficiency by 50% since 1990. nevertheless, poland remains a low-performing country compared to the european average. the introduction of a single binding target will cause political damage and will result in the costs of the changes being unevenly distributed between member states.
mr. chairman, please! since september 2009, europe has been replacing traditional light bulbs, which europeans have become accustomed to, with energy-efficient ones produced using new technology. the need for this was motivated by the slogans of energy efficiency. this was despite indications that the financial cost of such an operation to community nationals was too high, especially in such a short period of time. the secret of the polysynel is that the data on the effects of this change presented by the european commission at the time, as many point out, came from the advertising bulletins of the manufacturers of these newly developed light bulbs. in this report, we see similar overly optimistic assumptions. they do not sufficiently address the development differences between community countries and, therefore, the costs which they would have to bear if they were to implement the recommendations. achieving an annual energy efficiency improvement of 2% for industrial plants while reducing greenhouse gas emissions will result in higher production costs and a shift of production outside europe.
i agree with the rapporteur that more emphasis should be placed on systemic innovation such as smart grids, smart metering systems, easier integration of renewable energy sources, and the development of a comprehensive strategy for heat producers and distributors. but the greatest savings and the greatest efficiency i see in creating personal responsibility for every european union citizen. just as we have learned to conserve water, we must learn to respect and use energy efficiently. any authorisation procedures for new infrastructure should be simplified and accelerated in order to maximise potential savings. energy efficiency and energy security will be the priorities of the next hungarian presidency of the european union. poland, as the eu's presidency, will also deepen its discussion on modern legislative and non-legislative solutions to maintain the competitiveness of the european energy sector while improving energy efficiency. i must say at this point that for me personally, the question of the realism of the forecasts and the quality of the eu's primes model is becoming critical, especially in the absence of a consensus in cancun. this is a separate debate, but i would like to call for a new, cross-cutting approach to energy consumption and demand in the european union. transport seems to be the most appropriate element for implementing modern energy efficiency solutions. energy efficiency in the european union should be aligned with the direction of demand, which is directly linked to spending and changing habits of citizens. i believe that the changes will bring tangible benefits to consumers and to producers through appropriate incentives and funding spread over time.
in writing. energy efficiency is most generally defined as the reduction of energy consumption per unit of consumption by rationalising the use of equipment. however, the main possibilities for increasing gross energy efficiency lie on the side of industrial physicochemical processes, which consist of: 1) better use of the heat flux released from fossil or nuclear fuels by: a) shifting the conversion in the carnot cycle to a higher temperature and pressure range, b) using appropriate waste heat recovery, e.g. in cogeneration processes; 2) reducing the ohm resistance during current transmission; 3) reducing the thermal resistance of heat exchangers; 4) increasing the thermal resistance through the use of insulating materials in buildings; 5) reducing the friction resistance; 6) reducing the magnetic field losses; 7) reducing the length of the chain over the conversion of one type of energy to another. so the 3x20 policy goal in 2020 is not simply to reduce energy consumption by 20% gross, for example, through price increases, because that will only cause a decrease in living standards, but through a rationalization that will allow 20% more useful work to be produced from the same amount of primary energy. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy objectives in the field of energy efficiency and renewable energy.
in writing. increased energy efficiency will directly contribute to improving energy security across the union. if the changes are implemented properly, they will also reduce emissions. this is certainly a very good development, supporting our efforts to tackle climate change. the use of modern technologies in the modernisation of infrastructure will also bring financial savings and, as a result, economic growth in the community countries. this, the author stresses, will create new jobs not only in urban areas but also in local markets and in the countryside. of course, all these objectives will require the necessary resources and investment at the outset, but i believe that the most worthwhile thing is to ensure that europe has an energy-efficient, efficient and environmentally friendly economy.

president of the council. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, and in particular the rapporteurs, one of the most important promises of the lisbon treaty was to bring europe closer to its citizens. i think it is not necessary to mention here the examples that showed us before and after the signing of the lisbon treaty in december 2009 how necessary this rapprochement is. it is therefore not surprising that any measure which pursues the aim of involving citizens in the construction of europe is a priority for all the institutions, including the council. i am therefore particularly pleased to be able to address you on the regulation implementing the citizens' initiative, the flagship innovation of the lisbon treaty in terms of better citizen participation in decision-making at european level. this regulation was of course one of the priorities of the belgian presidency of the council, because it is perhaps this citizens' initiative that most symbolizes the new role of the citizen in the union after lisbon. the rapporteur has already said that a citizen's initiative allows one million european citizens to submit a legislative proposal to the commission, with the obligation for the commission to study it and take a decision on it. we must stop for a moment to appreciate this innovation we are making today, which is nothing more than the first element - as mr lamassoure said - of participatory democracy at the supranational level. it is not only a first at european level, it is simply a world first. let us return to the legislative matter we are discussing today. i can only welcome the compromise reached on this regulation in the negotiations between the three institutions and, of course, i also welcome the spirit of cooperation and the willingness to compromise which prevailed in the three institutions throughout these negotiations. i would of course like to personally thank the rapporteurs of the afco and peti committees, mrs gurmai of course, mr lamassoure, mrs wallis and mr häfner for their efforts and constructive contributions in the preparation of this regulation. i am particularly pleased that the vote in the afco committee on monday confirmed the text adopted by the institutions. if the vote in the afco committee confirms the same text, this agreement at first reading can of course be regarded as a model for rapid and effective legislation at european level. i would also like to thank commissioner šefčovič for his willingness and his willingness to help. in short, i feel that we have enriched each other on this issue by the many opinions expressed at the negotiating table and it is the european citizen who has benefited from this trilogue and this agreement. i am convinced that the compromise reached between the institutions is a good compromise, not only in the sense that each institution has been able to obtain the elements that were dear to it - in writing. with the lisbon treaty, we gave citizenship to eu citizens. the second step is to grant eu citizens a citizens' initiative. it's a rare moment when the legislative or executive branches of government give some of their power to the citizens. that's a lot of maturity. that's how we're gonna address the democratic deficit. we are not only based on representative democracy, but also on participatory democracy. the previous development policy, the consultation of citizens in the decision-making process, did not always meet the expectations of the citizens of the european union. the citizens' initiative, which was a difficult compromise, first ensured full transparency. second, we simplified the whole system. we also made an innovation in the way that we could submit electronic signatures. today we also have a great deal of promotion of the citizens' initiative, both by the commission, the european parliament and the member states. it is necessary to consider whether openness to the citizens' initiative may be threatened by demagogic or populist proposals. i don't think he did. each of the citizens' initiatives will require increased responsibility from the commission and the european parliament.

the rapporteur. - a few months ago, the european parliament gave the council its consent for the first time to the enhanced cooperation procedure. for the first time in the history of the european union. this is a very important step, opening up a whole new formula for cooperation between parts of the european union, if it is not possible to obtain the consent of all 27 member states. this is a very important decision. today we confirmed that this procedure is working well. i would like to thank the council very warmly for the position it has taken in cooperation with the european parliament. it's a perfect example of interagency cooperation. the parliament was only consultative when it worked on this regulation, but the frequency of meetings and the fact that the council took into account all the proposals that were drawn up in the european parliament, voted on in the legal affairs committee and incorporated in the final document is a perfect example of a procedure that bodes well for enhanced cooperation in the future. i also thank the council for its strong support for our request for a rapid revision of the brussels iia regulation, which is necessary to resolve, for example, the forum necessitatis issue, which allows the member states to maintain certainty about the functioning of their internal legal systems and gives our citizens hope that in the future they will be able to make a free choice not only of law but also of the court. i thank my colleagues and fellow co-rapporteurs on the legal affairs committee and the opinion committees.
in writing. - first of all, i would like to express my satisfaction that the european parliament and the council have agreed on the financing of the lifelong learning programme and the competitiveness and innovation programme. i am particularly interested in the lifelong learning programme. it comprises four sectoral programmes. the erasmus programme, which allows for student exchanges on a mass scale, is particularly important in my view. this is extremely important both in terms of acquiring new knowledge and skills and in terms of making new contacts and learning about the cultures of the member states. comenius plays a similar role for school-age children. these programmes not only pay off for the european economy, but also ensure the creation of a european consciousness based on a transnational network of contacts. these programmes should be given high priority regardless of the budgetary situation. they are an investment that will benefit the european union in many ways. not just economically, but culturally and politically. the decision to help palestine has a different dimension, but i also consider it to be justified.
in writing. − an agreement was reached between the council and the european parliament on the 2011 budget. i voted in favour of the budget because of the political and institutional demands, which include a stronger role for the european parliament in the negotiations on the new financial perspective after 2013 and participation in the debate on new sources of revenue, including the european tax. the budget has the added advantage of being more flexible in the face of unforeseen circumstances. we have eliminated the threat of acting on the basis of a provisional budget, which would have paralysed the functioning of the union to a large extent. this would be particularly unfavourable at a time when the economic crisis and the implementation of the treaty of lisbon need to be tackled intensively. the socialist and democrat group in the european parliament has a lot to be thankful for.
in writing. − the vote on the 2011 budget shows that a compromise within the european union is possible. the draft financial plan for 2011 was accepted and voted on thanks to the goodwill of all the institutions involved. this compromise is particularly valuable given that the decision-making procedures are new since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon and that, for the first time in history, the european parliament has co-decided on expenditure alongside the council of the european union and the european commission. it is not an ideal budget, but i believe that it has been allocated in a sensible way and covers all the priorities of the european union. in voting for the 2011 budget, i also expressed my support for further development and the idea of european integration.
in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? the threat of a provisional budget for 2011 has mobilized the european parliament and the council of the european union to intensify the debate, the outcome of which - the draft budget put to the vote today - can be considered a pragmatic compromise. the negotiations between the institutions have led to the adoption of most of the demands made by parliament. we have received the assurance from the council that it is willing to cooperate in the preparation of the financial perspective for 2014-2020, which will be the practical implementation of the provisions of the lisbon treaty. parliament also reached agreement with the prime ministers of hungary, poland, denmark and cyprus, the countries that will hold the eu council presidency for the next two years. we also welcome the council's decision to maintain the flexibility mechanism in the eu budget at 0.03% of eu gdp. these funds will finance key expenditure not foreseen during the negotiation of the previous financial perspective, such as the european external action service or the galileo system. the european parliament's concession is to postpone the debate on the future sources of funding for the european union, which the european commission is also calling for. the idea of relieving national contributions to the eu budget has fallen on deaf ears in the face of strong opposition from a group of countries concerned about public reaction. we will probably return to this debate in the summer of 2011, when the commission presents some new options for eu funding.

in writing. - i would like to congratulate the rapporteur for tackling so thoroughly the difficult issue of the choice of law applicable to divorce and legal separation. the sensitivity of this issue is demonstrated by the fact that the rome iii regulation is the first example of enhanced cooperation in the eu's history conducted under treaty procedures. the territorial scope of the regulation will therefore be limited to 14 of the 27 eu countries, excluding poland. i believe that by introducing the principle of the choice of law applicable to divorce, rome iii will contribute to greater predictability and legal certainty. however, given the limited scope of this regulation it will concern only the law applicable to international divorces it is also necessary to answer the question of which court has jurisdiction to rule on the case. this problem is the subject of another regulation at eu level brussels ii bis. i therefore agree with the rapporteur that it is necessary to amend this regulation as soon as possible in order to introduce the so-called forum necessitatis principle. it will allay the fears of many countries that their courts will be forced to grant divorce to unions that are not recognised as marriage by their legal system, and thus encourage them to adopt european-wide rules on international divorce, which will no doubt make life easier for many eu citizens.

in writing. − ecr meps believe that energy efficiency has a crucial part to play in helping the eu meet its renewable energy and emissions reduction targets. it also has a crucial role to play in ensuring our energy security and contributing to our economic competitiveness. we support much of the content of this report, such as the focus on smart grids and metering, financing from the eib and the private sector, and also the potential for r&d to further energy efficiency. ecr meps do not, however, support binding energy efficiency targets. we believe that the eu and member states are already incentivised to implement energy efficiency policies through renewable energy and emissions reduction targets, as well as energy saving targets under the energy services directive. ecr members therefore abstained on this report.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, this morning we heard a very good debate on the citizens’ initiative and tonight we are discussing the very important topic of comitology. i think it is a very good sign that here, after the lisbon treaty has entered into force, we are actually finalising the main pieces of the legislation necessary for its full implementation. the regulation on implementing acts will have a major impact on the way the commission implements european law in the future. it will have a very important influence on the union’s ability to deliver its policies in the interests of its citizens. when we presented our proposal we set out its main objective: that new rules should put in place a system for the adoption of implementing acts by the commission which would be simpler, more efficient, and more transparent and in full compliance with the treaty. how did we achieve these goals in the proposals we are about to discuss? as in the past, the control mechanism foreseen by the regulation is based on comitology, meaning committees composed of representatives from member states to which the commission will submit draft measures but, contrary to the present system, there will no room for intervention by the council as such. as the treaty makes clear, only member states and not the council can control the exercise of the implementing powers by the commission. moreover, the regulation provides that all special procedures will disappear and that all implementing measures including those on trade – various measures such as anti-dumping or countervailing measures – will be subject to the regulation. this will represent a real revolution in the field of commercial policy. we want to have simpler procedures, so not only will the new regulation establish just two procedures – advisory and examination – instead of four, but it will also provide for an automatic adaptation of the existing comitology procedures. the new procedures will begin to apply to all existing legislation from day one. of course this is without prejudice to the nature of the powers conferred on the commission on the basic acts. the commission has committed in a declaration to review all the acquis in order to adapt it as far as legally required to the regime of delegated acts, and i know how important this is for this house. we have so far identified 153 acts which were not submitted to codecision before the lisbon treaty, and which confer powers on the commission that have to be turned into delegated powers. in addition there are 299 acts which were previously aligned to the regulatory procedure with scrutiny, which will now have to be reviewed in the light of the provisions of the treaty on delegated acts. but our aim is that before the end of parliament’s present legislative period all existing legislation will be fully in line with the new provision of the lisbon treaty. this means full alignment. you know how ambitious this goal is and therefore i am particularly pleased that the belgian minister mr chastel kindly asked me to deliver to this house the commitment and the statement of the presidency. it states that the presidency is aware of the ambitious intentions of the commission in this regard; it welcomes these and supports the objectives. it can confirm that it is willing to do its utmost to make sure that this alignment is concluded as soon as possible once proposals by the commission have been submitted. the presidency is ready to cooperate in a loyal manner with parliament and the commission to achieve these objectives. of course we would like to have this statement enshrined in an official written record, but i think that we have to welcome the very cooperative spirit and collegial approach from the belgian presidency. we want to have a system which is more efficient; accordingly the new rules fully reflect the commission’s role under the treaties – with just one regrettable exception which i will come back to later – because only a qualified majority vote by the committee against the draft implementing act can prevent the commission from adopting it. the one exception i just mentioned, where the commission explicitly needs a positive opinion of the committee before being authorised to adopt the draft implementing act, relates to definitive multilateral trade safeguard measures. even though only a limited number of acts are adopted in this area, we were against these exceptions on institutional grounds as we would have preferred a full alignment with the new rules. i wanted to make this institutional point here although in the end this was the only possible basis for the compromise for the legislator and we welcome it. we want to have a system which is more transparent; the whole procedure will be conducted in full transparency. all documents submitted to the committees are simultaneously sent to the european parliament and to the council; these two institutions will have a right of scrutiny on a completely equal footing. at any time during the procedure they may indicate to the commission that they consider that the draft implementing act exceeds its powers; if we are overstepping our powers you have the right to make it very clear to us. to conclude, all in all the text presents a very good result for europe; it clearly strengthens the community method and it clearly expands parliament’s power of scrutiny into all areas. for instance, the new regulation provides that in some cases the commission might be obliged to discuss the matter in an appeal committee. however this committee will be a normal comitology committee chaired by the commission and subject to the same rules; only qualified majority against the commission’s draft can then prevent the commission from adopting it. if the new comitology regulation is approved today by the european parliament it will enter into force very soon, already on 1 march 2011, and this is indeed very good news. we need to have the new legal framework operating as soon as possible, and i also hope that in parallel we could launch a common reflection about the line of demarcation between the delegated powers and the implementing powers of the commission. we need these not only to avoid further conflicts when discussing proposals for the new legislation but also to streamline the alignment exercise. to conclude i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr szájer, for all the work done throughout the negotiating process and also to all political groups for their cooperation and the flexibility they demonstrated. a final word of thanks goes to the belgian presidency who did a remarkable job in getting this file through the council, in finding this very difficult compromise. i believe that what we are about to discuss, and i hope tomorrow approve, is very good news for europe.

in writing. - i have today supported the report on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council establishing a european union action for a european heritage label. i believe that this is an interesting and valuable initiative which will contribute to the promotion of european culture and heritage and to the development of tourism and the regions. it is right that parliament has stressed that the european heritage label will be complementary, not duplicative, of other initiatives in the field of cultural heritage, such as the unesco world heritage list or the council of europe's european cultural routes.
in writing. − as a member of the committee on culture, education and sport, i supported the ep resolution on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council establishing a european union action in favour of the european heritage label. the idea of establishing an eu trade mark is important in terms of bringing the history of the european union, its cultural heritage and the building of european identity and links between countries closer to citizens. by designing sites in each member state to be eligible for the eu's european heritage label, we are building a sense of awareness that the history of europe is relevant to all of us, regardless of where we live, our language, or our culture. the transformation of the european heritage label into a european union initiative will contribute to its credibility, visibility and prestige. this in turn can translate into economic and social benefits, such as an increase in the tourist attractiveness of the awarded sites. the award of this label will also contribute to increasing the interest and knowledge of the younger generation about the ideas and people of europe. and in doing so, bring our continent closer to its citizens.
in writing. −the european heritage label initiative aims to promote the places, figures and activities of people who have contributed to the process of integration in europe. it is intended to bring citizens closer to the fundamental values on which our community is founded, such as democracy, solidarity, cultural diversity and tolerance. the list of sites awarded the european heritage label will constitute a map of the traditions and culture of our continent, a map of places that have played an important role in shaping european identity. europe's common but diverse heritage can strengthen its citizens' sense of identity and deepen european cohesion. this initiative will create a platform for cooperation between the countries and regions of europe. in addition, it can have a positive impact on the tourism sector, contributing to the improvement of the attractiveness of the regions and at the same time their economic situation. i agree that this project should become an official initiative signed by the union, which will increase its visibility, credibility and prestige. the increased visibility of the project will allow more citizens to identify with the symbols that symbolise and commemorate european integration. the project should operate in parallel, on a complementary basis, with the international unesco project or the european capitals of culture the dimension of the european heritage label is educational and symbolic values and to a lesser extent aesthetic or architectural values. we should look for solutions that increase the sense of belonging to europe among its citizens.
in writing. - we all know how important a good education system is for every country, providing young people with the best possible education. good skills, knowledge and education have a direct impact on the culture, the labour market and, as a result, the standard of living of citizens. every country wants to be proud of its youth, and every young person wants to have the opportunity to learn new cultures, languages and gain professional experience abroad. the european union boasts a well-developed system of student exchange as well as open labour markets. this gives every young european a wide range of opportunities for intellectual and professional development. by participating in the 'youth in action' programme, switzerland is demonstrating its commitment to cooperation with the european union, especially in the field of education. we should not deny the young citizens of this country the privileges and opportunities of a community education.
in writing. - switzerland is a country which, despite its excellent education programmes, has to deal with the problem of unequal access to higher education. it is hoped that cooperation with the union will improve the chances of young people in switzerland, especially those from immigrant backgrounds, to have access to education. the experience of member states with youth exchange programmes clearly shows that they not only promote the acquisition of a good education but also play a positive integration role in europe through the knowledge of the languages, cultures and traditions of the respective countries. the lifelong learning programme is also a great opportunity to highlight the role of women in switzerland. as a social group, women were granted the right to vote at the federal level at the latest in europe, because only in the 1970s, for a long time, they had difficulty not only in participating fully in civil society, but also in education and professional self-realization. today, middle-aged women who wish to enter a new professional activity often face the problem of lack of qualifications or experience, as a significant proportion of them - due to the high cost of childcare - have not taken up a job to devote themselves to the family.
in writing. − respect for human rights is one of the union's fundamental values. this issue is receiving particular attention in the s&d group. it's on practically every agenda in the group. it is important that the whole parliament should also pay attention to this. we are seeing some, albeit slow, improvement in the world. we still have countries whose governments persist in human rights violations, and we also have countries where there are changes. the rapporteur's oral amendment reflected these good trends in russia. the situation in cuba is still very much alive, as the 2010 sakharov prize ceremony demonstrated. i voted for this report with conviction.
in writing. − i am extremely concerned about the establishment of a permanent mechanism to safeguard the financial stability of the euro area. this is a vital issue for the euro area countries as well as for the rest of the european union. more than 150 million citizens remain outside the euro area. stabilising the euro will help them to meet their aspirations for membership of the area and may protect the whole system from further disruption. the resolution will not solve the problems by itself, but it can be an important signal to the council and the commission and to the member states. the resolution expresses parliament's strong will to strengthen the union's approach and to strengthen european solidarity. i voted for the resolution with high hopes.
in writing. - i voted against the resolution, although i strongly support protecting animal welfare. it is necessary to comply with the requirements of the directive introducing the necessity to remove conventional cages, but all member states should be given the same time to implement it. the difficulties experienced by many european producers in adapting to the rules due to enter into force on 1 january 2012 will result in a shortage of eggs for human consumption on the market and a significant increase in their prices, a decrease in the competitiveness of this sector vis-à-vis imports from third countries and a likely cessation or serious reduction of production. before the final ban is imposed, an assessment of the state of implementation of the directive should be carried out, which would help to propose transitional solutions in the phasing out of unimproved cages without prejudice to producers who have already complied with the rules.
on behalf of the ecr group. we welcome the fact that malaysia is developing economically and that the living conditions of its people are improving, but we also welcome with disbelief the report by amnesty international describing the widespread use of flogging in malaysia. indeed, it is a severe punishment, often directed at the adult, sometimes for minor and very questionable transgressions. it seems particularly cruel to apply it to illegal immigrants or people in malaysia without valid documents, including political refugees from burma. however, behind the fact of its harsh wording, there is a hidden truth about the traditional terms and the wording of the whipping penalty used in malaysia. many of the offences punishable by flogging are related to the violation of islamic religious law and its customs. take the case of kartiki sari sukarno, who was sentenced to a lashing in 2009 for drinking beer in a bar. we need to respond to this situation.
the use of whips and all forms of corporal punishment and inhuman treatment should be strongly condemned. malaysia cannot invoke its domestic law, which provides for the punishment of flogging for at least 66 offences, to justify its ruthless methods amounting to torture, which are considered illegal by international law and conventions. also alarming are reports from amnesty international that a growing number of refugees and migrants are being flogged in malaysian prisons. the european union, which has more effective methods of protecting human rights since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, should take greater initiative in combating the brutal treatment of people in the world. in addition, respect for human rights should become a key condition for the european union to develop further political cooperation with malaysia.
malaysia is an economic tiger. it's a highly developed country that's a model for the entire southeast asian region. but this tiger has a serious problem. that's the punishment of the whip. of course, one can speak of respecting a certain cultural distinctiveness, of the fact that we europeans should be particularly sensitive when it comes to imposing our models on other continents. but what this issue is really about are human rights that are indivisible, that transcend continental boundaries, race boundaries, religion boundaries. i believe that the european parliament should not only defend, but must defend, the basic human right to human dignity, which is certainly being violated by the whip.
the practice of flogging has been practiced in malaysia since the 19th century, when britain colonized the area. the malaysian government has recently increased the list of crimes punishable by flogging, with 66 different cases of flogging being carried out. prisoners sentenced to be flogged are kept in prisons without any information about the time they will serve their sentence. amnesty international estimates that about 10,000 such sentences are handed down each year, with 60 percent of the cases involving illegal immigrants who do not even understand the sentence because of the language barrier. however, the authorities do not see the need to change the law, since they consider flogging to be an effective means of fighting crime. the european union has been working more closely with malaysia for the last eight years. the budgetary perspective for 2007-13 includes eur 17 million to support the development of the local economy. it is therefore appropriate to call on our partner to ratify the united nations convention against torture, strongly condemning the practice of flogging as incompatible with the position of the un human rights council.
- mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. attempts to discriminate against citizens based on sexual orientation in uganda is a serious matter. uganda has the support of many african countries who do not want the international community and the european union to push for the decriminalization of homosexuality. the misunderstanding is that in our view, as mrs de keyser has said, the prohibition of discrimination in this area is a universal human right. in most african countries, they don't agree with that, which is why dialogue is so difficult. we say we can't keep quiet about such things, and they say we meddle in other people's affairs. the draft laws in uganda are really radical. they introduce the potential death penalty for repeated violations of existing prohibitions or for particularly severe homosexuality, it is not known what that would mean. we do not agree with these proposals and hope that they will not be adopted.
on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. this is an interesting and important discussion. i would like to draw attention to two problems. first, uganda is not really an island of discrimination in this area in an ocean of human rights. three-quarters of african countries have very strict laws on this issue that are discriminatory. this is absolutely not so much a problem for uganda as it is a broader problem for this continent and african culture. secondly, uganda is obviously not the hub of human rights in africa. we know a lot, we have many examples of human rights violations, and this case is part of a larger problem, and of course it needs to be spoken about.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the situation of eritrean refugees in sinai is dramatic. they seek a better life, and often they meet death, torture, and oppression. they're being used and deceived. egyptian authorities have tried to combat human trafficking, but their response has not always been effective. we must help the refugees, the hostages, and all those who need our help. we should support the israeli and egyptian authorities in their fight against human trafficking. it is also worth considering the causes of these dangerous phenomena. i think we need to work to improve the situation in eritrea itself and in other countries in the horn of africa. improving the situation in african countries could reduce migration pressures. and just fighting the pathologies of migration alone is not going to solve the problem. we can only limit the negative phenomena and the exploitation of the refugees' determination. i'm asking for your support on the ppe bill. in this case, we are convinced that our project is better than the joint project.
the situation of eritrean refugees is tragic. but as we reflect on their plight, we should also keep in mind the cause of the situation. well, eritrea is a country that is pervasive in its violation of basic human rights. there's mass persecution on a massive scale of political opponents, christians, but also thousands of random people. and that's the cause of this tragic problem that we're talking about today. therefore, we must do everything to change the policy towards the eritrean authorities, especially when we remember that in 2007 the current leader of that country, responsible for the terrible and massive suffering of the people who are causing them to flee and for the subsequent tragedies, was warmly welcomed by the european commission in brussels. so it's time for a pragmatic and decisive policy against the tyrant.
